UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, March 15, consideration of the motion of Hon. Norman McL. Rogers (Minister of Labour) that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the general interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, and also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, and for the appointment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue the discussion of the motion respecting unemployment and agricultural distress which was introduced by the minister about four weeks ago, I feel that my position is not unlike that of a ghoul about to feed on the fresh corpse of a dead debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Hear, hear -that is a new one.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
In introducing this resolution the minister made a statement in regard to unemployment and agricultural distress. Even though his statement was made a matter of some four weeks ago I imagine that as a result of the nature of it most hon. members not only heard the speech but read it carefully in Hansard, and it will hardly be necessary
2732	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
for me even at this late date to refer to it except in general terms, and to one or two paragraphs of it in particular.
But we noted this aibout the speech, Mr. Speaker, that it was the most apologetic and defeatist speech that we have heard yet in this chamber. Since that speech we have been given the government's legislative program for the remainder of this session. It is notable that in this program there is no provision whatever to deal with unemployment as a permanent problem. It has now become evident that the government has no intention of taking action in connection with this most vital matter, which affects either directly or indirectly every man, woman and child in Canada. Even though the situation is shockingly obvious even to the most casual observer, and is becoming daily more and more acute, all that the government has to offer to him who is unemployed, and to his family, and to the youth who is endeavouring to find his first job, is a resolution which in essence says and says only, " You do not have to worry; the government is aware that you are on relief; it will not let you and your family starve to death. We are not prepared of course to introduce any constructive measures to give you a permanent job or to assist you to find a job, but do not worry, we won't let you starve to death."
Hon. gentlemen opposite are constantly complaining because we who speak on this side of the house, here and occasionally outside of it, refer to the present administration as a "do-nothing government." Perhaps it is not very important what we call the government, but it is the condition of the would-be wage-earner in Canada to-day which proclaims the truth of that phrase, and proclaims it more effectively than anything else that may be said by those who speak in this house. I have unbounded faith in the people of Canada; I have unbounded faith in the individual Canadian, and I feel confident that if the government were to give any indication of a real and sincere effort to meet the unemployment problem at its source by the opening up of new and permanent jobs, by dealing with the cause of unemployment rather than temporizing with its results, any such effort would meet with the spontaneous support of the people of Canada.
Let us listen for a moment to the words which were put into the mouth of his excellency at the opening of the present session by the right hon. gentleman who leads the government. They are to be found on page 4 of Hansard:
(Mr. Massey.]
My ministers recognize that the plight of those who are still unemployed cannot await necessary constitutional amendments, nor the summoning of any conference. They are prepared therefore, notwithstanding constitutional impediments to effective action, to join with the provinces in a further determined effort to meet the immediate situation.
To this end it is proposed further to expand the government's long range program of public undertakings. In pursuance of the policy of the active encouragement of employment, it is also proposed to undertake, with provincial cooperation, to provide assistance to municipalities which, as an alternative to the provision of direct relief, desire to expand their normal programs of civic improvements.
As a means of providing an opportunity for useful work and national service to single unemployed men, the assistance given to forest conservation will be extended to include other work of national importance.
The beneficial results of the youth training program, have demonstrated the wisdom of this experiment, and a measure will be introduced to increase its efficiency and expand its usefulness.
In the light of such a statement as this it was reasonable to assume that the government had some plan to introduce to the house this session, some plan designed to deal with unemployment at its source. But instead of that, what do we find? The legislative program for the remainder of this session is blank, bleached and barren of any constructive measure to deal with this problem in any permanent way. The very resolution which the minister introduced the other day was the same old relief resolution, hidebound and hamstrung by the red tape which has been manufactured by the joint efforts of the federal administration and the various provincial legislatures. Over a million people on relief in Canada, countless thousands of men looking for work but not yet on relief, with the conditions for them growing more desperate every day, and still further countless thousands facing the hazards of part time employment at-oftentimes-shockingly low rates of pay. The whole situation as reflected -in any release of the Department of Labour shows that this problem is getting worse every day. It seems to me that the attitude of the government in the present economic crisis in this country is not unlike that of the mule in the thunderstorm, when it stands stockstill and merely closes its eyes.
The minister's speech of a month ago, if analysed carefully, is, as I said in my reply to it at the time, a frank admission that the measures which have been taken so far have simply served to nibble at the problem. It is now apparent that the minister's admission of failure is recognized by the government itself, as is dramatically shown by the absence of any legislative program to deal with the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
situation. The minister essentially admitted this in his own speech. If we turn to Hansard
of March 15, on page 1920 we read this:
Like my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) I have had in these last few years some experience with the administration of social services on a basis of dual responsibility. I shall not conceal from the house that when I studied this question in the abstract, before I entered parliament, I was impressed with the possibilities of cooperation in this field of dual responsibility. I have not entirely rejected the possibility of cooperation, but I have found by experience that this indefinite area which applies particularly to social services in this country is not only susceptible of cooperation but is perhaps even more susceptible of conflict and friction. Therefore when it has been urged upon me from time to time as Minister of Labour that in the absence of any constitutional changes, before serious consideration of any constitutional changes and without such information as may proceed from the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, we should take over the entire burden of relief, I have said that we should not assume financial responsibility without securing administrative control. I submit that this is the only position with regard to this matter that can be taken by those whose attitude toward it must be based upon a sense of official responsibility.
An utterance, Mr. Speaker, which of itself sounds emptiness, hopelessness, and defeat. All that the minister said to the distressed of this country was, as I have already stated, "If we cannot arrange properly this question of dual responsibility we will continue to feed you and you will not starve to death." Then he went on to tell the million on relief in Canada, and the scores of thousands who are compelled to eke out an existence as a result of lack of work or of part time employment, that we should be grateful that we are better off here than they are in other countries. He said, at page 1929:
Why cannot we take encouragement from the fact that the situation in this country is relatively better than it is in others?
And further, on page 1913:
So far as relief and unemployment are concerned my position from the beginning has been that it was the part of wisdom to search out and present the truth, however unpleasant it might be.
Not for a moment am I saying that we should not be grateful that we in Canada do not have to face hazards in the same degree as that in which they have to be faced by people in other countries.
At a time like this it is strange that the Minister of Labour should attempt to take shelter in a position of assumed gratitude that things are no worse than they are. As we survey the legislative activity or lack of activity of this government in the last three and a half years, perhaps we should all be grateful that things are not worse than they are.
The minister said further:
So far as relief and unemployment are concerned my position from the beginning has been that it was the part of wisdom to search out and present the truth, however unpleasant that it might be.
I am not going to say for a moment that the minister did not make an honest statement, but I will say that in his statement, instead of facing the cold facts, he resorted to academic definition. For it was apparent that his chief concern was to make his figures appear in as favourable a light as possible. He took umbrage, or should I say he became righteously indignant, at figures which have appeared in the press from time to time, figures from the Canadian youth congress and from other sources which were not his own. These figures did not happen to coincide with his own academic definition, and therefore, as I say, he took umbrage at them.
I have in my hand the report of the unemployment survey conducted by the Ottawa youth federation, dated November 21 to 26, 1938. I presume the minister has seen this report. It was sent to me as well as to other members of the house, and I have perused it carefully. I congratulate those responsible for it. In this report there is a record of what was done under the survey. Two thousand homes within the city limits of Ottawa were visited, that is, one home in every ten. Let it be remembered that essentially Ottawa is not an industrial city; and yet in this city of Ottawa, in these 2,000 homes visited, there were found 562 unemployed young people between the ages of 16 and 30. It does not take an Einstein or anyone skilled in figures to multiply this figure across the dominion and to realize that such figures as have been presented by the Canadian youth congress and others are, after all, not so very wide of the mark.
The most glaring example of the minister's effort to present figures in a favourable light was in regard to those on relief. With all due deference to his desire to "search out and present the truth", I could not help being amazed at the way in which he presented his figures with respect to those on relief.
At the time of his speech a month ago the latest figure available showed 978,000 on relief. In presenting this figure the minister said, with no small degree of pride, that those who were on rural relief were less in number substantially than those who were on rural relief a year ago. He admitted, quite frankly and properly, that the number of those on urban relief was slightly in excess of the number last year. Since that speech there has been given out by his own department, under date April 8, a press release dealing with
'4	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
the unemployment relief figures. In February of this year, there were 1,012,000, an increase of nearly 4 per cent over January, according to the figures revised to date, but slightly more than 3 per cent less than in February, 1938. The dominion total of unemployed but fully employable persons on relief in February this year was 190,000. The figure for February of this year represented an increase of 8-6 per cent over February a year ago. A total of 694,000 persons were receiving non-agricultural aid, which shows a net increase of about 6 per cent over the February figure of 1938. There were 318,000 persons reported as receiving agricultural aid or subsistence in February, which is 18 per cent less than in February, 1938.
It was in that figure that the minister found his chiefest joy when he reported that those on rural relief were less in February. That is according to academic definition. In making that statement, in his desire to search out and to present the truth, the minister ignored completely the heaviest bill for rural relief which this dominion has ever paid. I wonder if the minister would regard pegging the price of wheat to the tune of $60,000,000 as a relief measure. It does not come under his department, but under the department of a fellow minister. But according to his definition, inasmuch as it is not under his department, it is not included in his figure. Would the minister regard $22,000,000 for feed and seed voted at the last session as a relief measure?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It was for drought.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Yes, but it is still relief.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What is the sense of putting that in with unemployment?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: We are discussing unemployment and agricultural distress. If the hon. member would pay attention he would be more intelligent in his interruptions. I have mentioned $60,000,000 for pegging the price of wheat, and $22,000,000 for feed and seed, and I ask, is that relief or is it not? Of course, it is relief of a sort, relief to prevent relief.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Is the hon. member asking me a question?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I would answer in these terms, that the pegging of the price of wheat at the price fixed might be regarded as a measure of relief, but the relief was not confined to those in western Canada. It established or maintained a market in western Canada which undoubtedly had beneficial effects throughout the entire country.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am not complaining about it, I may say to those who are applauding to my left. I am not complaining in any manner whatever, nor did I complain when the measure was introduced, nor shall I complain. But I do say that it is a measure of relief and therefore the minister cannot boast of a decrease of 18 per cent of those on relief. If we had spent $82,000,000 and had not obtained a decrease it would have been a peculiar state of affairs.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Include all subventions and subsidies, then.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am citing only one by way of illustration. My hon. friend has made my point very much stronger, because the figures the minister presented of those receiving relief did not embrace all who were given assistance.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: All the manufacturers receive relief when we give them protection.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: And the hon. member is one who would take it off.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

this house, because that other hon. gentleman used an illustration in the course of an argument which did present facts, facts which were not very pleasant. Again the minister took umbrage and said in regard to this gentleman, "At all events it has been stated by one who ought to know better, regardless of where he now is." I cannot help Ibut feel, as I review some of the statements made iby the minister during the course of his speech, such as that " no one can seriously urge that this government has not met the challenge of unemployment," and further that " this government has done as much as any government could do in order to stimulate the building industry of this country," they are made by one who as a result of his position " ought to know better."
Prior to the minister's speech I had prepared an extensive summary of the unemployment situation in this dominion, and was prepared to present it to the house under four headings, namely: the size of the problem; the nature of the problem; a review of such efforts as the government has made to meet the problem; and what can and should be done to meet the problem.

I shall come to it. I am not sure what useful purpose can be served by any of us making suggestions to the government when its policy has been disclosed as a " do-nothing " policy, except to pay out money and more money for temporary work, public works, and supply moneys to buy food barely sufficient to keep those on relief from starving to death. That is the policy of this government. I am, however, prepared to take the time of the house to-day in an attempt to present a true picture, to search out the truth and present the truth of the present situation in Canada in relation to this great problem of unemployment. Being a confirmed optimist, I plan to present to the government, before I sit down, several constructive suggestions in connection with the problem of unemployment, suggestions which are designed to provide permanent employment in Canada and to develop the resources of this dominion in the fullest possible way.
Before entering upon this discussion, however, may I refer hon. members to my own remarks in reply to the minister, as reported on page 1937 of Hansard of March 15:
I shall not, however, attempt to discuss the problem of agricultural distress, though I plan to speak upon this great question at a later date. I realize fully that this problem is irre-ducibly linked up to its twin problem of unemployment, and that a healthy condition of agriculture is tantamount to a prosperous Canada.
Does the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) hear that? I repeat it:
I realize that this problem is irreducibly linked to its twin problem of unemployment, and that a healthy condition of agriculture is tantamount to a prosperous Canada. Sufficient to say now that the government has treated the agricultural situation for the last three and a hall years as a succession of emergencies. By reason of this policy the problem of agricultural distress has in fact become a succession of emergencies. Surely the facing of these successive crises as isolated individual phenomena does not constitute an agricultural policy.

Everyone in Canada-no matter what his position, no matter how anxious he may be to minimize the facts, no matter what his desire to point out, in the words of the minister, that the situation of this country is relatively better than that of other countries, and that there are those in other countries who look upon the position here with envy and respect -is forced to admit that we are facing the most acute economic crisis in the history of our dominion, and that to-day democracy is threatened internally in Canada as never before.	.
I do not criticize the minister for not presenting exact figures; for, as I said, such figures are not available. But I do take issue with him sharply when by resort to academic definition he attempts to minimize the situation and fails to face the facts.

It becomes readily apparent, then, as one looks at this chart that the size of the problem of employment and unemployment has increased rather than diminished during the term of office of hon. gentlemen opposite; for the slight increase in the number of those employed is in no way commensurate with the increase in our population; and even in these figures which I have placed upon Hansard there is no recognition of the scores of thousands-I believe there to be hundreds of thousands, from my own contact with the situation-of young Canadians who have yet to find their first jobs.
The very nature of the problem with which this government is supposed to be dealing apparently has been ignored. I have in my hand one of the most excellent publications it has been my privilege to read in connection with unemployment. It is issued by our own bureau of statistics and is entitled "Census monograph No. 11: Unemployment." I regard it as a most important publication; for within its nearly four hundred pages is given in understandable detail the whole theory of unemployment and its possible cure. I should like to read many extracts from this publication, but without taking time to do so I would refer hon. members to page 23, where it says in part:
It has been shown that nearly a third of the wage earners received less than $450 in the year preceding the census, their average being $220, i.e., at best they had only part time work and not enough to live on. The conclusion seems to be that there is a tendency for these to increase in proportion to the others with the passage of time. It goes without saying, then, that the proper picture of the employment situation is not given when viewed from the standpoint of industry. From the latter standpoint it is expansion and contraction that are emphasized. It is taken for granted that increase in employment means decrease in unemployment. From the standpoint of the census of workers this does not follow. Decrease in employment may merely mean that a considerable proportion of the workers are little worse off than before, while the remainder are very much worse off.
Then I find these words on page 34:
The usual view of unemployment assumes that the person who is unemployed to-day may be employed to-morrow, and that in general if A is employed to-day and B is not employed, the situation' will be reversed another day. The present findings are that this is not so-
I commend to hon. members the conclusions stated at the bottom of that page:
(1)	that a concentration of the workers in such a way that in a large country like Canada they are found in spots, not evenly distributed, increases the distance between the producer and consumer and thereby decreases consumption;
(2)	that any activity which tends to create workers for temporary work is injurious. But another principle must be recognized first, viz..
that the Euclidian axiom "The whole is greater than its parts" is not true when applied to humanity. Rather humanity must be looked upon as an aggregate of individuals to each of whom his daily bread is more important than what happens to the whole; moreover, the satisfaction of this need of the individual will determine what will happen to the race.
Then on pages 29 and 30 there is a short discussion of the effect of immigration on unemployment, which I further commend to the attention of hon. members. There are many pages in this book which I should like to quote fully, but time does not permit.

speechtext:
I will read it to my hon. friend:
The immigration occurred during low unemployment but kept up until unemployment rose almost to the peak. Emigration then started and it was accompanied (or followed) by decreasing unemployment. This, of course, introduces a widely different concept of unemployment from that generally accepted, viz., that unemployment is merely the opposite of employment.
Unemployment only partly declined with increasing employment. As noticed, it also increased with increasing numbers of wage-earners and decreased with decreasing numbers of wage-earners. Immigration was no doubt accompanied by other inward movements into the ranks of the wage-earners-from farms, small owned establishments and from school; emigration was accompanied by return to these sources, so that immigration and emigration were only symptoms of more general movements. The conclusion is that unemployment (in so far as the population is concerned) can be caused by two things (1) decline of shrinkage in business and (2) increase in the number of wage-earners; it can be cured by (1) increase in business activities but only if accompanied by (2) exodus from the ranks of the wage-earners. The lowest point of unemployment would logically be not at the point of greatest business activity but at a point w-here activity becomes normal after a period of exodus and before a period of in-rush.

It will be noted that in 1925 the population of Canada in the age group of sixteen to sixty-four years was 5,363,000; by 1938 this figure had increased to 7,135,000, a net increase of 1,772,000. Of course, it is obvious that all those between the ages of sixteen and sixty-four years, both male and female, are not going to look for work, either on the farm or in our manufacturing or primary or secondary industries, but it does follow that if we increase our population in that age group by just under 2,000,000 in thirteen years, there must be an increase in the number of available jobs unless unemployment is to increase shockingly.
This brings us to the point raised by the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding) a few moments ago, the shifting of vocational pursuits. As a result of technocracy and other such matters, new vocations must constantly be found for those whose jobs have been replaced, either by machines or by shifting

economies. For example, as more hydro electric power is consumed, as more oil is consumed, the less coal will be required. Therefore, there at once comes a slack in the coal industry of Canada, and unless that slack is taken up by some outside means, there is at once permanent unemployment in our coal fields. There has been a shift in our economy-not as a result of inefficiency, not as a result of exploitation, not as a result of any one thing; but that there has been such a shift in our economy is beyond question.
Next, there is the problem of the stop-gap job, a problem which is seldom mentioned in this house but one which is of immense importance. I fancy that the minister has found in connection with his work, as I have found in my own small way, that there is an ever-increasing number of young men and young women who are taking any job they can get in order to tide themselves over " until the day breaks and the shadows flee

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
away." There are hundreds upon hundreds, yes, thousands upon thousands of young people in Canada to-day who have been trained well and efficiently, either in our secondary schools, in our technical schools or in our universities, who are doing anything at all in order to keep some small amount coming into the home. All through this dominion we have those who have been trained as skilled artisans, as machinists, who are doing odd jobs for a few dollars a week. There are those who have been trained as engineers, there are those who have been trained in other professions and who are doing any kind of work they can get in order to earn a living. There is a great readjustment necessary throughout this whole country in order to bring into line those who are out of line with their training.
Fourth, there is the question of the reestablishment and readjustment of Canadian youth. I do not think I can touch upon any single subject in this chamber that should have a greater humanitarian appeal or a greater national appeal to all hon. members, regardless of where in the chamber they sit, than the appeal of youth, the very lifeblood of Canada. After all, if we dissipate our youth we are paving the way to the complete ruination of this country; we are undermining its very foundation. I have full sympathy for the one who is older, the head of a family, the man of fifty or sixty who is unemployed; I have full sympathy with him, and let that not be misunderstood. However, such a man has passed the prime of life, but here we have the youth coming on to fill the job which the older man had. As a result of conditions beyond his control, as a result of his unfortunate inability to procure the necessary training, he has been required to drift about this country from one place to another, bringing on the gradual degradation of the individual himself.
The transient unemployed, of which the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) was speaking this afternoon, presents one of the most serious problems in this dominion. Perhaps there are those who regard these splendid fellows-I speak of them as such because I know many of them-as being ready to propagate sedition throughout Canada, as having lost touch with the spirit of democracy, as being essentially rowdies or persons who are prepared to take the bounty of relief and do nothing about it. I disagree with that. I know many of these men personally and I am ready to place them among our finest Canadians.
Next there is the great question of seasonal occupations. After all, if we revert to academic definitions, when we see that a man
is employed we write him down as one who has a job, even though that job may be for only eight months in the year. His earnings during that period must carry him over the other four months of the year. What about unemployment insurance? I shall return to that shortly.
Then there is the most pathetic of all the problems with which we have to deal, the problem of the unemployable unemployed. This is the man who would probably still have a job had it not been for the conditions that faced this world of ours in 1929 and 1930, had it not been for circumstances over which, God knows, he had absolutely no control. To-day he finds the "not wanted" sign hanging out for a man of his years. As a result perhaps of a physical disability incurred during the period of deprivation, such a man is no longer physically capable of doing the work which he used to do; or perhaps he is a man, advanced in years, and although he be physically fit and able-bodied, ready to go to work, he is told he is not wanted because he is too old.
I cannot possibly overestimate, Mr. Speaker, the gravity of the situation from the humanitarian and moral point of view, nor can the incipient danger to democracy as a result of ineffective or inactive government be overestimated. I wonder how much longer red-blooded Canadians, to use a phrase not unknown to my honoured leader, will be satisfied to eke out an existence on part-time wages or upon relief. How much longer will Canadian youth, noted for its virility and vigour, be satisfied to find that one hopeless day is destined to follow another hopeless day? Patience, Mr. Speaker, ceases to be a virtue after a while. Patience is a virtue only up to a certain point, and hon. gentlemen opposite must bear in mind that intolerable conditions will be endured for just so long. When government inaction or ineffective action becomes unpalatable, action is sought by other means. That has proven itself through history to be axiomatic. If we would retain our present form of government in Canada, if we would retain the democracy which is ours, the government of Canada is called upon to take swift and courageous action, action to meet the problem of unemployment by the creation of permanent jobs, to eliminate the hazards resulting from part-time employment, and to develop opportunities for the ever-increasing number of our unemployed young wage earners who have yet to find their first job.

In the opinion of the Canadian Federation of Labour, unemployment is the Achilles heel of democracy. The creation of casual employment through public works is only a palliative -by no means a cure. It must be borne in mind that whereas public works have their place and are desirable up to a point, they do not create permanent employment, and if we put every man to work to-morrow on some public works project, the minister himself would foe the first to admit that we are still a long way from meeting the problem of unemployment. The fact of the matter is that due to increases in our population as a result of immigration and patural causes, due to a changed economy both within and without our nation, it becomes perforce necessary for the federal administration to apply a principle which has been used in -business successfully ever since business became successful.
I have always understood that when a business man finds a surfeit in the markets for his product he is alert and astute to find new uses for it, new variations, new adaptations, and so he either discovers or creates new markets. The only possible method by which we can hope to cope with the problem of

unemployment is by the simple method employed by the business man, of finding further outlets for the activities of those who would be employed. Increases in our export trade alone, when domestically we consume eighty per cent of our own production, are not enough to absorb our employable unemployed and those who come on the labour market every year. The primary activity of this government then should be the development of our domestic market, the expansion of our internal industries both primary and secondary. Here is a practical function of government the neglect of which constitutes the most hideous betrayal of the electorate of Canada.
The unemployed of this country are not interested in theories of government; they are not interested in political theories or in the political patronage which this or any other government chances to operate under and dispenses. They are interested solely in getting jobs-a fair day's pay earned by a fair day's work.
Let us turn to see what the government has done in discharge of its obligation toward the development of Canada for Canadians. From the figures I have already brought to the attention of this house it is obvious that the problem of unemployment is still with us, and in spite of what the government may claim to have done, this problem has really changed only to the extent that so pathetically many of our unemployed have become unemployable. In 1935 when this government came into power it did so with the understanding of the Canadian people that it would improve the lot of the man on the street. But I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite, in the face of the facts, in the face of results achieved after three and a half years, to meet the man on the street who is still unemployed or who is looking for his first job and convince him that the present administration has a clear conception of the problem at hand and is dealing with it in a productive and a constructive manner. Speeches alone are not enough. Academic theories and theoretical discussions are not enough. It is not sufficient for the government merely to say that it is deeply concerned with this whole matter. The man who is out of work, the youth who cannot find a job, is concerned with one thing and with one thing only, and that is results- what this government can do and should do and is prepared to do to improve his lot and to build for the security of his home, if he is fortunate enough still to have one. Men will be patient if they recognize that the government is trying. Men will be patient if they realize that everything is being done
which can be done. But men will be impatient when they realize that apparently, from the point of view of results, the federal administration is blind and deaf to the situation.

When we ask ourselves how we should approach the economic problem it seems to me it is evident that short range and long range measures will have to be applied. It is our view that if we are to secure a proper revival of industry in Canada it must be upon the basis of trade policies which will permit a more satisfactory exchange between this and other countries.
There, epitomized in the minister's own words, is the policy of the Liberal party, the pet theory of the Prime Minister, which he rushed to put into practice almost the day he came into office in 1935; and now again we have had brought into the house, to the accompaniment of fanfares and what could hardly be called refreshing modesty on the part of the Prime Minister, a new trade treaty. It is therefore abundantly evident that the intention of this government to assist in the revival of industry in Canada has been the development of an external rather than an internal policy, and that the position we are in at the moment may be regarded as the direct result of the application of this policy.
It is crystal clear that it has been the cherished hope of the Prime Minister and his government, that an increasing and heightening world condition would have the effect of so improving internal conditions in Canada that it would be necessary to do little or nothing internally, and that good times throughout the world would, to use the old hockey expression, skate us on-side. Let me say at once that even though on this side of the house we have been accused in the past of endeavouring to bring about a degree of economic nationalism in Canada at the sacrifice of foreign trade, this accusation is, of course, without foundation. The policy of my party has always been and always will be, I trust, to regard the development of our domestic market as of primary importance and the development of the export market as secondary. We are in no wise averse to trade treaties. We favour them of course, but we are Canadian enough, and. Mr. Speaker, note it, we are patriotic enough in our point of view to feel that in making a trade treaty we should place Canada first and give first consideration to the development of jobs for Canadian workmen and to improve the lot of the Canadian farmer. If any prime minister of this country does not take this attitude, then I feel that he is derelict in his duty and untrue to the people who put him in office.
Not so many weeks ago we in this house listened to the Prime Minister as he virtually lectured those of us who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, on the glories of patriotism and willingness to contribute to peace on earth and goodwill between nations. After the Prime Minister made that speech, the situation in Europe, I noticed, grew steadily worse. That is coincidental. We on this side of the house will take second place to none in our love of the mother country, of the empire, and of peace throughout the world, nor will we take second place to any man in our regard for patriotism in its purest and best form when it is not cloaked in a disguise, a pseudo-patriotism cloaking that which is virtually some pet political theory. Personally I feel that a policy which places Canada in a state of dependence upon the other countries of the world is fraught with the gravest dangers. WThereas export trade is of great value to Canada. I submit that we should never fail to realize that it is secondary, coming next to the domestic market.
If employment in Canada is to be dependent primarily upon the sale of our goods in world markets, then we are placed in a most precarious and hazardous position. For three years we have operated under the last trade treaty with the United States, and the net result of those three years, from 1935 to 1938, has been a reduction of 19,000 in unemployment, or four per cent. There was an increase of imports in what hon. gentlemen opposite choose to call the good year of 1937 over the year 1936, of 27-4 per cent, while exports increased only 8-4 per cent, less than one-third of the imports. I readily recognize that this plan has met with some success, and I gladly give the government credit for that success. Apparently, with all due deference to the enthusiasm of some hon. gentlemen opposite, including the minister himself, the government's efforts to reestablish the construction industry so far have not been dramatically successful.
There is another project, however, which was designed primarily to promote employment in the construction industry as well as to aid municipalities in the development of self-liquidating projects. Early in March, 1936, I made my maiden speech in parliament on a resolution which I introduced asking that consideration be given to the setting up of a national youth reestablishment commission. To my unbounded
delight that resolution passed this house unanimously. I listened to the minister as he spoke in reply to my speech, and took courage, as did the youth of Canada, when he said as reported on page 919 of Hansard of 1936:
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would repeat that the government is fully in sympathy with the reestablishment of the youth of this country and, like any government conscious of its responsibility in relation to unemployment at this time, we will take every possible step to see to it that young men and women are given opportunities within which they may realize their desire for remunerative employment. I do not believe the youth of this dominion expect ready-made jobs, nor do I believe that the solution for unemployed youth lies in public employment. If I did believe that I should have some misgivings for the future of Canada. It is our duty to create conditions within which our Canadian youth may once more, as in other years, find their own opportunities and make the most of them.
The 1936 session of parliament passed into history. There was no legislative action to further the interests of youth, and these high-sounding and encouraging phrases of the minister were "full of sound and fury, signifying nothing."
Shortly after the opening of the second session, the minister stated on February 24, 1937, as reported at page 1208 of Hansard:
In considering our obligations, particularly at this time, I do not believe we can ignore the primary obligation we have towards those younger people who are now unemployed. As members of the house will be aware, the speech from the throne contained an explicit reference to measures which would be undertaken for the reestablishment of unemployed young people. I feel quite certain that at this time members of this house and the country generally would feel that this type of assistance should have priority over any far-reaching change in the existing establishment of studentships and fellowships by the national research council.
I claim that such statements as those I have just read, with all due deference to the minister who made them, are nothing more than vapourings and pious platitudes, high-sounding sentiments which subsequent experience has taught us have little or no practical value.
Nothing having been done for a full year and a half to indicate that the government was sensible in any way, great or small, to the plight of our youth, we were asked late in the session of 1937 to vote one-fifth of one per cent of our governmental income to be devoted to the reestablishment of youth. about SI,750,000 in three and a half years for youth reestablishment. What great speeches! What little action!

A permanent officer has been attached to the Department of Labour, Mr. R. F. As we look back upon the decades of this century in Canada's story, in the light of our experience of these immediate years, we can see the situation in a three-pronged challenge to our progress.
1.	The problem of assuring gainful occupation on a self-supporting basis for a large supply of necessarily mobile and necessarily young labour;
2.	The problem of assuring reasonable social care for these men whose very modes of life have defeated marriage and the establishment of homes; and
3.	The problem of tying down both employment and social care facilities on a basis of residence.
And, later on page 17:
Surely we cannot continue longer to suffer, in indifference, this shifting movement, back and forth across the land, and this concentration, in the centres of congestion, of hundreds of men, many of them young, who now pass the greater time of each year eating the bread of idleness and bitterness, and with no more hope than "two meals and a bed" and "move on" to-day, to-morrow, and for the duration of life in Canada. That way lies resentment, and fierce revolt: for many, apathy and despair: for others, something close to mere rotting, and for all, and for Canada the loss of vigour and of manhood, much of it in the prime of life.
No one can deny that the situation is as here described. Any hon. member of this house who has read this pamphlet issued by the Canadian welfare council knows that it is true, knows that the work was carefully

carried out by those who had no political axe to grind. But what recognition has the situation received? The minister will no doubt refer to the work done on the rights of way of the two railways, which was merely temporary work affording casual employment. It was only a palliative measure. He will also refer, no doubt, to the farm placement scheme, which has been successful as far as it has gone, but which has proven to provide only 33^ per cent permanent work. I have given credit to the government for their efforts as far as they have gone, but surely hon. members must realize that such schemes as have been put forward are only stop-gap proposals, holding out no hope of a remedy. The situation in Vancouver last May and the situation existing in Toronto at the present time indicate that no permanent plan has been evolved. Single transients to the number of thousands upon thousands beg here and there in an effort to keep body and soul together, and thousands have died as a result of exposure, illness, actual starvation or lack of care.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
The national employment commission is terminated now, ended abruptly, and its main recommendations have been treated as I have said. Why they have been so treated is for the government to answer. Many had based high hopes on the report of the national employment commission. It was the keystone in the arch built by the Prime Minister in his election campaign of 1935. It is gone now; its great efforts have been put to use by the government to alleviate rather than liquidate unemployment, while the Prime Minister and his government remain to pay lip service to the worthy work done by Mr. Purvis and those associated with him.
Let me refer again to a speech of the Minister of Labour on January 23, 1939, as reported at page 220 of- Hansard:
In the first opportunity I had to speak in this house I stated my own firm conviction that regardless of what might have to be done in the way of expanding public employment it was the first duty of government in a democratic state to take measures to expand private employment. And we have done just that.
How can the minister possibly claim that private employment has been expanded as a result of any action taken by this government, in the light of the figures I have presented this afternoon? In 1938 employment was retarded, not accelerated. The figures are upon Hansard; I placed them there this afternoon, and they cannot be denied. I agree with the statement of the minister that the first duty of government in a democratic state is to take measures to assist in the expansion of private employment. In the light of such facts as I have presented, however, it is amazing to hear a minister of the crown lay claim to achievements in this regard when such claims are without foundation or categorical proof. Again on January 23, at page 225 of Hansard, the minister stated:
Apart entirely from what has been indicated here, I should like once more to stress the importance of this government or any government receiving the broadest kind of cooperation from employers generally throughout this country in doing what they reasonably can do, even at some risk, to increase their working staffs during this coming year. I have been told sometimes of employers who have done this and who have received a large measure of satisfaction from knowing that in this way they were making their own contribution to the problem. Because-let us make no mistake about it-if private employment is not able to take up the slack; if private industry acting with governments, and having a knowledge that governments are doing their part, does not itself do its part toward that objective, there will be thrown ultimately upon democratic government such a pressure of opinion in favour of public employment that government itself will be asked to undertake burdens which it is not equipped to bear.
I think we should remember that. During the course of the same speech the minister said:
I should like to assure this house that this government from the beginning, although at times its progress may have seemed slow and at times perhaps it may have been open to the charge that we were taking too much care before we proceeded in a given direction, at all events lias proceeded resolutely upon lines which we felt would lead us ultimately towards a sound solution. There is no defeatism here; there is no discouragement; and although there are times, I confess, when one encounters reverses, let us remember that this battle of unemployment is not fought on one front alone; it is fought on a long battlefront, and sometimes we may have to retreat on one sector, sometimes we may have to consolidate our position along the whole line; there is not always an advance. But I believe that, given the kind of cooperation, the kind of enterprise and initiative that exists in this country, at least potentially, it is not beyond the powers of government, and citizenship, to make steady progress towards the solution of this problem of unemployment.
I wonder if in those statements the minister is insinuating that industry is not cooperating with the government, and is still unwilling to cooperate. When the minister complains about the lack of cooperation he is forgetting his ability to get it if he so desires; for he has stated that the government has power to get cooperation if it wishes it. Let me refer your honour to the minister's own words spoken on April 20, 1936, as reported at page 1983 of Hansard:
The power is here if we desire to use it, to enter into agreements with industrial corporations for the purpose of expanding employment.
If there is lack of cooperation, why has not use been made of the ability to gain that cooperation? I think I can answer the question-because the internal structure of Canada has been so neglected by this government, and because industry can have no confidence in a government which is constantly tinkering with tariffs.

If we face the facts of the record of this government, face them fearlessly, and judge the government on the -basis of those facts, we are forced to the conclusion that hon. gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches either do not comprehend the gravity of the unemployment situation, or do not know how to combat it, or both. The phrase " do-nothing government " may not be palatable to hon. gentlemen opposite, but in the light of results obtained so far, as I have endeavoured this afternoon and evening to outline them to this house, the phrase seems to be an extraordinarily accurate description of the present administration.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us leave controversy. Let us turn our attention to what the government can do, or if you will, might have done. I should like to present to the house several suggestions in connection with this problem. I have regard for the suggestion which has been made from time to time Iby hon. gentlemen opposite that we who criticize the administration do not always offer anything in return. I should like to say, however, that in offering these suggestions to the government I realize full well it is probably taking the time of the house uselessly, on account of the fact that the present government has already announced its program for the balance of this session, and in that program, as I have already drawn to the attention of hon. members, there is no constructive measure relative to decreasing unemployment, other than through such measures as we have already noted as palliative measures.
However, as I have said, I am a confirmed optimist; I am prepared to take at this point more time of the house to offer these suggestions to the minister, and I do so in all sincerity. I am not in a position to make a declaration of policy for my party, but I am going to point out a few ideas which I do not claim by any means as altogether my own, but which I present personally. There are ways and means for productive governmental effort towards the solution of this problem, and the ways I shall mention are perhaps the most obvious ones. They will not be presented with any degree of completeness, and I put them forward only to indicate a few of the methods which could ibe applied by the minister and those who sit about him.
The first constructive suggestion I throw out for the consideration of the government is the development and opening up of the northwest territories and the northernmost parts of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba and also northwestern Ontario and northeastern Quebec. Northwestern Ontario and northeastern Quebec are likely to

be just as rich in mineral deposits as areas already under development, but they are at present completely inaccessible except by aeroplane. We who live in Quebec and Ontario realize what a vitally important part the mining industries of our provinces have played in our provincial development, and it is not without significance that mineral production in Canada has increased 58 per cent since 1929 and 76 per cent since 19,33. Here is an example of a new and permanent type of undertaking, productive of new and permanent jobs, of which I have been speaking. Engineering surveys of the northwest territories, the northern parts of the prairie provinces, the northwest corner of Ontario and the northeast comer of Quebec reveal an essentially untouched wealth which is virtually staggering -wealth which cannot be reached unless governments make ingress and egress possible. I think it is no exaggeration to state that there is work for hundreds of thousands of present and possibly new Canadians in this one undeveloped part of Canada, but the work cannot go forward unless the government is prepared to do its part. I commend to the attention of hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches the development by the Swedes of their iron mines within the arctic circle and Lapland as an illustration of how successfully a government and private capital may work together for the opening up of a new empire within the state.
Second, I suggest an extensive and intensive nation-wide program of afforestation and reforestation. We all realize how vitally important in our national scheme of economy are our forests, but we have been profligate in the treatment of our forests and have virtually decimated this priceless asset. The other day I took the trouble to make a rough calculation as to the possible practical limit of life of our commercial forests, and I came to the sickening conclusion that it could not be more than thirty years. Hardly daring to believe my own figures I consulted one whom I regard as an authority, and he told me that according to his calculation I was fifty per cent out, for he would make it about twenty years. Again let me point hon. members to Sweden. There, cutting in earnest started about 1850, or ninety years ago, and yet today Sweden has available forty per cent more timber and pulpwood than she had in 1850! It has -been demonstrated that our young men are willing and anxious to go into our forests and, with proper training made available, to become foresters. Here again are tens of thousands of jobs that could be made

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
available in a most constructive project, constructive not only in rehabilitating a vast number of our youth but in reestablishing a priceless national asset as well.
Third, I suggest an extended program of water conservation and flood control. My good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who has made a detailed study of this most important question, has pointed out in this house and outside of it on more than one occasion not only the necessity of such a program but its desirability from the point of view of creating work for thousands of our Canadian people. I shall not attempt to add to what he has already so ably said.
Fourth, I suggest a nation-wide intensive and immediate program to make Canada more attractive and accessible to the tourist. We cannot read the statistics of the trade of Canada without realizing what an invaluable asset to us are the natural beauties of our country, which attract tourists so that now millions of motor-cars with their cargo of tourists enter Canada every year from the United States and other thousands of Americans come by train and boat for our summer and winter sports. It seems to me that this trade is more important to us than ever this year because of the uncertainty of the European situation, the result being that a great many people who normally go to Europe for their holidays will not be going there this summer, and they might be attracted to Canada.
An important part of the maintenance and development of our tourist paradise is the construction and extension of national highways that will permit ready access for the tourists to those beauty spots in Canada which are a source of inchoate wonder for the visitor and native alike.
Hon. members may remind me that the construction of highways is public works. True. And that it is casual expenditure. True again, up to a point. But here are public works that would provide prolonged casual employment, and return of themselves manifold benefits to the dominion.
Another class of work which should be done to attract the tourist trade is in connection with the preservation of our game and game fisheries. Our game waters are rapidly being fished out; our game areas are rapidly being shot out; and provincially we are doing very little to restock either of them. Here is a long range program of work which would demand the employment of a countless number of our presently idle Canadians.
Fifth, I suggest a cooperative nation-wide housing plan sponsored by the federal and provincial governments in conjunction with
the municipalities. It is obvious that there is no greater need for the stabilization of our national life than the need of homes. Bad housing and slum conditions do more to promote ill health and crime than any other single factor within the national fabric. Couple with such conditions unemployment, which means idleness, and the results are what we are experiencing in Canada to-day. Recently we have been informed that the public works program for the year will include the building of parks and other similar municipal developments. Slums are the reciprocal of parks, and if parks are to be built, why could they not be built in our present slum areas? We have only to look at such countries as the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Denmark to realize how governments have been cooperating with private capital in the elimination of slums and the building of low cost comfortable dwellings. The results have been spectacular.
In Toronto those interested in housing and its allied problems recently met in conference, and it was brought out at the conference how successful had been the cooperative housing scheme in Nova Scotia. Here perhaps may be a Canadian model to be followed in a national way under the aegis of the federal government and with its support. A great part of the difficulty in the way of progress is, of course, realty taxation, but surely it is not beyond the realm of the activities of the federal government to confer with the provinces and the municipalities towards the end of lightening the ghastly and impossible burden of taxation which the home owner now has to carry. The Technical Education Act of 1919 had an electric effect upon technical education, and, as the minister well knows, has been of untold value. Within the last few months I have talked with practically every deputy minister of education in Canada, and I have yet to find one who does not feel that the application of an act designed along the lines of the former Technical Education Act would be extraordinarily helpful, particularly at this time.
On our statute books, chapter 59 of the statutes of 1931, is the Vocational Education Act, which is described as "An act for the promotion of vocational education in Canada." This act provides for an annual appropriation of 1750,000 over a period of fifteen years to be made by the federal government to the governments of the various provinces. In a letter dated September 15, 1931, signed by the then deputy minister of labour, all provinces were notified that the

operation of this act would, in the terms of the letter, be postponed "until such time as economic conditions of the country warrant expenditures being made in connection with the work to be promoted under the terms of the act." What a contribution it could have made to our already heavily overcrowded technical schools!

Seventh, I wish to suggest to the government for their most serious consideration the establishment of camps similar to those of the civilian conservation corps in the United States. I have before me a considerable quantity of literature concerning them, which I have perused with a great deal of interest. One type of camp-a combined work project and training scheme-should be for men under twenty-five years of age. In these camps, men should be housed, fed, clothed, and paid a wage of a dollar per day. Their daily schedule should be almost equally divided between honest work, under rigid supervision, on useful works projects, and between training of a vocational and educational nature fitting them to enter primary or secondary industry as self-reliant citizens.
A second type of camp, for men over twenty-five years of age, should be established on a straight works camp basis, paying 35 cents per hour for work honestly done, less reasonable charges for medical care and housing. Here again, for the good of the men, it would be advisable to make a further division in age groups, setting aside some camps for men over forty years of age. .	.	.
We should also suggest a general housecleaning of government employment bureaux- a matter which is sadly overdue-so that they might be able to give aggressive and efficient assistance in finding employment for men at the conclusion of their camp work.
The possibilities along this line, Mr. Speaker, are legion. The way is clear; the challenge is there. Something must be done if we are to save democracy. I am a firm believer in youth, particularly in our Canadian youth; so I feel that one of the greatest of all challenges to the government of Canada is to give leadership and opportunity to our youth.
Eighth-not a direct suggestion for the creation of jobs, but rather an indirect, and certainly not an original suggestion, since it was contained in the report of the national employment commission to which I have already referred-is the setting up of government employment bureaux under federal administration, and to have those bureaux efficiently operated from coast to coast. It is true that the government itself said the cost of operating these bureaux, amounting to upwards of half a million dollars a year, was too great; but what is half a million dollars a year if thousands of jobs could be found by modernized, efficient bureaux, compared with the cost of relief, let alone the contribution to the humanitarian side of the question?

Ninth, I suggest that the government give some leadership by cooperating with private capital along the lines of internal, industrial, economic readjustment. The need for such readjustment arises not alone as a result of depressed internal trade or depressed external trade but also from our own shifting economies and new world economies. To use the illustration I mentioned this afternoon, as more oil is consumed, less coal is required; as further hydro electric developments are completed, less coal is required. Thus if we contract in our coal fields, why should we not expand in our oil fields, developed and undeveloped, when we have the oil we now possess?
Tenth, I suggest an intensive, nation-wide, government sponsored campaign under such a title, perhaps, as "Canada's prosperity year." Public relations, a comparatively new phase of advertising and publicity, has been employed successfully by particular businesses or industries in the United States to move large inventories and to expand markets. We have a national radio in Canada and a press that I think would be willing to cooperate fully with the federal government in a nationwide, well directed publicity campaign to help restore the confidence of business and industry and create a public interest in the purchase of made-in-Canada goods. As an example of what I mean the minister will recall the "Eat more fish" campaign conducted in Great Britain not so many years ago, and the campaign conducted by the egg producers' association of the United States more recently, which lifted an inventory of millions of dozens of eggs. Unlimited are the domestic results and the consequent increases in employment possible under an efficiently controlled campaign. For instance, if the 11,173 secondary industries reporting to the bureau of statistics were to add ten per cent to their staffs, one hundred thousand men would be put to work to-morrow.
Finally, the eleventh suggestion I have to make is for a great dominion, provincial and municipal conference to be presided over by some outstanding empire figures such as Lord Willingdon, who has a knowledge not only of Canada but of the empire. The purpose of this conference would be to determine legislative steps to be taken toward the end of a social reform program to bring the economic system under which we live up to date and to purge that system of some of the evils practised within it. Unemployment insurance, minimum wages, hours of work, social services, housing and many other such vitally necessary reforms could be discussed and determined upon, so that the parliament of Canada, in

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
cooperation with provincial legislatures and municipal and town councils, could work towards the end of reestablishing our social system on an equitable and fair basis. I plan to discuss this suggestion more fully at a later date.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker-and I am sure the right hon. minister will be pleased to hear these words-I am convinced that no shocking or conspicuous revolution is necessary in the Canadian institution of parliament. What Canada needs and expects of its government is resolute and forthright action, and the application of that energetic and intelligent set of principles usually referred to as common sense. We must forsake the political charms of lethargy and assume the responsibilities of action. We must forget that doctrine which says to those in high office, " If we will sit quietly, with folded hands, and express nothing but amiable platitudes, well calculated to avoid all friction, it will all come out all right at the next election." The path for us to follow is not the primrose path of doctrinaire socialism or monetary inflation but the difficult British method of clearing away one obstacle at a time. These are days of progression, not retrogression. Never was the challenge more clarion in its note. I should like to read a few words from the notes of a speech I made in Toronto on December 8 of last year:
Those of us who have sat in parliament realize with painful obviousness the tragedy that there is when a government temporizes with difficulties that are by no means insoluble and when only palliative and emergency measures are employed to deal with permanent vexatious problems. Our problems in Canada to-day are by no means emergency problems, hut are by way of being permanent problems, and for three years we have temporized with their results rather than dealt in a forthright manner with their causes. If we would retain our present form of government, if we would maintain our democracy, let us realize that if inactivity is permitted to continue in Ottawa we are paving the way for a revision, perhaps violent, of our present system of government. If I were asked to sum up in one or two words the greatest need in Canada to-day, I could give you an answer, and that would be "courageous, federal leadership."
In view of the situation which prevails in Canada relative to unemployment and its accompanying distress, and relative to agriculture and its distressed condition; in view of the plight of our Canadian youth, I urge the government, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, to forsake the charms of lethargy and to accept the challenge issued to it by every citizen of Canada to give our country the courageous leadership which it so sorely needs.

Nonsense? Quite true. There can be no more complete nonsense, but they continue to argue it as they have always done. Lower tariffs move goods, and more goods mean cheaper goods. There is the problem which the Dominion of Canada requires to solve to-day.
Then there is the question of an equilibrium between farm prices and prices of manufactured goods. Finally, there must be an effort to extend to the consumers of Canada the gains which accrue to industry from improvements of the technical and mechanical means of production. I read not long ago an able speech by an American, Doctor Nourse, in which he pointed out that it was his firm belief that in the period between 1900 and 1914 the failure to raise the standard of living in the United States was on account of the fact that monopoly control at that time took for the industries and did not give to the nation the result of the improvements which occurred during that period.
The other day I picked up a copy of Canadian Business. It too recognizes the movement in this direction. Here is a special article by a gentleman named S. C. Scobell, which touches the point:
Some way must 'be found to allow the masses to buy more, so that we can resume the vital expansion in the capital goods industries which, in a saving society, is necessary to maintain income and employment.
To increase such purchasing power, there must be a progressive decrease in manufacturing costs to enable prices to be reduced and potential markets tapped. Unhappily, there is a tendency in this country towards a rigidity of selling prices which prevents such expansion in domestic markets and closes the door to new private investment for increased facilities.
There is the problem which confronts the nation, the simple and direct problem of bringing the price of goods within the capacity of the nation to buy. If you cannot solve your problem in that way, believe me you will not solve it by things like this:	a program of
water conservation and flood control, extra nation-wide afforestation and reforestation, the opening up of the northwest territories and northern Ontario and Quebec. A gallant program-yes.
But I want to relate briefly the story of five boys on a farm. They were called A, B, C, D and X, and sometimes X was given the name of Denton. These boys and the old man were discussing farming operations. The boys argued about what they would do. Some said they would increase their investment in poultry, and some were going to extend their dairying. Then X spoke up and said, "You are all wrong, we must create things which we do not need. Let us have
a goldfish bowl in the front yard, and let us have a monument to protection in the backyard, and a lot of other things, and the creation of these things, while it may not give us much money, will give us employment." Then the old man spoke up-and in these instances sometimes the old man is wise-and said to them, "Boys, there are three things you can do. First, you can produce goods for your own consumption, to the full extent that you need. Next, you can produce goods for export. Next, you can develop your capital facilities if it is within your power to do so. But you must do economically whatever you do, and do the thing which it is within your capacity to do."
My hon. friend suggests that we should go to the farthest points, to the north, the east, the south, all over, and do these things, not stopping to consider that the intensive development of our resources within the existing provinces is perhaps the most profitable thing to do. Profit does not come into his mind. There are in the province of Ontario vast areas of splendid farm lands capable of producing immense wealth if we but had the capacity to get a market for these products- and it can be found. There are ample fields for development fairly close to our railways or close at least to our waterways. But neither this nor any other nation can afford to go into remoter spheres of development without first doing the tasks which lie close at hand. We have over-expanded in Canada; we have built railways to places where they were not needed. What is required is not only a conservation but a concentration of effort with the idea of using all our forces in industry and in the national economy to produce the maximum wealth with the minimum of cost. My hon. friend may not, perhaps, feel an impulse in that direction. He may not have come in contact with the necessity of economy. But the Canadian people have learned in a hard school. We have spent too much. We know our lesson. We will develop what lies close to our door, and in doing that we shall develop our wealth to a greater extent than we could do in any other way that may be brought to our attention.
I submit these matters to the house for consideration as an appropriate attempt to solve the problem which faces Canada to-day.
