Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), who has just resumed his seat, referred to the groups in the house and to their policies with regard to the economic problems which confront us. From the reference he made to the group to which
2774	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
I belong, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, I feel that he could not have read our program; either that or he did not understand it. I do not think the latter is the case, because I have a high regard for my hon. friend's intelligence.
I was interested in one remark which he made, when, after referring to an article in Canadian Business by Mr. Scofeell, he said that the problem which confronts the people is to bring prices of goods within the capacity of consumers to pay. I should like to tell the hon. member that is exactly what cannot be done under our present economic system because the producers of commodities, who are also in large measure the consumers of commodities, must first of all sell their labour power, and every employer of labour is trying to get that labour power at the cheapest possible price. The larger his balance over and above what labour costs him, the more profitable is his business. The farmer is in the same position. The hon. gentleman shakes his head, but I know businessmen. I have negotiated with businessmen in regard to wages, and I have always found that the lower the wage, the more satisfied they were. As I say, the farmer is not in a much better position than the city worker. There are a great many factors in connection with his economic position which I do not wish to go into- to-night, because I did not prepare myself for a consideration of the farmer's point of view; but he is in the same trap, caught in the same system as his brother the industrial worker. First of all, he is selling in a market over which he has no control, a market that is absolutely uncontrolled as far as he is concerned, and if it is ever controlled it is controlled against him, as was definitely proved in the price spreads and mass buying commission's report. He is buying in a market that is doubly controlled. In the first place it is controlled by the large industrialists, and it is still further controlled by the fiscal policies of governments. It is therefore absolutely impossible for producers of wealth under the capitalist system to consume what they produce. May I say for the benefit of hon. friends to my left that this is not because there is not sufficient money, but because the people who need the money also need the goods and have neither, and the people who have the money also have the goods. That is the reason why the end desired as much by my hon friend (Mr. Deachman) as by myself cannot be brought about under the capitalist system,
We listened throughout the afternoon and for a considerable part of this evening to a trenchant criticism by the hon. member for

Greenwood (Mr. Massey) of the government's policy or lack of policy in regard to unemployment. I found myself in large measure in agreement with what he said, but in my opinion there were certain weaknesses and a few contradictions in his lengthy speech. Throughout his address, which concerned itself with unemployment and its effects on the individual and the community, there was not a word as to the cause of unemployment. It seems to me it is difficult to deal with a problem if its cause is not first ascertained. The hon. member did, of course, refer to the government's fiscal policy, but I hope I would be doing him an injustice if I said that he considered the economic stress we have been going through for the last few years as being entirely a result of the fiscal policy of any government. I do not think he would say that. There must then, I believe, be some underlying and fundamental cause for unemployment.
I have stated in this house on many occasions my own opinion as to the cause of unemployment and I will not repeat it at any length to-night, except to say that I still believe that unemployment is the natural result of our system or method of production and distribution. To convince ourselves of the correctness of that statement, I think it is only necessary to observe that the more the means of production increase and the more the instruments of production are perfected, the greater the economic insecurity of the masses of the people becomes.
The economic depression which began in the fall of 1929 and which is still with us is a depression of abundance and not of scarcity, and until we have satisfied ourselves as to the reasons for these paradoxes we are not likely to make much progress in solving unemployment and other related problems.
I have sat in this house since the election of 1930, and I remember that during the greater part of the life of the last parliament it was admitted by all parties that unemployment was the most serious problem facing the people. Indeed, the chief charge which the Liberal party then in opposition brought against the former government was that it had failed to end unemployment. This government has been in office now for three and a half years and it, too, has failed to end unemployment. Not only has it failed to do that, but it has failed to make decent provision for those on relief. It has failed to organize any plan whereby unemployment as a social and economic problem can be definitely disposed of. The number of the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
unemployed is increasing, and the misery and degradation resulting from unemployment are also becoming more widespread.
During the five years the Conservative party was in office, not for one day was it allowed to forget the promises it had made to end unemployment. But those members who were so vociferous then have been strangely silent during the past three years. It would seem that their interest in the unemployed has evaporated. For instance, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), who I am sorry is not in his place to-night, was one of the loudest in his condemnation of the former government. The miseries of the unemployed weighed heavily on his heart during the whole time from 1930 to 1935. On February 20, 1935, a little over four years ago, he moved an amendment to the motion to go into supply. His amendment came at the end of a lengthy speech, and it will be found in Hansard at page 1194. It reads:
This house regrets that, notwithstanding the specific promises made prior to the election of 1930, and many times since reiterated, and despite the fact that extraordinary powers to deal with unemployment have been repeatedly secured from parliament, the present administration, after nearly five years of office, has not yet submitted to parliament any definite or effective policy to deal witl} widespread actual unemployment or distress which continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem.
As I said, we have been here for another period of four years, and the mover of that amendment is a shining light in the government of the day, yet unemployment still continues to be Canada's most urgent national problem. There has not yet been submitted to us any definite or effective policy to deal with it. The. minister's mind, which was so fertile when in opposition, has been exceedingly barren since 1935.
Unemployment statistics make very distressing reading indeed. I have been examining the reports of the national registration department for a number of months. They show that the difference between the number receiving relief at the end of 1938 as compared with 1937, and at the beginning of this year, is getting less. For instance, in October, 1938, the number on relief had dropped 155,000 from October, 1937, but the decrease was only 26,186 in January, 1938, compared with January 1939.
When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) spoke to this resolution on March 15, he endeavoured to show from statistics that, to use his own words, "we have been making substantial progress in reducing the number of unemployed." In one set of figures he showed
that the total number on direct relief decreased from 1,326,000 in January, 1936, to 1,178,000 in January, 1937, and again to 1,015,000 in January', 1938, and to 978,000 in January, 1939. I believe that last figure was a preliminary one, and the final number may possibly be greater. The figures therefore show a decrease, although not a great reduction. But I submit that the figures given are not all the figures, and do not show all those who are getting assistance from the government. What has really happened from January, 1936, to January, 1939, is not so much a decrease in the total number receiving direct relief as a change in the heading under which relief is given. For example, the number receiving old age pensions in 1935 was 101,000. In 1938, that number had increased by 75.000 to 176,000. I think it is fair to assume that in 1935 many of those
75.000	were listed as receiving direct relief. It must also be noted that there is no registration of persons as receiving relief in New Brunswick. In January, 1935, 26.500 persons were listed as receiving direct relief in that province. But assistance is being given to New Brunswick on account of unemployment. Last year the amount was $225,000, which amount I suppose corresponds to the 30 per cent paid to the other provinces towards direct relief. It is reasonable then to suppose that if there were unemployment registration in New Brunswick at the present time, the number unemployed and receiving assistance would be somewhat larger than in Nova Scotia, because the assistance given in 1938-39 by the federal government is slightly more for New Brunswick than for Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia in December, 1938, there were almost
11.000	receiving direct relief. We may assume then that some 11,000 were in receipt of assistance in New Brunswick in view of the amount of money paid by the federal government. Adding that number to the increase of 75.000 in old age pensioners, makes 86.000.
In Quebec a law providing for mothers' allowances recently came into effect. The latest estimate I obtained is that some 6,000 mothers, heads of families, with approximately 25,000 dependents, are receiving assistance under that legislation. It is fair to assume that most, if not all, of that number, some 30,000, would be receiving unemployment relief.
Since 1935 we have had a considerable number of persons transferred from unemployment to relief of another kind through the operation of the War Veterans' Allowance-Act. This act was extended in 1938 to apply to all veterans not capable of maintaining

themselves. The number of veterans receiving assistance under this head at the close of the fiscal year ended March 31, 1939, was 5,150. The annual report of the war veterans' allowance board has this to say in regard to this class of relief recipients:
When considering expenditure under this legislation, it is well to remember that the allowance is awarded to those in necessity who are incapable of maintaining themselves and even had the act not been enacted, the great majority of those receiving its benefits would of necessity have had to be maintained by the community in one form or another.
The War Veterans' Allowance Act was enacted only in 1930, yet on February 1, 1939, returned men to the number of 19,250 were receiving assistance under it. It is exceedingly significant that the number receiving assistance in this category increased by 4,230 from February 1, 1938, to February 1, 1939. It seems to me then that it is very little use for the Minister of Labour to tell this house that the number on relief is decreasing. It is not. We are just transferring people from the form of state assistance which we call unemployment relief to some other form of state assistance.
But that is not all. During the last few years provincial governments and the municipalities have been "chiseling" on the unemployed and thus reducing the relief rolls but increasing the sum total of distress and want. Early in 1938 the government of my own province notified the municipalities and cities within its borders that under a ruling of the federal Department of Labour the provincial government would no longer be able to contribute any portion of the cost of relief for unemployable persons. I have since been informed that the federal Department of Labour did not make any such ruling, but that the provincial government just had a bright idea for putting more of the burden of unemployment relief on the municipalities. To some extent they succeeded in doing that, with the result that the cities and municipalities in British Columbia have been for the past year carrying thousands of unemployed who were formerly getting assistance from the dominion and provincial governments.
The municipalities are also doing their share of "chiseling" on the unemployed. In [DOT] Vancouver, when an unemployed person gets work for a short time and then comes back on relief, he must give a strict account of every cent of wages earned by him during the period when he was working, and for every S75 of wages received during the period of employment he is supposed to keep himself 
and family for one month. No allowance is made for the number of dependants. No account is taken of the fact that clothes and household goods wear out. No account is taken of the fact that dental and medical needs are postponed during periods of unemployment. Indeed, regulations of this kind put a premium on Shiftlessness.
What I am stating now is clearly demonstrated by the employment and relief statistics of the Department of Labour and the bureau of statistics, as the following figures will indicate. While the number estimated as being unemployed is increasing, the number actually getting unemployment relief or assistance is decreasing. I think the following figures are interesting:

It might interest the house to learn that during the first eleven months of 1938 only 36 per cent of the estimated unemployed were receiving relief at all. The report on employment by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for March makes rather interesting reading. But in December, 1938, the estimated number of wage-earners was 61,000 less than in 1937. That is rather absurd; surely we had as many wage-earners in 1938 as we had in 1937. These figures, I think, are ample and conclusive evidence that the policy, or lack of policy, of this government is not even checking the failure of private industry to put the people of this country to work. From Victoria to Sydney comes a despairing cry from people crushed and broken by poverty, destitution and degrading misery. Almost every issue of every newspaper in Canada has its story of misery and want. A few weeks ago I saw in one of the Ottawa newspapers a heading over a news item from northern Ontario,

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
"Starvation brings great suffering in northern Ontario." The article reads as follows:
Ansonville, Ont., March 7. Dr. E. J. Clouthier, medical officer of health, said to-day five cases of scurvy have been discovered in this northern Ontario village three miles south of Iroquois Falls. He said the disease was the "direct result of starvation and deprivation of the essential foods." . . .
The disease is caused by a lack of vegetables and fruits in the daily diet. It was said many residents of the village who are employed at paper mills in Iroquois Falls are working only part time and are unable to purchase these essential foods.
So not only are the unemployed suffering; in many instances those who are employed are suffering as well. Then a Canadian press dispatch from Stellarton, Nova Scotia, under date of November 29, 1938, gives another story of poverty and destitution. The press dispatch referred to was based upon a survey made by a committee appointed by the United Mine Workers of Stellarton, employees of the Acadia Coal Company, operating in that district. I should like to read at least part of this dispatch which appeared in the Halifax Herald:
Stellarto i, N.S., November 28. The following is a Irief prepared by the U.M.W. committee on the conditions of the Stellarton school children whose fathers are employed by the Acadia Coal Company.
These are not the children of unemployed but of employed workers.
Local union 4481, U.M.A. of A., Stellarton, has made a house to house survey of living conditions of the families of coal miners living in the different sections of the town, and the results of this survey have convinced our organization that these facts should be placed before the Nova Scotia government in an effort to have financial aid sent into Stellarton, to relieve some of the distress that our survey has disclosed, before the cold weather sets in, otherwise a serious epidemic will be the result of this shortage of clothing and undernourishment that to-day faces the large per cent of the population of this town.	,
A statement taken from eighty-four families covering 040 children, and this is only one-quarter of the survey taken, reveals that these people are living in a state of starvation. The average earnings of these people for the last nine months has been ($8) eight dollars per week, to supply food, clothing, milk, medicine, lights and dental care, resulting in the fact that eighty per cent of these children do not know the taste of cow's milk, and milk in any form is a luxury in most of these houses.
Another fact that our survey has disclosed is that these people are living, or trying to live, on the magnificent sum of 19 cents per day, which is below the rate allowed^ to maintain inmates of any prison or industrial home in the Dominion of Canada.
The town of Stellarton, in an effort to assist these people, has put into effect a work project that is insufficient to begin to take care of the distress that is apparent in Stellarton. Miners who have not received any work for weeks are given twro days work under this project at
$2.50 per day for nine hours work. Some of these miners have families ranging from five to twelve people, which our survey had disclosed, in a great majority of cases, have been receiving a wage for the last six years that is, at least, 40 per cent below a decent Canadian standard of living, resulting to-day in the fact that most of these people's clothing, both bed and wearing apparel, is worn out, also their furniture, and under the present set-up of the work project that is being put into effect in Stellarton, and the conditions of the mines which are only operating one and two days per week, these people cannot supply to their children the necessary food that will keep them in normal health, to say nothing of getting warm clothing that will supply a measure of protection against the cold winters that we experience in Nova Scotia and allow these children to attend school and equip them with the necessary education that will allow them in future years to take their rightful place in our society and become good citizens of Canada.
There is a picture of want and degradation that demands attention. It is not a solitary instance; it is something which can Ibe duplicated in almost every province in Canada. Conditions may not be as bad in some sections as in others, but if they are not it is because the people over the years have been able to organize and have worked and agitated for better conditions. It would not be so bad if there were any just cause for such conditions, if this were the result of a poverty of resources. But that is not so. It is the result of bad economic organization and ruthless exploitation. It is a striking example of poverty in the midst of plenty, of starvation in a land of abundance. As I listened on March 15 to the recital by the Minister of Labour of how the government was overcoming unemployment, my mind went back to perhaps happier days when I found pleasure in reading Lewis Carroll's classic, "Alice in Wonderland." Hon. members who have had the pleasure of reading that fantasy will remember how Alice and the red queen had to keep going at top speed in order to remain in the same place. My good friend the Minister of Labour is doing just what Alice was doing. No matter how hard he goes, he merely manages to keep in the same place. But I doubt if he will be able to keep in the same place much longer. I am sorry to have to say it, but the fact is that all the efforts of the minister and the government since they came into office, as far as unemployment is concerned, have left them in the same place as they were when they started.
In going through my papers a few days ago I came across a leaflet which was distributed by the Liberal party during the election of 1935. It makes interesting reading to-day, interesting I presume for everyone but Liberals. This is headed in large type, " Jobs or doles-

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
which?" Then follows a quotation from Mr. R. B. Bennett, on January 2, 1935:
Canada on the dole is like a young man in the poorhouse.
Then the leaflet states:
After five years of Conservative government more than one-tenth of the Canadian people are on direct relief.
During these five years to March, 1935, the dominion government has spent $312,328,098.97 on relief. This does not include the wheat guarantee which may be estimated at anywhere from $150,000,000 to $250,000,000. It does not include the public works program of 1935.
This was election propaganda. It continues:
The national debt has risen by $800,000,000 between 1930 and 1935.
It goes on to give unemployment figures, showing 596.946 persons on relief in May, 1932, and 1,341,942, in February, 1935. It continues:
When the Liberal government was in office men and women had jobs. Vote Liberal and get back from the poorhouse.
The people voted Liberal, but they are still in the poorhouse. And they are more likely to stay there than ever before. When the minister was speaking on March 15, he made this statement:
. . . and when it is considered also that, despite the sharp recession in the United States in the latter part of 1937 and 1938, our figures of employment kept relatively constant, there is evidence here of the recuperative powers of this young country-
That reminds me of Mr. Bennett.
-and if only we had more faith in the recuperative powers of Canada, if only leaders of industry had more faith in the recuperative powers of Canada, it would be possible, I say, for us to make a substantial reduction in the number of unemployed this year.
Is the welfare of the people of Canada to depend upon the faith of the industrial leaders of Canada? If the industrial leaders of Canada will not show faith, is this government going to say that nothing can be done about it, that we must continue to remain in poverty? I am satisfied that the government cannot do that and hope to continue this as a democratic country. During the last few years we have heard a great deal about democracy, but if there is one thing that stands out clearly, it is that the greatest democratic progress occurred during the last half of the nineteenth century and the first two decades of this century, during which time we had the greatest period of economic expansion the world has ever known. We must make the wealth of this country available to the people of this country if we hope to maintain our democratic institutions. If we do not do that, regardless of whether or not our industrial leaders have faith, we are bound to be over-
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
taken by the malady that has already overtaken a great part of the world.
I wish to say a few words in regard to the single unemployed. I am not sure that the plight of the single unemployed is worse than that of the rest of the unemployed, but it appears to be. The national economy of Canada, as was pointed out by the national employment commission, demands a large army of unattached men who can on short notice move from one place to another to meet the demand for labour. We can all remember the thousands of men who were required to harvest the grain crops in the prairie provinces prior to 1930. That work lasted for only a few weeks, and then those men moved on to other fields of activity. The demand for that type of labour is not as great to-day, but there is still a certain need for it. In its final report the national employment commission drew attention to this problem. At page 88 of appendix D to their report, the commission had this to say:
Development of Canada's resources demands a large supply of vigorous, mobile labour. A shifting labour reserve, without definite residence, while aggravated in recent years by lack of opportunity for gainful occupation, is not only a natural but almost an essential feature of production in this country. Our great primary activities, along with closely allied secondary industries, employ almost half of the gainfully occupied population, the overwhelming percentage of whom are unskilled or semiskilled wage earners. As such they are dependent for gainful occupation upon circumstances quite outside their own control. In many cases their occupations are seasonal and carried on in the isolation of frontier or "new" country. These men must move with employment demands. or lack of the same, and thus have not a free choice as to their place of residence. It is practically impossible for a man in this category to establish residence anywhere. Although he may have five or ten years' history of almost continuous employment it may be spread over widely different occupations in varying localities, one place in summer, another in winter, and so, when idle, he keeps "moving on" in search of work, always hoping that somewhere the job he finds will last long enough to let him get "settled."
The commission, as the Minister of Labour well knows, give a general review of the so-called transient unemployed problem, and they conclude by saying:
Until these two distinct phases of the one problem "residence" and "social need" are segregated and each dealt with along appropriate lines, on a dominion-wide basis, the problem of bewildered shifting families, and of thousands of men. in unceasing trek in search of a "toehold" will continue to defeat the best and most determined efforts of local and voluntary services to effect reestablishment.
Yet with this report before them now for two years, the government have not yet begun even to touch this problem of the transient worker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so much has already been said about the sorrowful plight of the unemployed and so many pertinent statistics have already been ' compiled and put on Hansard that I think any additional remarks of mine along that line would be entirely superfluous at this time. I do feel, however, that all thinking people must by this time concede that there is absolutely no reason or excuse for present conditions in a country so naturally wealthy as this dominion. I think everyone must concede that the condition to-day of such a large section of our unemployed and of those who are living on subsistence incomes constitutes one of the saddest reflections on modem government. I am quite satisfied that if proper methods were pursued in Canada our system could provide for every adult citizen an income of at least one thousand dollars' worth of consumable goods a year, and I do not think it requires any stretch of imagination to concede that.
I am not going to enter into the controversy that is usually carried on between Liberals and Conservatives as to what adjustments in tariff and trade are necessary to bring about a proper relationship. I think the history of the last seventy years in Canada indicates to us that the remedy for our troubles does not lie in the realm of tariff and trade adjustments. Surely to goodness if there is an ideal arrangement to be made in that field the Liberals and Conservatives would have found it at some period during the last seventy years of our history.
The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) sarcastically referred to the proposals of the Social Credit party for remedying present conditions. He rather discounted the suggestion that money tickets were necessary to the solution of the problem, and if we may judge from remarks and speeches that are made from time to time in the house a great number of members discount the fact that money tickets are an essential factor in solving our problems. Surely everyone who has made the slightest study of economics must realize that in this highly complex age, an age in which the systems of production and distribution are extremely complicated, we can do nothing without a medium of exchange. Surely it is obvious to anyone that, unless we employ a medium of exchange, in the first place we cannot produce the goods, in the second place that we cannot distribute them when they are produced, and finally that we cannot consume them. Therefore there is a definite relationship between the money tickets required and the goods which should be distributed, and to suggest that money tickets have no relationship to
economic policies or to the production and distribution of goods is idle.
I should like to say a few words on the cause of our unemployment situation. Before we can intelligently prescribe a proper remedy for our present conditions we must first analyse the situation. Unemployment is not a cause; it is a result. It is the natural consequence of the technological advancements of our modern age. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) this afternoon did not, I think, place sufficient emphasis on one of the factors, in my opinion the major factor, contributing towards unemployment not only in Canada but in every country in the world, and that is the substitution of mechanical for human energy. I have here a few statistics which I have gathered in my reading, showing the extent to which human labour has been displaced by solar energy and power machinery, and indicating that it is physically impossible to employ all the unemployed in industry.
One of the most remarkable substitutes for human energy is the development of the production of electrical energy. Back in 1832 a water turbine produced only fifty horse power; in 1891, at Niagara, each electrical unit had a capacity of 5,000 horse power; to-day, we are informed, units are produced which have a capacity of 300,000 horse power, and we are also informed that a unit with
1.000.	000 horse-power capacity could be built. Translated into human energy, a unit of
1.000.	000 horse power capacity would provide the equivalent of the labour of 10,000,000 men for an eight hour day, or of 30,000,000 men if it were on a twenty-four hour basis. According to the Canada Year Book, the available water power of Canada is 34,000,000 horse power; the developed horse power is, I believe, about one-fourth of that, or around eight millions. If this 34,000,000 available horse power were developed we should have the equivalent of ten times that quantity if translated into man power, or an average of thirty-four mechanical slaves for every man, woman and child in the dominion. In other words, the substitution of electrical energy for human energy has increased to such an extent that to-day our mechanical man power is forty or fifty times as great as it was before electrical energy was discovered.
In his address on his resolution, the minister suggested that it was the duty of industry to employ idle labour. I do not agree with him, but I am not going to discuss that at the moment. The point which I wish to establish is that, to begin with, it is mathematically impossible for industry to absorb the unemployed to an extent that they would have sufficient wages to buy back the pro-
27SO	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
ducts of industry; that is, provided they are going to take advantage of power machinery as we have it to-day. And surely we are going to do that, we are not going to tolerate retrogression rather than progression.
I have here a few statistics with regard to the extent to which in certain industries human labour has been reduced. In the days of Athens and Rome one miller could grind from one to one and a half barrels of flour a day. We are informed that in Minneapolis a machine in one mill has a capacity of 30,000 barrels a day. In 1899, the number of plants was 9,500; in 1929, it was 11,500. In 1899, 32,200 mills ground .471,000,000 bushels of wheat; in 1929, 26,400 mills ground 546,000,000 bushels. There was a decrease in the number of mills and an increase in the number of bushels ground. All these figures, by the way, relate to industry in the United States, but the same thing holds good of industries in Canada, and the same effects would be produced if an equivalent amount of machinery were installed.
In the shoe-making industry, we are informed, in Roman days one man produced a pair of shoes in five and a half days; to-day, with the aid of power machinery, one man in the same time can produce seventy pairs of shoes. The shoe-production capacity of the United States is 900,000,000 pairs a year.
The same conditions apply in the brickmaking industry. For 5,000 years the highest production per individual was 450 bricks a day; to-day one machine can produce 400,000 bricks a day. The same statisticians inform us it is estimated that one hundred men in five plants situated strategically throughout the United States could supply the total brick requirements of the whole of that country.
Let me give a few similar facts with regard to the steel and iron industry. In 1900, it required seventy man-hours to produce one ton of steel; in 1929, the same amount could be produced in thirteen man-hours. The same trend is evident with respect to pig-iron. In 1879, 73-7 tons per man per year were produced; by 1929 the output per man had been raised to 1,710 tons per man per year.
In the automobile industry it required, in 1904, 1,291 man-hours to produce an automobile; in 1919, 313 man-hours; in 1929, only 92 man-hours.
We have also a few interesting figures with regard to agriculture. By the spade method one man can dig one-eighth of an acre in twelve hours; so that ninety-six man-hours are required to dig one acre. With a twenty-horse hitch and six fourteen-inch steel-bottom ploughs twelve to fifteen acres a day can be ploughed, representing -83 to -67 man-hours an

acre, a reduction from 96 hours to -67; and to-day, with a tractor drawing a 60-disc plough the number of man-hours per acre is reduced to -088.
In the meat-packing industry the number of man-hours per 1,000 pounds of meat production has been reduced from 25-56 to 17-86.

speechtext: The hon. member mentioned the number of pairs of shoes that can be produced in a day. Has he the price, in both instances?

speechtext: I know, but I thought the hon. member might have that.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext:
No, I have not the prices here. The point I am trying to make by means of these statistics is that our unemployment is largely a result of the substitution of power machinery for human energy.
In the face of these facts I fail to understand how the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) can suggest that it is the obligation and the duty of the industrialists of Canada or of any other country to absorb idle labour. It is a mathematical impossibility, and furthermore I do not think it is the proper objective. I believe that the proper and common sense objective of an economic system is to provide the maximum amount of goods with the minimum of trouble. We have therefore on our hands to-day leisure which is called unemployment. It is misnamed when it is called unemployment; it is leisure, and the real problem we have to deal with is the proper distribution of this leisure. As it works out to-day, those who have this leisure, for which people are not paid, and which, therefore, is not leisure proper, have not the training or the education which would give them the ability to appreciate their leisure time. On the other hand, those who are employed in industry are obliged to work so hard and to put forth so much effort that they are unable to appreciate the little leisure that they have over and above their hours of labour. So that the first problem is properly to distribute this leisure, and the other is to provide security for those who have been displaced by machinery, without reducing the standard of living of those employed.
I believe that the reason we do not make progress in adopting a proper solution of this problem is that we build up arguments on false premises. It is assumed by most economists to-day that industry is self-liquidat-

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
ing, that each industry in the course of the production of its goods pays out in that production an amount of income equivalent to the prices of the goods produced. That is a false premise, and an analysis of the statistics will readily indicate that this is so. I have here a chart given in the Canada Year Book of 1939 at page 123. It gives statistics for fifteen leading industries in the dominion. It shows salaries and wages paid out in the production of goods and gives the costs of materials and the gross value of the products, which, I presume, is the selling price of the articles. The total gross value of these products of fifteen leading industries is $1,507,580,073. All payments made in these industries in Canada, to labour in the form of salaries and wages, and payments for raw material for processing and so on, total $1,165-, 110,975. Therefore there is a difference of $342,469,098 between total payments made and the prices of the goods. That is the difference between total prices and total income.
It should be apparent to anyone that it is impossible to buy $2 worth of consumable goods with $1. In this instance the statistics indicate that if the people are expected to buy the goods at the prices at which they are offered for sale, they are short $342,000,000 plus. That is the deduction I draw from the figures I have given. I do not know of any other deduction that can be drawn from them, and as has been pointed out from time to time, particularly by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), that situation is due in the first place to the substitution of power machinery for human labour, second, to reinvestment from savings, and, third, to other charges the equivalent of which is not created as purchasing power.
If the people who are entitled to the goods are to receive them they will never receive them through wages. As I have already indicated from the statistics quoted, it is mathematically impossible to absorb the unemployed in industry; consequently the difference between total prices and total income must be distributed to all the people in an equitable manner. The difference between total prices and total income exists as prices only. It is not income; it is not money that exists in the pockets of people; it is merely the price written on goods, the equivalent of which does not exist as money. And unless the equivalent is created in money or tickets or whatever you wish to call it and issued to consumers in various necessary ways, I fail to see how we can distribute to the people of Canada the goods which we produce in Canada. The same applies to every other country.
I realize that we cannot overnight bring about an entirely new system and that we must necessarily pass through a transition period. I quite agree with the hon. member for Greenwood that in this period there are many necessary public works that could be done until the whole economic system is adjusted to function smoothly.
The hon. member for Greenwood put forth a number of suggestions which -are worth while and certainly necessary; but the one thing that he failed to tell us, and it is the one thing which all hon. members who make such proposals always fail to tell us, is how these projects are to be financed. They continually suggest to us social crediters that our proposal of new money is not sound. At the same time they do not offer any suggestion as to how the necessary money can be raised except by increasing debt or taxation. I should like to know how the Conservatives, if they were in power, would finance such a program. It is a wonderful program; I agree that many of these things should be done; they should have been done a long time ago. The Liberals should be doing them now, but they are hamstrung in the same way as the Conservatives would be; under the present system they have only one source of money-either taxation or borrowing. Apart from the social credit proposals no other method is suggested by which the balancing of consumption with production can be accomplished. If there is any other way we should like to hear of it.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext: There is no doubt about that. The more hon. members come to know of our proposals, the more they will see it.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext:
All is wrong,
but you cannot put it right; many problems but no solution.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext: You have no solution but taxation.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext:
These suggestions of ours
could be elaborated further, but I do not think it necessary at the present moment. Every problem that arises in this house, it makes no difference what it is, always resolves itself finally into a question of finance: Where is the money to come from? One does not need to be a parliamentarian or university graduate to suggest public works, reforestation or any of the proposals which have been made; any everyday school boy could do the same thing. The question which the public wants answered and which we want answered is how these projects are going to be financed. The answer to that question should be forthcoming. It is a simple matter
2782	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
to make these suggestions, but how are they going to be financed outside of parliament assuming and exercising its prerogative so as to make financially possible what is physically possible? I know of no other way by which this can be financed.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext: Nor does anyone else.

maintopic: NET INCREASE IN POPULATION OF CANADA-AGE GROUP 16-64 YEARS
speechtext:
And as far as a long range
policy and. a permanent solution of the question of unemployment are concerned, I am satisfied that if the Conservatives or the Liberals were to have another fifty years of office, under the present financial policy they would be further away from a solution than they are to-day. Without a change in monetary policy the problem is insoluble and will proceed from bad to worse.
I am not going to discuss further at this time the application of social credit principles to adjust the situation, but will conclude simply by emphasizing once more that it is a problem of finance and nothing else, and until the present or another government devise a new scheme of financing, adopt a new financial policy, the problem cannot be solved, and consumption can never be equated with production.

speechtext:
The
motion of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the general interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, and also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, and for the appointment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.
That resolution has been before the house for three or four sessions. The agreements with the provinces are for some provinces but not for others; there is no equality of treatment. The British North America Act calls for equality of treatment in such matters, but for some bankrupt provinces the total burden of relief is borne by the high court of parliament here and these provinces do not contribute anything. In other provinces some municipalities can get all kinds of municipal improvements, while in others they can get nothing. Ontario has not taken full value of what it should get here because the provincial government is not altogether in accord with the present government at Ottawa on this question.
When the present government came into office after the last election all the billboards in the country were covered with abuse of the [Mr. Khul.3
government of the day: "Beat Bennett and bad times, end unemployment, vote Liberal." The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) told the house before the election in 1930 that Conservative provinces would not get one five-cent piece for unemployment. Between 1926 and 1930 I asked the government nine or ten questions about unemployment, and the Minister of Labour of that day replied that the federal authorities had nothing to do with unemployment, it is a matter for the provinces and the municipalities. In 1935, in the first session of this parliament, the present Prime Minister was asked what he would do to cure unemployment, and he said he would appoint a royal commission. A royal commission was appointed; the commission reported, and according to some of the Prime Minister's own following the report was valueless, so much so that the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) took the report and threw it on the floor in the presence of this house, and it has proved valueless in practice. I may say that on this particular question the church's one foundation-I am not a member of the continuing Presbyterian church and for that reason I cannot speak longer than forty minutes; but we read in the Scriptures, "Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher, all is vanity." "Humbug of humbugs," say the unemployed, "all is humbug," with the many commissions who do nothing for unemployment.
As far as the unemployed are concerned, this parliament is not doing its duty with any leadership, or cure, or action. With the great natural resources which this country has, the magnificent forests and abundance of raw materials and products of every kind, there should be no one out of work. In the present session of parliament I introduced a resolution. which was not reached. The resolution stated the case of the municipalities for help. It said:
That, in the opinion of this house, in view of the present social and economic conditions of this country, including unemployment and unemployment relief, the time has come for the government to consider assuming the total cost of it all, including that of hospitalization, as well as providing more adequate grants for education and public health for the people, and that the federal authority should deal directly with the larger municipalities on municipal relief works and relief unemployment, instead of as at present by way of the provinces, notwithstanding the provisions of any law. statute, usage or custom to the contrary.
In my opinion the municipalities are not getting fair treatment. This parliament makes the immigration laws, the financial laws, the laws regulating trade and commerce; it can make treaties of all kinds with a foreign

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
country and do a great deal to injure employment. The government of the day saw fit to change the policy adhered to by the Liberal party from 1921 to 1930, which was that they had nothing to do with unemployment, it was a matter for the provinces. When the depression came and the industrial workers were out of work and the farmers could not get back their costs of production, this government came along and said "We will do something," and they appointed a royal commission and wasted two years. This parliament has appropriated the revenues of the municipalities in the way of income tax. The income tax enabled the municipalities to carry on the services in connection with relief, hospitals, education and so on. Then this parliament came along and invaded what had been the exclusive field of the municipalities since confederation, and imposed a duplicate tax and in the case of some provinces a triplicate tax, with the result that when the depression came along and all these people went on relief, the municipalities had not the money to carry on, deprived as they were of their revenues. Now agreements are made with the provinces, and I hope that under the present agreements the minister will earmark this money, because in some of the provinces they have been making deductions for costs and other reasons, and the total federal grant is not passed on.
I do not wish to criticize Quebec, because the industrial workers of that province are suffering acutely, but I do say that if Quebec is able, under this act, to have money advanced by that province for all kinds of municipal public works, the same thing should be done in Ontario, British Columbia and the mari-times. One example is the Montreal terminal, for which $12,500,000 was voted. This work was said to be mainly for unemployment relief, but this government did not deal directly with the province at all; they dealt with the city; that work was commenced, and neither the province nor the city gave anything. I see no reason why that principle should not be extended to the other large municipalities throughout the country.
With regard to unemployment insurance, that should be divisible between the employables and the unemployables. In 1909 they had unemployment insurance in Great Britain, and it was part of the Liberal platform in Canada in 1919, but we do not have it yet. We were told a month ago that we would have to await the report of the Rowell commission. Dear knows when that report will come in, if it ever does; and then probably it will be put in the archives. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) did not pay much attention to the Rowell report, or even
wait for it. When it is a case of crop and farm insurance versus humans, what does the minister do? A month or more ago this house adopted a resolution proposed by one of the government members for the appointment of a select committee to inquire into the question of crop insurance. But the Minister of Agriculture introduces a resolution, on which he speaks from 3.15 to 5.30 o'clock on the Wednesday afternoon of last week in order that no one can reply, notwithstanding the fact that this house decided that a committee should be appointed to deal with this very question. You see how quickly the present administration can side-step the rule of anticipation and how quickly they can formulate government policy. They are going to bring about crop insurance in the twinkling of an eye, or certainly before this parliament prorogues, but unemployment insurance can wait. How have they dealt with the question of unemployment among the industrial workers in our large cities and towns, who have been driven to the wall? They get none of these prairie hand-outs, these many kinds of subventions, bonuses and subsidies from the party now in power, who are free traders on the prairies in regard to grain. How do they feel about unemployment insurance? Have we got it? No, although they have had it in Great Britain for two decades.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we could have unemployment insurance right now under clause 1 of section 91 of the British North America Act. Under that section this parliament can make any grants of money it sees fit to make out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada in regard to public debt and property. That was the way in which they voted money for technical education, pensions and other services. So, if only the government would do the same in regard to unemployment insurance, they would relieve a great deal of suffering throughout the country.
In regard to a public works program, the committee on education and labour of the United States senate held a hearing some twelve years ago, under the chairmanship of the late Senator Couzens, during which they investigated conditions the world over in regard to seasonal unemployment, technological unemployment growing out of the use of machinery, casual unemployment and so on. They dealt with the question of the employables and those permanently unemployed. Mr. Daniel Willard, president of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad, in giving evidence, had this to say:
It is a dangerous thing to have a large number of unemployed men and women

dangerous to society as a whole-dangerous to the individuals who constitute society. When men who are willing and able to work and want
2784	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
to work are unable to obtain work, we need not be surprised if they steal before they starve. Certainly I do not approve of stealing, but if I bad to make the choice between stealing and starving, I would surely not choose to starve-and in that respect I do not think I am much unlike the average individual.
If Canada had appointed a committee fifteen years ago to go into the question of unemployment we would have been ready when the depression came along and we would have had a survey and register ready to act on. In comparing this United States report with that of the Purvis commission, I find that both deal with the questions of youth and unemployment insurance, and many of the findings of our 1937 commission are the same. I am sorry that under the youth program little or nothing has been done, nor is anything being done to take care of the senior employees who have been driven to the wall. There are industries in this country that will not give employment to any man over forty-five years of age. These senior employees should be provided for. So I say not only should provision be made for youth- and dear knows we need some provision of this kind-but in addition we should not have the law of the jungle or the survival of the fittest apply to our older men in connection with employment, because that is what it amounts to. There should be equality of treatment for the senior employees as well as for youth, and with leadership all would be taken care of.
We are having a great deal of trouble in the city of Toronto as a result of the depression. To-day we have practically the confiscation of property for non-payment of taxes.
On motion of Mr. Church the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the course of his speech the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) made the startling assertion that thousands of single transients had died as a result of exposure, illness, actual starvation or lack of care. His exact statement as appearing in Hansard is as follows:
Single transients to the number of thousands upon thousands beg here and there in an effort to keep body and soul together, and thousands have died as a result of exposure, illness, actual starvation or lack of care.
As might have been expected, this quotation has caught the headlines of newspapers and has been carried to all parts of the country by press reports. On my responsibility as Minister of Labour I denied absolutely the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
truth of this statement when made, but the hon. member for Greenwood refused to withdraw and placed me in the unusual position of disproving an assertion which he on his part was unable or unwiUing to confirm, and in support of which he did not produce a word of evidence.
When the house rose at six o'clock I gave instructions to have an inquiry sent immediately to all provinces in order to obtain accurate information on the point raised by the member for Greenwood. The message, I might say, was sent officially by the commissioner of unemployment relief to the appropriate heads of relief departments in the various provinces. The message sent by the commissioner of relief here was in the following terms:
Please wire rush collect if you know of any cases of death due to starvation or exposure in your province during past four years. Would appreciate answer in respect to categories viz those on relief and transients.
H. Hereford, Department of Labour.
It will be noticed that this inquiry goes beyond the class mentioned fey my hon. friend. His reference was to transients alone. I am going to place upon Hansard the replies received thus far from seven provinces.
The first is from Ontario:
Re telegram: know of no cases of death due to starvation or exposure of unemployed residents or transients in Ontario.
That is signed by S. J. Gadsby, accountant of the relief branch, acting in the absence of the deputy minister of that department.
From Saskatchewan:
No deaths have occurred among those on relief or transients from starvation and no deaths have resulted from exposure or lack of clothing among those on relief or transients. Only deaths from exposure are those caught in severe blizzards. In no case has a death resulted from refusal of relief authorities to provide shelter.
W. W. Dawson, Director of Relief.

Our officials cannot recollect any cases of death due to starvation or exposure of relief o-r transient cases during past four years.

Re telegram thirteenth. In Alberta no deaths of those on relief due to starvation or exposure for last four years or previously. Messages have yet to be received from Quebec and Prince Edward Island. I have no reason to believe that they will disclose any different situation in those provinces. When the answers are received I shall place them before this house.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, April 13, consideration of the motion of Hon. Norman McL. Rogers (Minister of Labour) that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of un-

employment and agricultural distress and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the genera] interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, and also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund, and for the appointment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I may say, having been in municipal life and on public bodies and boards of health and hospital boards for a great many years, that as regards the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), while I cannot speak as to the numbers involved, I agree as to the principle he expressed in connection with long-continued unemployment and its ruinous effect on public health and its wastage, because the way things are to-day an unemployed man who has a wife and family to keep, and perhaps others dependent upon him, might almost as well lose his life as lose his job, his only security-that is the way things are to-day, as I read the returns of the boards of health. In fact the trades and labour council of Toronto, in presenting a resolution the other day to the board of control, dealt with this matter of health in relation to unemployment and the damage resulting from it, in dooming thousands to a life of permanent ill health. I know the matter was commented upon; I have here the reports of the board of health meeting and other health reports, but I do not wish to read them now because I have only another thirty minutes in which to speak. As I said last night, I am not a continuing Presbyterian, therefore I am limited to forty minutes.
I should be sorry to see this made a party question. It has never been so treated by me, because I believe that the care and welfare of our people and the health and peace of our citizens constitute the first duty of a government. We have been asssembled here some sixty-four or sixty-five days, and have appointed committees of all kinds, but in my opinion the most important which we could appoint would be a labour or an employment committee. We have many committees and they are not functioning the way they should. Let me say that this country does not belong alone to those who at present inhabit it. It is an inheritance from the past, a possession for the present, and a trust for the future. After all is said and done, the wealth of Canada is not comprised solely in our magnificent natural resources, our raw materials, our chain of great lakes, our splendid harbours, the products of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mine, our great transportation system by land and sea and

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
in the air. There is a more glorious treasure than that in the character of our people and in maintaining their morale. That is what is being destroyed to-day by this canker of unemployment in the state and the failure of the government to do anything on practical lines to remedy it. The returns brought down by the minister deal largely with the past. They speak of the present to some extent, but so far as the future is concerned, I can find little or nothing in them to offer us any encouragement except a small-sized youth training program. It seems there are two things that the government have been unable to do. They have been unable to look after the youth problem, and they have not taken care of the senior citizens of the country who have borne the heat of the day in the matter of unemployment.
It strikes me that this country is in need of mathematicians who can do some counting up to ten millions, consecutively, of our people, because we have never been able to find out exactly what the population of the country is. We have never had an, exact estimate as a result of any decennial census. The decennial census covers a house to house canvas in urban and rural Canada, but the work is carried out in a deficient sort of way.
