maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for drawing attention to the fact. This is one of the most important questions before the house. I wonder what those hon. gentlemen who are carrying on conversations, who are talking to their neighbours, are going to tell the people when they get back to their constituencies of what jobs we have found in Canada for Canadians. What are they going to tell the people are the concrete views of 245 members of parliament in regard to the all-important question of getting jobs for those who are out of work? The greatest problem which faces Canada to-day is that of providing work for unemployed Canadians, but what have we been doing here? May I ask the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley)? This matter concerns his department; as head of that department he has something to do with it. I should like also to get the attention of some of the other ossified conservatives sitting on government front benches-gentlemen who are opposed to adopting practical measures for the solution of the problem. They are by the commission route divesting the House of Commons of its rights, privileges and prerogatives. Instead of helping parliament to discharge its responsibilities, the government are appointing numerous commissions. There are so many officials and employees in connection with all these-commissions that if they lined up two abreast the line would reach from here to Lansdowne park. That is the object and reason for appointing these commissions, to prevent any actions being taken here, and they do this admirably. The government appointed the Purvis commission and that body brought in a report, which was not acted on except in a small way. One hon. gentleman flung the report on the floor, and in my opinion that is the proper place for it, the wastepaper basket, because it was nothing but a copy of some of the findings of the Couzens report submitted to the United States senate fifteen years ago. The Purvis report, on its presentation, was referred to another Doomsday commission, the Rowell commission, which is still on its rounds and still not doing anything.
This government seem to think they can relieve unemployment by adopting a lot of trade pacts, but as far as I can see these trade agreements simply aggravate the situation. They create unemployment instead of providing work, because they are destroying our own markets for our own Canadian products and our own work for our own workmen, and depriving Canadian workmen of employment at home. Is it any wonder there is unemployment in our industrial centres? No business man is going to extend his activities so long as we have tariff tinkering and numerous trade pacts, with consequent instability in industry and commerce, and widespread unemployment.
One important matter that calls for the consideration of parliament at the present time, in view of the emergency that exists in the world to-day, is the defence problem. After all, as Adam Smith said, security is better than opulence. I suggest therefore that it would be better to deal with the government's program for the expenditure of 863,000,000 next Monday or at once, and pass that at any rate. It would provide some immediate employment, and the time spent in the discussion of the matters involved in that program would not be wasted, because we may be actually face to face with the enemy at any moment. Who can tell? May first is only two weeks off.
The heavy burdens of relief, hospitalization and other things of that sort are hampering the business man to-day and threatening the municipal institutions of the provinces. The situation is so highly unsatisfactory that no one wants to own real estate. Real estate at the present time is groaning under an incubus of heavy taxation in consequence of a state of

Un'employment and Agricultural Distress
over-taxation and over-government in the country, with tens of thousands of Canadians out of work through no fault of the municipalities of Canada. This widespread unemployment throughout the land is having its effect on property owners and the federal burdens imposed wrongly on cities and towns. Confiscation of property is at times being carried out extensively and property owners are reeling under high mortgage and interest rates and other heavy charges. And the shark loan companies add to the evil. Yet nothing is being done here by the government to relieve this situation or hold an inquiry into these excessive rates. The municipalities were here all this week and when they asked for bread they were given a stone. Relief to them was denied and deferred, presumably until the Rowell commission's report is received, which will amount to nothing. It has cost, up to January 1, 1939, $357,500, and more would have been accomplished by a round table conference with the provinces.
Canada to-day is threatened from within by unemployment. Indeed, it is threatening the existence of confederation, the British empire, and the party system, because nothing is being done to solve the problem and to deal with the question of distributism. The government is doing nothing to remove the evils of the capitalist system and to provide work for the unemployed. On Febuary 17, 1936, I brought forward a motion dealing with this matter and it was debated from 3.20 in the afternoon until 6 o'clock and again throughout the evening. But, as usual, nothing was done. The motion was as follows:
That in the opinion of this house, Canada should immediately adopt a comprehensive national housing building reconstruction, renovation, slum clearance land settlement and reforestation policy adopted to its circumstances, and also embracing as one of its main features a national policy for youth in relation to education and industry and employment, so as to get people off the dole and back to remunerative employment.
And further, that this house is also of the opinion that in any such national reconstruction policy a lower rate structure for bank mortgage and insurance loans is an immediate necessity. Such a reconstruction policy to also embrace protection for industrial workers in urban and suburban areas from forfeiture on the same principle as farmers and fishermen are now' afforded by existing legislation.
So far as Toronto is concerned, little or nothing is being done there to relieve the overburdened taxpayers, those who contribute over 90 millions of revenue to this government, or to help them. The work that is being done in connection with the Island and Malton airports, both construction and maintenance, is being borne by Toronto, whereas in other places, Canada pays for it; and so fMr. Church.)
far as post office facilities are concerned, although a very large percentage of the postal revenue, over seven millions, comes from that city, we cannot get a proper new mail order building. On March 13, 1939, I received from the Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty), in answer to a letter I had written him regarding the new Toronto post office building at Fleet and Bay streets, a communication in which he informed me that the plans had been prepared and the Department of Public Works advised that they expected that tenders would be asked for that week.
' We are getting little or no assistance from the dominion government. I believe in the principle of confederation of each for all and all for each, but I do not want to see Ontario and Toronto made the goat of confederation for taxation purposes and not getting anything in return; and if the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act does not make satisfactory provision for Ontario, I suggest that the sooner it is amended by the Minister of Finance to take care of the situation in that province, the better it will be for all concerned. Where a province fails to take advantage of this act the federal government should take steps to see that equality of treatment is maintained throughout the country and thus Toronto would get aid for its trunk sewer. Many cities and towns in Ontario have made applications for assistance under this act but they are getting nothing because Ottawa and Queen's Park cannot agree. I have a return showing what has been done in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island under this act but there is not a cent for the city of Toronto.
The minister has announced that if the province of Ontario will agree to a dollar for dollar payment on the Toronto sewage disposal plant lie will take action. In this connection I should like to read the following item from the Toronto Telegram of Thursday, April 13, from the reply of the Ontario legislature to the proposal of the federal Minister of Labour.
Premier Mitchell Hepburn angrily rejected to-day the proposal of Hon. Norman Rogers that the two governments should contribute "dollar for dollar" for the cost of Toronto's new sewage disposal plant. The Ontario premier branded the federal labour minister's offer as "a barefaced attempt to bribe the voters of Toronto on the eve of an election."
"If he thinks he can get us into such a deal -into competitive spending-just to bolster his dying government he has another think coming," the premier declared.
"Why didn't Mr. Rogers make such generous offers long ago, long before an election was in sight? Both Toronto and Ontario have been paying far more than their fair share of relief

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
costs because Mr. Rogers callously refused enough assistance. Now he thinks he can bribe the city on the eve of an election. Such a barefaced attempt is an insult to the intelligence of the people of Toronto."
That is the opinion of the premier of the province, and the provincial leader of the opposition, Colonel Drew, the other day spoke in much the same strain about Ontario and the need of helping real estate, of overgovernment, and of Ontario being made the goat in the matter of taxation and receiving practically nothing from the federal power in return for all the federal taxes it pays. I have some protests here from the building trades unions and officers of the stone industry, which I have not had time to read yet, concerning the harm done to the construction industries if this post office building is not proceeded with, because it would mean work for two or three thousand men. The delay in building for postal reasons cannot last much longer because the province needs this post office, and the Post Office Department needs that public utility there, where nearly thirty per cent of the postal revenues come from, for the efficiency of the sendee.
I asked for a report about the Alien Labour Act and unemployment in Canada, but I find the departments are utterly helpless to regulate it. The question I asked was in regard to the enforcement of the Alien Labour Act and the number of aliens who have been admitted under the said act in 1937, 1938 and 1939. The justice department in the return say they have no information and they start to plead the rules of the house, some of which are more than a hundred years old. They say that question number two appears to relate to a matter of policy. The Department of Mines and Resources say:
This department is not aware that any department of the dominion government is charged with the enforcement of the Alien Labour Act.
Anyone seems to be able to come here and without taking out naturalization papers take employment away from our own citizens. Did you ever hear of such an absurd way of enforcement? As far as immigration is concerned they have no information. Immigrants are admitted to Canada from many alien places under the Immigration Act and they get jobs and remain un-naturalized. The non-enforcement of that act has led to a great deal of unemployment in the industrial cities of Ontario and Quebec.
One of the most important things the minister has overlooked is the export of brains from this country. Canada should utilize the talents of its youth as one of its greatest natural resources. I referred to this two or three years ago in connection with the mining
estimates; the thousands in the universities, high schools and the technical schools could go into the north country during the summer and learn a great deal about our natural resources in mines and minerals, and prospect and help develop our great natural resources.
What is more distressing or more pathetic than to see men willing and able to work, at the peak of their physical and mental capacity, unable to get employment because of the governing policy of industry which discourages the employment of middle-aged men, over forty-five years of age. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has said that we are on the eve of an election. Of course we are. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) tells the municipalities that nothing can be done about unemployment relief until the Rowell commission presents its report. When the commission does present it, it will be sent to the archives and that will be the last heard of it. It will be committed to the ground of the archives, earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; that will be the last we shall hear of this famous report. They have already buried the Purvis report. But on the other side of the ledger what do we find? We had the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), when a motion was adopted appointing a committee to deal with crop insurance, rising in his place with a resolution and a bill to provide for the very crop insurance, before the committee met at all. That is the way in which we deal with crops, material things, but how do w7e deal with humans? In England they have had unemployment insurance since 1909; it was part of the Liberal platform at the Ottawa convention in 1919, yet we have not got it to-day. If we had, unemployment would have been reduced.
In January of last year there was a byelection in Montreal, and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) on January 5, 1938, must be mind-readers; for they told the electors that the Canadian National station in Montreal would be gone on with, notwithstanding the duplication it involves. Nothing more was heard until December 5, 1938, eleven months later, when the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways approved the project, an order in council, P.C. 746, was passed, and in March of this year work was begun. Up to December 31, 1938, they had spent $16,651,000, and since then, $12,862,343, or a total of $29,513,343, over the head of parliament and without regard to the coordination of the railways, and now it is proposed to spend a further $12,500,000 for a terminal that is not needed.
2790	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
What has become of cooperation between the railways? Where does the taxpayer stand while all this wasteful expenditure goes on over the heads of parliament and the railway board?
In the city of Toronto a home for transient unemployed was started by the Reverend John Frank. A man like him should be congratulated upon what he has done for the unemployed. I have here a picture taken in the parish house of Holy Trinity church, Toronto, last Christmas week showing the unemployed sleeping on the floor where they had been for several weeks. To-day many of these men are in the new John Frank home and going on a John Frank farm, and others are in the coliseum. I have not time to read the letter or what has been said in reference to it. A couple of Sundays ago these men marched to St. Paul's Anglican church, and Reverend Doctor Sclater then declared that it was a surprise to him when he first came to Canada to learn that in this country the one place where a man could be sure of getting food and a bed was the gaol. And Sir William Mulock said:
I do not know the solution to the problem, but what an unspeakable condition it is when our fellow citizens must go into the ice and cold to-night with no homes and through no fault of their own.
Yet literally nothing is done. This week there has been a meeting here in Ottawa of the Canadian mayors, and they laid on the door-step of parliament the Whole question of Canada's most important problem, unemployment. Unless this parliament bestirs itself, lack of employment will disrupt confederation and threaten the fate of the British empire. Those who have been engaged in municipal work-and theTe are many in this house-are brought daily face to face with this problem. The loss of a man's job is fatal to him, he loses his whole outlook on life, through fear and lack of security his health is destroyed. These worries prey on him day and night and are a nightmare to him.
I fail to find any actual measure taken by this government to cope with this problem. We have a war in Canada to-day, a war between millions of our fellow men and poverty and starvation. This enemy is just as dangerous-as I said in my remarks on a similar resolution on April 1, 1936-as a foreign foe in war-time. Against a foreign foe we unite, but against our internal foe we are disunited, and do nothing to check or repel this enemy. When the invader is at our gates the country mobilizes its entire resources, its man power, its transportation system, its capital, but in times of depression and unemployment, driving people to the wall, the industrial workers are left without

any protection at all. The workers bear the brunt and we do nothing but sit around and appoint commissions.
Nothing is said in this bill as to the relation between the industrial and the agricultural worker.
The mayors were told yesterday that the federal relief policy stands pending the report of the Rowell commission, who have been all round the world collecting information which was already known and available. This commission should be instructed to hand in its report at once. When it is received it will be consigned to the archives. That is one of the reasons why these commissions are appointed, namely to postpone action by the government of the day on Canada's most vital problems.
The first of May is only two weeks away. So far we have had the ambassadors' cure for unemployment, the professors' cure for unemployment, the Purvis 'commission's cure for unemployment, and the Rowell commission's cure costing $357,000, and the sum total of their efforts has been to befog and becloud the facts and prevent this high court of parliament from dealing with the problem.
One of the main causes of unemployment has been the destruction of the home market. The Liberal policy has been to rely on a multiplicity of trade treaties. This policy has been weighed in the balance and found wanting, and we see the result in the present impossible economic conditions in Canada. The youth of the country coming out of the high schools, whose only fault is that they cannot secure a job, are left to take to the roads all over Canada, or ride the rods in search of employment. The government's policy is one of inertia, coma, inaction, drifting, evasion, postponement, somnambulism and refusal to face the facts or the actual situation.
I have some constructive suggestions to give the government regarding unemployment. In a country with the natural resources and abundant raw material that Canada has, no one should be out of work. Bonuses, subventions, subsidies have been created for coal so that Canada may use more coal from the maritimes, Alberta and Wales. This policy was launched in 1922 on a resolution introduced by me. Notwithstanding the free trade policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, that policy has created employment. In my opinion this policy should be followed only where work is created. The machine has taken the place of labour on the prairies, in Canada's basic industry. It is being utilized more on the prairies in everyday life and in the United States and Canada, and there are no countries in the world where want and waste have

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
been more clearly evidenced or where more unemployment has been caused. We hear a great deal about the building trades. We are doing nothing to get armament contracts. The other day an air force contract for $60,000,000 went to San Francisco. We are not getting food contracts from Britain's rearmament program ; they are going to Australia and the United States. Little or nothing has been done to establish food reservoirs either in Canada or in England for emergency reasons, and at the present time Great Britain has two thousand fewer merchant ships to transport food from Canada and from overseas than she had before the great war. Canada spent over a million dollars on some of her government merchant marine ships, some of which were sold only recently for $50,000. These could have been converted into food vessels and rearmament cargo boats, which would have been of assistance to Great Britain in an emergency, because she imports 90 per cent of her food and 95 per cent of her raw materials. We got nowhere in all this, which would have helped unemployment.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, something should be done to provide work by reopening peacetime shipping plants and converting them into marine buildings for defence purposes, for rearmament and shipbuilding purposes and for storing defence materials.
The Conservative party has been consistent in upholding the doctrine that one of the causes of unemployment has been the destruction of Canada's home markets for the products of its own workmen. The removal of the 3 per cent excise tax, the uncertainty, instability and tariff tinkering, have led business men to reduce staffs and have caused great and widespread unemployment, especially in the industrial cities. The same can be said in regard to the building trades.
I would like to say a word or two in relation to industrial employment, because I want to contrast with the precepts of Christianity the way the industrial workers are used. Contrast our professions with the ruthless competition, the cruelty and vice of present day business and industry. Here personality counts as nothing, the dollar is all supreme. Modern life is machine life, soulless, a life of standardization, high speed production, a highly efficient organization for the making of profit. Everything is done in the mass, and life is made uniform, monotonous and artificial. Dividends are the chief objective; to get dividends human beings are sacrificed. Wages are shockingly low, often below the level of mere subsistence, so that people are forced into immoral and criminal ways of life to eke out a precarious livelihood. The maximum 71492-176
in hours of work is exacted in return for the minimum in wages. Senior employees, whose lifeblood has been drawn from them by long years of faithful service, are in many cases cast out without retiring allowance to make room for younger and cheaper people. It matters not what suffering is entailed for human beings so long as the stockholders are paid their dividends. This amazing selfishness and shortsightedness of the modern industrial system is creating a progressively lower standard of living and a vicious struggle for existence philosophy on the part of the people, increasingly serious social problems which must find their tragic solution either in war or in revolution. In the face of modern methods of competitive living the royal law of love, bear ye one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ, is a hollow mockery in Canada, presumably a Christian country. This is the contradiction of modem life: a truly wonderfid appreciation of the value of the single soul in some quarters, but an absolute denial of any such value in others.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me unemployment is the most important question before the people of Canada to-day. Trade pacts are important only as they make for a higher standard of living for the masses. Elaborate government machinery is worse than useless if it serves merely to protect the privileges of the few or, as is often the case, permits and assists the few to exploit the nation. The welfare of the common man must be the measure of the success of any democratic government, and measured by this standard I am afraid this government has failed. In his speech on March 15 the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) stated that the government was charged with responsibility. Well, that means the government must necessarily assume responsibility for the conditions that exist to-day, and the only way we can hope to improve the situation is by bringing the facts home to the government.
I do not intend to burden the record with further statistics; statistics have been given in abundance by the minister and by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). As a matter of fact I feel weary of trying to portray the conditions which are known to all, and still more weary of listening to the apologies of the government. Granted that they have set up many projects; granted that they have assisted the provinces, granted too that they face a difficult world situation-as I see it the fact is that the government is not meeting or facing the situation. The minister pleaded certain constitutional difficulties and said that he had little patience with those who urged that the

2792	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
constitution should not be allowed to stand in the way. He read me a lecture. Well, if I may say so, I have little patience with those who magnify the difficulties of the constitution, or who insist on a narrow interpretation, or who place the letter of the constitution ahead of the present needs of the people. The minister has been generous enough to credit me with being one of the pioneers in the movement seeking amendments to the British North America Act, but let me say that no small portion of our difficulties arises because of the indefensible interpretations that have been placed upon that act. For example, only recently have women been recognized as "persons" under the terms of the act, and other similar absurd interpretations have been expressed. Our most pressing needs-and I believe even this question of unemployment-can be met under the act as it now stands. It is true that contributory insurance could not be enacted under the British North America Act, but under existing circumstances contributory insurance is no solution and indeed is not possible. The difficulties are not primarily those of jurisdiction.
The minister's next line of defence was that our difficulties were due to the international situation, and he spoke of economic nationalism. Undoubtedly our difficulties are aggravated by economic nationalism, but I submit that they are due to much more fundamental causes. Speaking of economic nationalism, the other day I came across a curious statement which illustrates its weaknesses even in regard to those countries that have adopted it:
According to Mr. Strachey, economic paralysis due to lack of markets had reached a tragic but amusing extreme in Holland, which illustrated the impasse to which capitalism has come. He told how, to mitigate unemployment, a part of the Zuyder Zee was drained as a "public works" project. The reclaimed land produced an excellent wheat crop, but the government did not know what to do with the wheat. It was finally sold at a low rate to the Danish government, which resold it to the Danish hog raisers as pig feed. It produced wonderful hogs which could not be sold, and were boiled down for fertilizer. Frantic search for markets finally resulted in the sale of the fertilizer, to the Dutch government very cheaply, and it was put back on the reclaimed land of the Zuyder Zee, whence the wheat had come to raise the hogs to produce the fertilizer.
It is in somewhat similar circumstances that we find ourselves at the present time.

speechtext:
From a review of
a book by Mr. Strachey. Despite all this, the minister goes back to his phrases of returning confidence, greater production and expanding

markets, and declares that never at any time has he or the government adopted an attitude of defeat or despair. Well, it is fine if the minister can maintain his morale; it is fine if the government can maintain its morale, but what about the 662,000 persons receiving nonagricultural aid, these being totally unemployable, partially employable or fully employable, together with their dependents? What about the 316,000 persons on agricultural relief? What about the additional thousands who are not on relief but who should be? What about the thousands of young people dependent upon friends and relatives? What about the men in camps and on farms, without adequate remuneration and with no hope? I wonder what about their morale and how they can maintain it under those conditions?
I suggest that not only is the government on trial and that it has failed lamentably to meet the situation; more important still, the present economic system is on trial. And as long as we as a parliament refuse to face this situation and deal effectively with it, in reality we are undermining the very foundation of the representative institutions of democracy. A warning came a few weeks ago, from the Monetary Times of February 4, 1939. I read two or three brief paragraphs:
When the Prime Minister says in the House of Commons that there is no way to deal effectively with the perplexing problem of unemployment in Canada because it is a worldwide condition, he but sends more people in search of someone who will tackle this condition with the will to get results. When the leader of the opposition finds three hours insufficient to bring out even one valuable point of constructive criticism in regard to the government's moribund policy, he but destroys what little there was left of hope in the possible leadership which might have been offered by the Conservative party. Either the country must turn to the socialistic doctrines of the C.C.F. or to the weird conceptions of the social credit group, or construct completely new political machinery upon which it can depend for constructive policy and sound administrative action.
The country might thrive under a C.C.F. regime, and certainly it is a growing political force. Conditions might be better under social credit. Prosperity might come as the result of dictatorship. But whatever happens, the change in the administrative policies of Canada will be the result of old party bungling and the inattention to internal problems on the part of the present government.

speechtext: I am quoting from the Monetary Times of February 4, 1939.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: By whom?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I think it is an editorial. It was published in Toronto and

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
can ibe readily looked up. I read this further paragraph:
True, the people of Canada do not want a dictatorship. The majority do not want a brand of radical socialism. But they do want an end of inactivity on the part of government, and some indication that the present government has a clear-cut policy with which to dissipate the serious internal problems of unemployment, unsatisfactory administrative relations between the provinces and the dominion, destructive taxation and the general want of confidence..
In short, the people want their problems and their needs put first and political party fortunes last.
I am not accusing the government of putting their own political fortunes first, but I do say that whatever the motive is, the government is failing to meet this very pressing problem.
The article to which I have referred speaks about the straightening up of dominion-provincial relations. Well, the government has told us again and again that it has appointed a commission. We were told a little while ago that the royal commission would report during this session of parliament. Then, later we were told that the commission found it impossible to do so, and that presentation of the report would be put off until after the prorogation of parliament. We are told, further, that probably the next step would be to secure some sort of constitutional conference in which the dominion and the provinces would be represented. That is the way the thing goes on. Now we are told it will not be possible thoroughly to discuss these immediate and practical problems because the king is coming, and it would be highly desirable that we should have the unique opportunity of having the king prorogue parliament. And so it would appear the discussion of these problems is to ibe curtailed.
Well, I would point out that whilst we take leisurely step after step after step and condone delay after delay, the people are suffering. I am not here to say whether or not the hon. member for Greenwood was quite correct in the statement he -made with regard to the number who are dying because of malnutrition, or because of accident and neglect. But anyone who has visited the hostels of this country, anyone who has visited the hospitals of this country, anyone who has visited the homes of the poor in the country, anyone who has been up and down the railroads and heard the stories of the boys who are riding the rods, knows perfectly well that scores, if not hundreds, have died through no other reason than the public neglect of the unemployed.

No, I am not going to present evidence for the minister. I said 71492-176^
it was my opinion, and my statement is perfectly in order. I said anyone who had been around the country and has heard the stories of these men from their own lips, who has visited the homes of the people, who has visited hospitals, knows that people have died of neglect. maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: One other question. Will he not acknowledge that other members of the house have shared the experience to which he has just referred?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, possibly; but I cannot quite understand how other members of the house can differ from my conclusions in that regard. I am not accusing the minister of heartlessness. Of course I am not. I knew him before he came to this house, and I know him too well to say that. But, to be perfectly frank-possibly it is because I have not been in a position of responsibility as a member of the cabinet-I have often wondered whether, because of the numerous duties which are placed upon ministers of the cabinet, it has not become almost impossible or, shall I say very difficult, for them to see the picture as it is. I sometimes wonder whether or not they are too dependent upon the reports of their officials, and whether they are not too close to the figures to grasp the human meaning of those figures. I have been almost inclined to interpret the situation in that way.
I say that because I cannot look across at the minister, or at other members of the cabinet, and think that they are less humane than those of us who happen to be sitting on this side of the house. I think the minister will absolve me from any suggestion that I am saying this merely to reap political advantage. I am not doing that. But I have had the opportunity of meeting with a great many of these people, and not merely during the term of office of this government. Unfortunately I have had to say much the same things during the term of the preceding government-and long, long years before that. In fact, I was dealing with similar conditions long before I ever came to this House of Commons.
This is not a recent problem. We have had unemployment with us for years and years- yes, even during the great rush in immigration days there were large numbers' of unemployed. But we all know that in recent years the unemployment situation has been greatly aggravated. I believe one of the troubles is that most of us are still going largely on the supposition that if a man is out of a job it is more or less his own fault. In the old days that was to a great extent
2794	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
true, but it is not true to-day. There is no doubt that a person with exceptional ability and exceptional perseverance will land a job ahead of others. But where one man in a hundred gets his job, the other ninety-nine are out of work. While a lot of our young people are getting along fairly well in life, a great many others have yet to get their first job.
It seems to me we must disabuse our minds of the old ideas which prevailed when we were children, and recognize to-day that this unemployment situation is in aggravated form. W'e must deal with it as it is. We must be fair to those unfortunate people, and deal with their problem at whatever cost to the public treasury! W'e talk about $63,000,000 for defence purposes; I do not feel like voting one dollar for defence purposes so long as there is a hungry man in Canada.
It seems to me we must adjust our scale of values in this matter. Sometimes we talk as if we could set this responsibility aside, and that the decision as to whether or not we deal with the problem is one which depends upon the generosity of governments. It is nothing of the kind. We come back to what I said in starting, that the success of a democratic government is surely measured by the way in which it deals with the unemployed.
A colleague has just handed me a note which I shall read:
At the moment there are approximately two hundred single unemployed men in front of the arliament buildings seeking to lay their case efore the minister. Seventy-five of their number are without provision for food and shelter.
I have not been out doors. The minister asked for my evidence. In this instance I have this evidence, this note which has just been passed to me by my colleague; that is all.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

Will my hon. friend permit me, because my name has been mentioned? A few moments ago I was called from the chamber to meet two of his colleagues, who quite properly presented to me a request that I should meet a delegation from these single unemployed men. Some days before I had met the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who had made a similar request to me. I told him then that it was not possible or desirable from an administrative point of view that a federal Minister of Labour should meet local delegations from the city of Ottawa, that it had never been done, and it would not make for successful administration. I said that if these men through their association wished to communicate anything to me by way of letter I would be pleased to receive it and would

deal with it courteously, and I would be pleased also to ' vr mv representation^ they wished to make through members of this house who approached me. At Uie same time, Mr. Speaker, I believe my original decision was right, not to meet local delegations of unemployed men. I explained that decision to my colleagues, and I propose to adhere to it. But that does not in any way suggest a lack of consideration for these men. I have made it perfectly clear that I shall be ready at any time to receive any communication they desire to make to me by letter or through my hon. friend or his colleagues.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am not criticizing the minister's policy; that is for him to decide, but I read this statement to call attention to the actual facts of the situation. The statement is made that there are two hundred single unemployed men in front of the parliament buildings and that seventy-five of their number are without provisions. I say that I have not been outside to investigate, and I ask the minister to take the statement as it has been given to me to-day and as I have just given it, that there are two hundred unemployed men outside the parliament buildings. I have only to go to my own city of Winnipeg to find similar conditions, only in much more aggravated form. I have been across this country and I find the same conditions everywhere. There are these two hundred men in front of our doors to-day, and the minister says: "I cannot do anything about it officially; I cannot meet them because that is not a good policy." But what are these men to do? My colleague suggests that they should write a letter to the minister. They have written letters until they are sick and tired of writing letters.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: My hon. friend has asked me a question: What are these men to do? I share his desire that they might find their way as soon as possible into employment, not necessarily public employment, but employment in which they would have an opportunity to earn a remunerative and self-respecting living.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Just where?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
In the last year some
fifteen hundred men from the employment office in the city of Ottawa were placed on farms in this area and at this time of year additional employment is being offered in connection with various government services. All who register at the employment office are eligible for that work.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I know they are
eligible, but it does not make any difference

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
whether fifteen hundred or fifteen thousand men were placed in employment last summer. The fact is that at the present time there are two hundred men waiting outside this building, and seventy-five of them have no means of eating. Is nothing to be done about them? That is the condition which prevails all over this country from Cape Breton right across to Victoria. Every mail that comes to me brings me further evidence of this kind of thing. What is to be done? The fact is the minister has no plan to meet the situation. The minister and the government say: If we cannot do it, we refer it to the provinces; and if the provinces cannot do it they refer it to the municipalities. The municipalities turn round and refer it back to the provinces, and the provinces to the dominion. In the meantime the men suffer physically-and they suffer demoralization. I must leave it at that I
Before my line of thought was interrupted a few minutes ago I was referring to some of the underlying factors that enter into the situation. The unemployment situation has been developing over a number of years-long before we ever heard of economic nationalism, which the minister has stressed. I quote a paragraph or two from Census Monograph No. 9. on the Dependency of Youth, published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, a document cited yesterday by the hon. member for Greenwood:
The average young person on reaching the age of 20 in 1911 had earned twice as much as those reaching 20 in 1931.
Social effects of the increased dependency are suggested by the unusual fall in the marriage rate among young people between 20 and 24 years of age (20 per cent for men and 13 per cent for women) as well as in the 100 per cent increase in the illegitimate birth rate from 1921 to 1931.
Again:
The development of large-scale enterprise has increased the proportion of wage-earners to independent workers.
An attempt is made to gain a conception of the actual number of boys and young men of ages 15-24 lacking gainful occupation in 1936. The combined percentage of those without work due either to loss of employment or to never having been gainfully occupied appears to be over 16 per cent; in round numbers, this group approximates 155,000. or one and one-half times the supply of new workers coming of age annually. Since nearly all of this group are non-farm boys, the average length of idleness for boys living in the city appears to be about two years.
The fact that industry for so long has come 10 per cent short of using the biological supply of youth, should make it clear that the youth situation is not just a depression phenomenon but a deeply rooted problem.
That is what I would impress upon this government. Let me quote from another
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
source, which may seem a little remote at first glance, the conclusion of the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada, at page 17:
ft seems safe to say that in the present state of international relationships broad recovery in the section of the economy to which I have referred is unlikely to be rapid. It therefore seems obvious that unemployment in its existing proportions cannot be regarded as entirely, or even chiefly, a short-term problem.
What are we doing about it year after year? Just shifting the problem a little bit ahead of us. meeting some of the more immediate pressing needs; if possible, cutting a certain number of people off relief or praying that spring may come and that some will be turned loose to forage for themselves.
I ask the minister: Is the international situation a provincial matter? Is the international situation a municipal matter? If not, can the municipalities be held responsible for those long-term widely-planned measures which alone can meet the situation? In the meantime should one-tenth of our population be allowed to suffer just because there have been international difficulties that have interrupted the regular course of trade and commerce or closed some of our markets to us? We have in this country all that is necessary to supply the needs of the Canadian people. We have our natural resources; we have capital equipment-the stored up wealth through which we can produce more wealth; we have money, whatever that is; and we have men. The trouble is a lack of proper economic arrangements. Fundamentally we have it within our own power to alter the present economic arrangements; but that this government will not do, and so they identify themselves with the maintenance of this antiquated economic system.
I should like to quote a few paragraphs from an article by a prominent economist, Professor Broadus Mitchell, associate professor of political economy, Johns Hopkins university, appearing in Current History, in its issue of February, 1935:
Social insurance is not enough because of fundamental defects in our prevailing mode of producing and distributing wealth. No insurance plan can be more solvent than the economic structure upon which it rests. Insurance means converting individual uncertainty into collective certainty. But when wre try to include the great mass of the population we suddenly discover that there is no social certainty. In other words, when we make the sum of the risks practically identical with the social causes of those risks insurance becomes impossible. As Mary Van Kleeck has said, "insurance conceived as provision in advance for needs which, though not foreseeable for the individual are measurable for the social group, breaks down
2796	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
when needs are no longer foreseeable on the basis of past experience but are expressed in a change of social trends." . . .
Our economic ups and clowns are not due to the eccentricities of nature. . . . Our vexation arises from the failure of our price-and-profit system to work in harmony with our productive capacities. . . .
What this system needs is not more plant, more production, but a relative enlargement of consumption. . . .
. . . but cyclical and technological unemployment burst all bounds. The beginning of wisdom in meeting these terrifying disorders is the recognition that they are inherent in the capitalist economic system. . . .
I cannot see that we shall get any further in solving the problem of unemployment or in straightening out the anomalies of our present arrangements in Canada until we as a people recognize that we must make fundamental adjustments in our whole economic system. I continue:
Men, since they learned to exchange goods and use money, have entertained three successive conceptions of wealth. The Mercantilists considered that wealth was cash. The laissez faire school thought and still thinks that wealth is commodities. The collectivists, their preachments at length confirmed by the march of events, know that wealth consists in neither cash nor commodities but in capacities. . . .
What we need is to control the energies at our command. We should not be anxious to socialize a part of the product, but resolve to socialize the whole of the power. . . .
The task of placing goods at the use of consumers is hindered at every turn by allegiance to the capitalist mode of production and distribution, which has become increasingly unworkable. . . .
Social security will proceed from economic stability and steady progress. This requires planning, and planning requires unquestioned control by organized society over the means of production.
I turn from the economic aspect of the case and I urge that at bottom this is a moral problem. It involves fundamental questions as regards both our economic system and the state itself. Recently there have been many eulogies of the late pope. May I pay my tribute :by quoting from him and thus seek to spread his teachings. I think I quoted some years ago a few passages from the encyclical letter Quadragesimo Anno on the reconstruction of the social order. The situation is outlined:
Towards the close of the nineteenth century the new economic methods and the new development of industry had sprung into being in almost all civilized nations, and had made such headway that human society appeared more and more divided into two classes. The first, small in numbers, enjoyed practically all the comforts so plentifully supplied by modern invention. The second class, comprising the immense multitude of workingmen, was made up of those who, oppressed by dire poverty, struggled in vain to escape from the straits which encompassed them.

This state of things was quite satisfactory to the wealthy, who looked upon it as the consequence of inevitable and natural economic laws, and who, therefore, were content to abandon to charity alone the full care of relieving the unfortunate, as though it were the task of charity to make amends for the open violation of justice, a violation not merely tolerated, but sanctioned at times by legislators. On the other hand, the working classes, victims of these harsh conditions, submitted to them with extreme reluctance, and became more and more unwilling to bear the galling yoke .	.	..	.	. the immense number of propertyless wage-earners on the one hand, and the superabundant riches of the fortunate few on the other, is an unanswerable argument that the earthly goods so abundantly produced in this age of industrialism are far from rightly distributed and equitably shared among the various classes of men.
Having stated the situation, his holiness then goes on to discuss the whole question of the rights of property. He says:
History proves that the right of ownership, like other elements of social life, is not absolutely rigid .	.	.
Again:
For it is rightly contended that certain forms of property must be reserved to the state, since they carry with them an opportunity of domination too great to be left to private individuals without injury to the community at large.
He speaks of the arbitrary power which is now placed in the hands of the few. I quote:
In the first place, then, it is patent that in our days not alone is wealth accumulated, but immense power and despotic economic domination is concentrated in the hands of a few, and that those few are frequently not the owners, but only the trustees and directors of invested funds, who administer them at their good pleasure.
This power becomes particularly irresistible when exercised by those who, because they hold and control money, are able also to govern credit and determine its allotment, for that reason supplying so to speak, the life-blood to the entire economic body, and grasping, as it were, in their hands the very soul of production, so that no one dare breathe against their will.
This accumulation of power, the characteristic note of the modern economic order, is a natural result of limitless free competition which permits the survival of those only who are the strongest, which often means those who fight most relentlessly, who pay least heed to the dictates of conscience.
This concentration of power has led to a three-fold struggle for domination. First, there is the struggle for dictatorship in the economic sphere itself: then, the fierce battle to acquire control of the state, so that its resources and authority may be abused in the economic struggles. Finally, the clash between states themselves.
There is one other brief sentence which I would commend to my fellow members of the Catholic faith, because I believe that the attitude of the church has often been misrepresented. His holiness says:

If these changes continue, it may well come about that gradually the tenets of mitigated socialism will no longer be different from the program of those who seek to reform human society according to Christian principles.
I wish I had time to elaborate on these pregnant statements.
If the problem cannot be solved under the existing economic system, then by all means let us try a new economic system. The minister and the government have no solution under the present economic system.
In the little time which remains to me I should like to quote from a memorandum which was presented by some of the transient unemployed who are connected with the John Frank's house in Toronto, an institution already alluded to to-day by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I do not know that I approve in toto this memorandum, but it struck me that since the unemployed were not able to be present here to put their own case I should like to have the honour of presenting their point of view just as they themselves presented it:
We, the members of John Frank's house, believe that every man should have the right to work and to receive a reasonable living wage for his efforts. We consider that, when potentially employable men are unable to find such work, great harm is done in a very short time both to the nation and to the persons concerned.
At present, many thousands of young Canadians who, during the past few years, left the municipality of their "legal residence" and went in search of work wherever they thought it might be found, are unable to find gainful employment. Many are wasting their youth and becoming prospective public charges by working in temporary jobs like serfs for their keep.
Many more are hungry, ill-clad, without permanent shelter. Undernourished or incorrectly fed, lacking preventive medical treatment, subject to merciless exposure to all seasons, their physical condition has suffered badly. Idle, or trekking a great deal of the time, their ability to do things has slowed down. Their plight, and their numbers, represent a situation many times more grave than federal authorities seem willing to admit.
These men set out to seek work at living wages and, despite the unfortunate effects of their experiences, that is what most of them still want. In our opinion it would be a serious mistake to provide them with relief or hosteliza-tion, except on a very short emergency basis, for such a course, if continued, might convert them into permanent relief seekers. The only answer to their problem is immediate rehabilitation and gainful employment.
Such a solution, on a final basis, may best be found through healthful stimulation of commerce and industry until Canadian business reaches that point where it can provide employment, at living wages, for all who honestly seek it. Such a happy situation, however, may be slow in arriving and at present there is urgent need for speed because idle men become daily less employable.
It seems to us that the only possible immediate solution, which can meet the need adeuately, is to be found in the establishing of works project and training camps on a scale sufficiently large to provide gainful employment for at least 200,000 men.
These camps, however, must be small-each with a capacity of 125 men at most-if they are best to serve their purpose in making selfreliant citizens of their members. These camps should be under the control of the dominion Department of Labour-not of the Department of Defence, and certainly not under the thumb of any self-appointed group of ex-military men or private citizens, however well-meaning.
In direct criticism of existing well-publicized plans for large camps, we submit that large camps become breeding places for discontent. We predict-with confidence based on experience and observation-that the regimentation, necessary for discipline in large camps, would bring immediate and serious trouble from transients. If, however, such regimentation were successful, it would merely increase the difficulty in reestablishing individuals in civil life at the end of their enlistment. In effect, it would fit them for little except continued life in camps or in a standing army. If, however, the underlying purpose of these large camp plans is to increase Canada's standing army, we should suggest, with all sincerity, that the best way to accomplish this would be by increasing the standing army, not by establishing a private army under another name.
To return to our suggestion of small camps, we should recommend that campers be divided into age groups and that the camps be of two types in order to met the distinctly different requirements of these age groups.
One type of camp-a combined work project and training scheme-should be for men under 25 years of age. In these camps, men should be housed, fed, clothed, and paid a wage of a dollar per day. Their daily schedule should be almost equally divided between honest work, under rigid supervision, on useful works projects, and between training of a vocational and educational nature fitting them to enter primary or secondary industry as self-reliant citizens.
A second type of camp, for men of over 25 years of age, should be established on a straight works camp basis, paying 35 cents per hour for work honestly done, less reasonable charges for medical care and housing. Here again, for the good of the men, it would be advisable to make a further division in age groups, setting aside some camps for men over 40 years of age.
It would also seem advisable that some plan were used to provide training for men in industries where skilled craftsmen are needed. It is generally acknowledged that, since the breakdown of the apprentice system in Canada, the source of supply for various types of skilled craftsmen has been cut off. Therefore, we should suggest that a limited number of carefully selected men be chosen from the camps and placed in industry-their salary being shared by government and employer during their training period.
We should also suggest a general housecleaning of government employment bureaus-* a matter which is sadly overdue-so that they might be able to give aggressive and efficient assistance in finding employment for men at the conclusion of their camp work.
I must thank you and the house, Mr. Speaker, for permitting me to finish the memorandum.

speechtext:
Since I have had the honour to represent the constituency of Brant I have spoken nearly every year to a resolution similar to the one at present before the house, and I think I should be remiss in my duty if I did not approach the question from the point of view of an agriculturist. It is possible I may not have that sympathy with the unemployed which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) shows, inasmuch as I have been associated with the farm throughout almost my whole life. Never since the time I left school have I had to face the ravages of unemployment. I have never known in my time what it was not to have something planned for me to do the next morning. That being so, perhaps I should make this qualification, because this is a serious question and we must approach it from the point of view of the actual facts. I qualify my remarks in this way because if I happen to say anything that suggests a want of complete sympathy with those unfortunate people whose lot we are considering, it will be because I have not experienced the difficulties which the unemployed of Canada are facing to-day.
May I also preface my remarks by congratulating the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) upon his able presentation. I regret very much that he is not in the house at present. I sat patiently for four hours yesterday listening to him, and I was greatly impressed with his ability to express his thoughts in such splendid phraseology. It is a great privilege to have that ability. His quick retorts to interruptions were also masterful. I noticed that he was extremely resourceful, because when he could not make a reply that was pertinent to the question, he would attempt to quote the classics. His frequent references to Shakespeare reminded me of my limited acquaintance with the classics, gained in an elementary education. After he aspired for the leadership of the great National Conservative party I was reminded of the immortal lines of Gray to the effect that:
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen,
And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
I am prompted to make a few observations by the fact that so many of the speeches to which we have listened emanated from the great industrial centres. From my point of view one tragic feature which has greatly aggravated the situation is the fact that the young people have been lured from the farms to the cities. I am inclined to the view that if the conditions prevailed to-day that we had thirty or even twenty years ago, when 
sixty per cent of the population of Canada was on the land, we should not have the present distress.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
May I ask the
hon. member, suppose we had sixty per cent of the entire population on the land, where would they find markets for their production?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should be intelligent enough to answer that question himself.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: We will turn the clock back thirty years for you.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: First of all, if the lord had seen fit to put Adam and Eve in a city he would have built a city for them. But he did not do so; he put them on the farm, and in view of the profession of the hon. member before he came into politics-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: He did not put them on a farm, he put them in a garden.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
What is a farm for? A farm is a place on which to make a living, it is a place where one can produce for oneself food, clothing and shelter by the application of labour. I do not know that it necessarily follows that because there are more people on the farm production increases to such an extent that there is more to sell than people can consume. But I do believe it would be very much better if this unemployed ten per cent of the population were back on the farm at least making their own living, growing their own food; then those on the farm to-day would not be taxed, as I contend they are as wealth creators, to maintain a standard of living for the unemployed which is out of all proportion to that of those who are maintaining them. If they were producing their own living we would not have to make it for them. That is my answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, whether or not it satisfies him. But I am convinced that this would be a solution of the major part of our problem.
I should like also to comment upon the contribution of the hon. member for Greenwood yesterday. Unfortunately he spoiled it by an extravagant statement, the sort of thing which has a tendency to undermine our institutions. He waxes eloquent about his high motives and ideals, so it was especially unfortunate that he spoiled a masterpiece in that way. I feel that a large part of the difficulty we have in Canada to-day is on account of the fact that we have lured young men to the city by contributing so much in the form

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
of relief. I do not want to be misunderstood, I do not begrudge any contribution we are giving to these unfortunate people-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Who does the hon. member mean by "we?"

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is a condition of affairs that has trained them to stand on the street comers instead of doing something for themselves. We have crowded people together in great numbers in the industrial centres, and they are something like the young birds in the spring, with their mouths open for the elders to drop worms in them; I am afraid that is the condition of affairs we are creating. I do not blame them for it, but I say that we are encouraging this condition of affairs, to the detriment of those who are on the farms, and so aggravating a serious situation. I think that the party to which the hon. member for Greenwood belongs has perhaps contributed largely to that unfortunate condition by the special legislation which it passed in 1930 when $20,000,000 was set aside for no other purpose than the dole. They started in this country a condition of affairs which my own leader warned could only bring about the situation that exists to-day.
The hon. member for Greenwood professed disappointment regarding the accomplishments of certain social legislation which in his view would have gone a long way towards solving our problem. We have no unemployment insurance to-day, and I believe the reason is partly that the confidence of the provinces was destroyed by the fact that legislation was attempted to be forced upon them which they felt involved a surrender of their rights, and which they therefore resented. I believe that had the former government seen fit to clear the deck and lay a foundation by amending the British North America Act at the proper time, and then passed its legislation, we would not have the disunity that hon. members opposite talk so much about to-day.
However, for my part I am not so impressed with the seriousness of this disunity as some hon. members profess to be. After all, Canada is a federation. We start right at the school sections. I had the honour to start right at the base of our governmental life, right in the school section. A school section demands certain things from the township; the township demands certain things from the county; the county demands certain things from the province, and the provinces of course are only doing their duty when they rise to the occasion and do everything possible for the people whose affairs they are 71492-177
called upon to administer. That is an indication that the men who hold public positions to-day in Canada are taking their duties seriously, doing everything they can for the people for whom they are responsible, and getting as much as possible for them. I was "guilty" of it myself; I quite remember going through all these stages of governmental life. I asserted my right, in the position in which I happened to be, to get as much as possible and to give the very best type of legislation I could when I had that particular responsibility of office. But I do not view so seriously these differences of opinion that prevail, because I believe we have men who are anxious to serve their people.
I wish to draw attention to some conditions as I see them in Canada, after listening to the speeches of hon. members opposite who have been bemoaning our troubles. One listening to the debates in this house at this time might well be led to think that we have on the other side the greatest exhibition of calamity howlers that any parliament has ever seen. But let us look at a- few facts and see if we have not even made some progress. Let us not be so pessimistic as to think that this whole country has gone to the dogs, because in spite of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said a few moments ago as to our system having broken down, if this is a broken-down system I believe people who are living on this northern part of the north American continent are enjoying a far higher standard of living than almost any other country in the world, including some which are carrying on under an economic system that some hon. gentlemen would approve in preference to what we have to-day.
I should like to draw the hon. member's attention to something I happened to see in the Toronto Telegram, which I purchased on my way from the train on Tuesday. I am sure the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) would approve anything published in this newspaper. Under the heading " Sparks from the anvil," there appears a table indicating the amount of bread that can be purchased with one hour's pay in different countries. Perhaps I might read a few words from the article:
There are many people who consider there should be some change in the monetary system-
Perhaps this will interest our social credit friends as well.
-and that goods should be based on definite units of labour. Along that line it may be of interest to quote a table which shows an hour of labour in Canada and the United States will buy about 7-5 pounds of bread-

The hon. member can make

comparable with what the average farmer would receive in cash. I realize, of course, that in addition the farmer gets many other things that are not purchased with cash. For one thing he gets a great deal of his living from the farm, and I think that indicates one great solution of our problem which the hon. member for Greenwood might have included in the list he gave the house. I think I might suggest two or three further additions to his suggestions. I believe that we should bring about such a state of affairs as will lure unemployed with agricultural backgrounds back to the land. We have had some advanced agricultural legislation brought into the house; some may view parts of it as unsound, but I believe it is emergency legislation that is necessary if those who live on the land are to get a fair share of the national income. Because I take that ground I am glad to support that legislation; for, if in a country like Canada we do not endeavour to maintain a strong, virile population on our farms, Canada will not long continue to be the country it is to-day.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

That is right, but
