maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I do not
hear what the hon. member is saying.
The hon. member for Greenwood also bewailed the fiscal policy of this country and said industry was going into a decline. I should like to direct attention to page 940 of the Canada Year Book, 1938, in regard to the dividends paid by industry in Canada. In 1934 those dividends amounted to $185,760,000. In 1935 they rose to $222,629,000, and in 1938 they amounted to $319,804,000, or an increase of almost $100,000,000 between the latter two years. Does that look as though industry is suffering as a consequence of the fiscal legislation of this government? I believe the figures for 1938 are very close to those for 1937, showing a difference of only about $2,000,000. I cannot understand a man rising in his place in the House of Commons and making statements to the house and the country when he knows the figures prove the contrary. He must have some other purpose in mind than to enlighten the public, and for that reason I sometimes question the sincerity of what comes from the other side of the house when hon. members decry our country to the world. After all, I am prepared to be sufficiently loyal to Canada to say we have the best country in the world in which a man can make a living.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
If that is not sufficient I should like to draw attention to the condition of business in general. Generally when conditions are bad there are more cases of insolvency and ultimate commercial failure. In 1934 there were 1,600 failures in Canada. In 1937 that number was reduced to 952, a reduction of 648. Surely this shows that we are on the right track and that something has been accomplished.
The hon. member for Greenwood went on to say that industry had lost confidence as a result of tariff tinkering; I think that was the term he used. I should like to draw the attention of the house to the figures in connection with the construction of factory buildings in Canada over a period of six years. In 1932 there was $7,820,400 invested in factory buildings for the promotion of industry in the Dominion of Canada. By 1937 that figure had gone up to $33,779,800. Does that look as though the policies of this government were bringing ruin to industry? If the hon. member for Greenwood wishes to face the facts he should revise his statement. If he is as good a Canadian as he purports to be, he must realize that kind of speech cannot accomplish anything for the good of Canada.
After all, one must compare Canada with other countries in which there is a similar standard of living and in which similar conditions exist. May I point out that in respect of trade Canada stands to-day in fourth place among the exporting nations of the world. Surely if we have advanced from sixth to fourth place some credit is due the Canadian people and to the administration which has found markets for the products of our labour. When we have been able to meet the competition of other peoples to that extent, it would seem that at least we are making progress faster than other comparable countries.
One of the major indications of the prosperity of a country is the rate of interest at which it is able to borrow money. After' all, if the risk is higher the rate also is higher. I am prepared to say that of a group of six countries including the United States, France, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand and the United Kingdom only one, the United States, is borrowing money at a rate lower than that enjoyed by Canada. The rate of interest in the United States is 2-69 per cent. Of course they may have issued more tax-free bonds than any other country, a fact which may have some bearing upon the rate I have indicated. Canada stands in second position with a rate of 3-53 per cent. We have looked upon the United Kingdom as one of the greatest financial countries of the
71492-177 J
world. Probably she has loaned more money and financed more enterprises in all parts of the world than has any other country. British sterling is recognized as a standard. Yet the United Kingdom is paying a rate of 3-56 per cent, or -03 per cent higher than we pay. One must not forget that the United Kingdom has age-old consols and perpetuals on which she pays only 2 per cent, all of which would have a tendency to reduce her rate. Despite that advantage we borrow our money cheaper than does the United Kingdom.
Something has been said about New Zealand, but I would point out that we borrow money considerably cheaper than does New Zealand. Their rate is 3-78 per cent, while that of Australia, where some of the most drastic methods of debt reduction have been made effective, is 3-98 per cent. Despite objections on the part of some people we have retained sound policies and have met our obligations, with the result that confidence in the Canadian people has been established, and to-day our credit position is one of the best in the world. These are some of the facts which cannot be disputed. I have secured my figures from those issued about June 30, 1938, by the League of Nations.
As a rule I am cautious about giving the opinions of other people. Generally my observations arise from a survey of conditions as I see them. My opinion is that this is the only useful contribution I can make. I am more or less practical and I like to state my impressions. For a moment, however, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the words of one who is considered probably the greatest authority on economics. I refer to Roger Babson. On his return from Europe last fall he made a statement in which he observed he believed that to-day Canada offered the best opportunities for the investment of money and of all the countries in the world was the most desirable in which to live. He said that a young man coming to Canada would have advantages he could get in no other country, and that while we have made some mistakes in Canada he believed we have made fewer mistakes in legislation than has any other country of which he is aware. I say to a large extent that condition is a result of the fact that for a goodly portion of the time since confederation Liberal governments have been in office. That, in my view, is the answer to Mr. Babson' statement. We have enjoyed sane, economic administration. If one were to check the debt of Canada as it stands to-day, if he were to add all the surpluses under Liberal administrations and those under Conservative administrations,
2802	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
and balance them against the deficits of these respective parties, he would find that only $23,000,000 of a total interest bearing debt of $3,100,000,000 can be attributed to Liberal administration. I point that out as one of the reasons for Mr. Babson^ statement that in Canada we have suffered less foolish governmental policies than any other country.
While I am on the point I should like to say I was deeply impressed with the sincerity of the hon. member for Greenwood in his appeal to youth. He waxed eloquent on what he would do for youth, and yet he is the man who has chosen to follow that reactionary party which has placed upon the backs of the youth of Canada the burden of paying a debt of about three billion dollars, a debt which is traceable to the party of his choice. How can the hon. member be sincere in his eloquence for the youth of Canada when the party to which he belongs has been guilty of saddling youth with more debt and has done more to mortgage future generations than any other party in Canada.
I take this opportunity to read the following newspaper article respecting Mr. Babson's views:
"Invest in Canada," he advised. "Canada's bullish outlook should mean some good investment opportunities in the securities of Canadian banking, utility and industrial concerns."
I do not think any higher tribute could be paid to a nation by one who is probably one of the greatest authorities in the world. The article continues:
Mr. Babson was in England during the European crisis last September. He believed that England is looking more and more for a stronghold for her supplies-a base for her industries that will be safe from the marauding of modern bombers. Such a stronghold is Canada.
"Conditions being as they are to-day in Europe, Great Britain must have a safe place to develop her industries. Few realize it, but the bombing plane will actually revolutionize English civilization."
He believed the mother country is looking across the sea to Canada. North America is practically immune to bombing attacks, provided an enemy cannot establish an air base on this side of the Atlantic. Canada is in the geographical centre of the empire, therefore, he said, it was only logical that England should look to Canada as the storm cellar for her reserves. It is reported that England is now investing $100,000,000 in Canadian aviation plants, he said.
Then the article goes on to refer to the visit of the king and queen. I believe there was no reason for his expressing an opinion such as I have read if that opinion did not express what he believed were the actual facts. I think it is recognized that in this particular
'Mr. Wood.]
line there is no one whose opinion is more sought or more respected than that of Roger Babson.
I have my own opinions about the solution of many problems of the individual, but whether they would apply nationally is a question. I believe in the system of democratic government, under which every man has the right to guide and direct his own life within our economic structure just as he sees fit. If a man chooses a course that brings disaster upon him, I do not know that there is very much we can do about it except to use our influence with those associated with us to try to show him the proper way. I am a great believer in self-reliance for the individual.
I do not know just how far government can go to relieve our present problems, but I will say that I know of no country under democratic government that has made a better job of it than has this dominion. Some countries have resorted to dictatorships, but a price must be paid for that, and are we prepared to surrender our liberties to any dictatorship? I believe that the great majority of the people of this dominion want to lead a self-reliant, ambitious life of their own choosing. But to-day there are so many distractions for youth that it is almost impossible for them to face the sober realities of life and make the sacrifices that are necessary to build a home and provide for their future. I believe that nothing can be accomplished without sacrifice, and until we ourselves realize that we have to make sacrifices we cannot expect others to make sacrifices for us.
Some may say that the standard of relief is not high enough, but at least the country is giving as much as it gets in return. I am sorry for those who are suffering under present conditions, but I have come to the point where I believe that some consideration should be given to a certain class of people in this country who are not wealthy, and I believe I represent that class of people myself, people who are trying to pay their taxes and carry their burdens, and taking the other fellow by the hand. I have no particular brief for the wealthy man because he can look after himself, but I am concerned for those who are trying to do their duty, paj'ing their way, helping the other fellow where they can, and who are getting somewhat of a raw deal in our present economic order.
We have developed in this country a standard of living that has some relationship to our economic situation to-day, and I sometimes wonder if we are not living beyond our means. In Ontario, for example, there is one automobile for every five people, and on the

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
other hand, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated, there was a group of young men outside these buildings this afternoon wanting work. It seems to me that there are too many people on wheels to-day. I do not wish to refer particularly to the youth movement, but a great deal of youth movement is on wheels. I am not 'blaming them for it, because sometimes I believe the blame belongs probably to people of our age, to the parents, the older grey-haired people who go out playing bridge and go to parties instead of staying at home looking after their children. Naturally when the parents go out playing bridge, the children get into the sugar-bowl and among the cookies. It is not altogether the young people's fault if they have become soft, because we may have failed to train them to meet the sober realities of life. Life is the product of labour, and it is well that we should prepare to give our children a little bit of a start in life.
It has been pointed out that there are four million depositors in the banks of this country, with an average deposit of over $500. So it cannot be said that there are not many people in this dominion who are trying to provide for their own social security. Will anyone say for one moment that when we have in Canada 3,500,000 insurance policyholders, with an average of two thousand dollars of life insurance, they are not taking steps to look after the future welfare of themselves and their families? True, we have not unemployment insurance, but I want to tell this house that unemployment insurance is not very popular among the farmers. They look upon it as only another policy that is going to add to their present load, which is already burdensome. We have to-day an Annuities Act under which any young man, 21 years of age, who will contribute S20.62 a year can draw the equivalent of an old age pension at sixty-five years of age, and if he dies before that, his contributions are returned to his estate with four per cent interest. So we have the machinery to-day whereby, if a man will intelligently direct his efforts and save a part of the product of his labour, storing it up for his own social security, he can in some measure provide for his own future. I am not sure that the question of unemployment insurance is a serious one to-day except that it gives hon. members opposite something to find fault with the government about. They call this a "do-nothing government," but that is a mere phrase in view of the accomplishments which I have mentioned to the credit of this government in the past three years. Such talk is not the way to establish confidence. It
does not do to be continually sniping at the government and bemoaning conditions, dragging out of the gutter all the foul and filthy things that there are in a country. If we would rise up and hold our chins a bit higher it would help us, and we can hold our chins up with a great deal of pride because Canada has the wherewithal that lends dignity to us as a nation.
I see that I have almost exhausted my time, Mr. Speaker. There are a few other matters on which I should have liked to touch had time permitted. There has been a great onslaught on governments and on certain institutions. There has been an organized attack made by some people on the salaries paid for by the taxpayers to men occupying prominent positions in public life. Canada to-day has probably one of the most brilliant cabinets we ever had, and what we pay for it is only twice as much as is drawn by Deanna Durbin, the motion picture star. I have here a list of people drawing high salaries in the United States, and some of the salaries are very large. I think it is unfortunate that we have in this country a type of mind that does not want to pay for actual services performed and results accomplished.. They do not like to pay for food, clothing and shelter, although Canada can provide that just as cheaply as any country in the world, as I pointed out just a few moments ago. Yet these same people have no objection to paying enormous salaries to those who provide them with entertainment and amusement. That applies to everything from baseball players to movie actresses. There is one man who has a salary of over a million dollars. One does not hear any objection to that, but if one endeavours to get a business administration-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I said that floods were
not of modern origin, and when I was interrupted I was about to remark that there is danger now of their reaching their maximum crest. We have not yet had a flood of maximum crest in this country, nor has there been one in the United States, but there, the people believe that the last flood on the Ohio river was not very far from that stage. Unless, therefore, we take drastic steps to cope with the situation we shall be faced with very grave danger indeed. In the United States the story of floods on the Ohio goes back to the capture of Fort Duquesne, afterwards named Fort Pitt by the British. After the British had taken that fort they kept records of the heights of floods on the Ohio. Surveying this subject in relation to many of the European countries and throughout America I find that most of the great nations to-day are adopting flood control programs, as well perhaps for the purpose of saving life as for safeguarding property; and another important object is to provide sound employment. It is a means of providing sound employment, because I find that in the United States they are proceeding on a large scale with flood control works. There, a vast program of flood prevention is assisted by the PWA, and at the present time from
200,000	to 300,000 men are engaged in the United States, directly, or indirectly, on these works, to which I shall refer in a moment.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They have a different monetary policy from ours.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I am not going to discuss that question now. Hon. members have dealt with it half a dozen times this session, and so has the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I have listened to all the speeches on monetary policy. In 1936 the United States
2806	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
government passed their first flood control act, a copy of which I have here. It contains twenty-eight pages setting out various projects, and the estimated cost is 8325,000,000. In 1938 they were so well pleased with what they had done two years previously that they extended their program under a new act containing twelve pages of projects at an estimated cost of $375,000,000, or a total of $700,000,000. These works cover projects in practically every state of the union.
It was my good fortune to travel over a great many of the rivers mentioned in these acts and to survey flood control works erected thereon, and I say to the minister I am convinced that he would be on sound ground if he brought forward a flood control act under his relief program, and proceeded upon a long term program of five or ten years, undertaking to flood-proof the rivers of Canada, commencing with those in the most settled territories and where the greatest damage has been done and the greatest number of lives have been lost. That would be just as sound as the work that has been carried out in the United States, and none of the money invested in these works would be lost. As a matter of fact, in the net result, these works would really cost the country nothing because they would annually save a great deal.
Some may say that there is no reason for floods, but there are many reasons. In the pioneer days our forefathers did not experience the floods that we have to-day, because in those days nature provided against such conditions. The outlets of all the small lakes and swamps were clogged by stumps of trees, brush and so on, and all down the course of the river, running zigzag like a snake, the land was covered with trees. But in these days the river courses have been straightened, the land has been ditched and drained, trees have been cut down and, in short, man has done everything he can to expedite the flow of water off the land into the river bed. God Almighty designed the river beds to carry off a certain amount of water, but man has frustrated this design by cutting down the trees, and so on, and he has done nothing to counteract his own work. These two acts that have been passed in the United States indicate that the people of that nation realize that the time has come for them to restore the defence that man has destroyed; and the time has come in Canada likewise for us to restore by our own works what we have taken away from nature in the way I have described. In carrying out such a program a great deal of employment could be provided. In my judgment it would be sound economic employment, and in the long run it would not cost the

country one dollar, as I shall show when I come to discuss one or two of the results that have so far been attained in the republic to the south of us.
My time is passing, and I wish to present to the best of my ability a plan which I believe the minister would be well advised to follow. Take the city of Belleville. We did not have a flood there this spring, it is true, but last year there was one that cost the people of Belleville $100,000. Belleville is in jeopardy every spring from the Moira river. Take Port Hope. Two years ago they had a flood that cost them about $300,000. Take the Portneuf river, in Quebec. I have a letter here, dated December 19, 1938, from the minister who looks after river and flood control in the province of Quebec, telling me that a number of rivers and creeks there have had disastrous floods; he names the Portneuf, creeks Blondel, Casault, Lemoyne, aux Chien, Sault-a-la-Puce and du Moulin. The loss in these floods last August was estimated at $200,000. The object of flood control is to eliminate such losses. The losses sustained by all these towns, cities and villages and factories annually can be eliminated, and in that way the work will soon pay for itself.
Now to speed along, because I want to present concrete examples in western Ontario that can be taken care of. To lay a basis for my argument let me refer to the Ohio river. Hon. members will recall that in January, 1937 I think, there was a very great flood on the Ohio river, the most disastrous in its history, which caused property damage amounting to $800,000,000, and which took a large number of lives and brought disaster to thousands of homes. I happened to be in Louisville a short time before that flood, and when I read later, that the restaurant in which I dined in a big store like Eaton's or Simpson's, had been flooded up to the second storey, I could hardly believe it. The United States at once decided to eliminate floods on the Ohio river. They had an example to go by. In 1913 there was a great flood on the Miami river-the older members present will remember it,-when the fine city of Dayton was almost swept off the map, 416 people drowned, and the property loss in that river valley exceeded $100,000,000. The communities along that river at once commenced to flood-proof it. They built five great dams and the necessary reservoirs, dams which work automatically. They are open in dry weather, but in the event of flood the gates automatically close and hold the water. Since 1913 the Miami river has carried off the waters from

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
eight major storms, any one of which would have been serious, and one of which would have been much more serious than that of 1913; yet the valley has been flood-proofed and the cities along its banks and the people adjacent thereto have not experienced any damage from floods since 1913. They tell you down there that the money they spent on flood-proofing that river, some $33,000,000, has been paid back to them over and over several times, in addition to the saving of the property and lives of the citizens.
The United States government, observing the splendid results from the flood-proofing of the Miami river, adopted that system of flood-proofing and is applying it to-using an arbitrary number-500 or some such number of streams, as mentioned in these forty pages of the two acts to which I have referred. After the dams are erected and completed, they use the young men in the civilian conservation corps camps for reforesting these reservoirs, which are dry in the dry season, and are used then as parks. They employ thousands of these young men in beautifying these parks which provide accommodation for holding picnics to which multitudes of people go and in which there are many small refreshment booths, which are another means of furnishing employment; in some instances they charge a small fee and in that way there is some return. In flood-proofing the Miami river 4,000 men were employed directly and approximately another 4,000 indirectly. They are now following the same system on thirteen other tributaries of the Ohio. One is the upper source of the Monongahela river. They erected a great dam. That dam is now completed; it is one of fourteen being erected to flood-proof the Ohio river; about 60,000 men are employed in the work directly and probably another 60,000 indirectly in making cement and other supplies and equipment. One dam, the Tygart dam, is 1,880 feet long, of solid concrete, 200 feet through the base and 167 feet high. That is only one of fourteen that they are erecting.
In my judgment employment on that kind of work is a sound investment because it adds to the national wealth. The army engineers at Pittsburgh, tell me that the results from the erection of those dams will produce a saving of perhaps $200,000,000. At that rate it does not take very long to pay for a program that will cost approximately $300,000,000. So this seems to me a sound method to take care oi unemployment. Any hon. member who contemplates motoring down in Ohio in the summer could not do better than visit some of these rivers and see the great works being constructed there. The Muskingum river is
another that for many years caused great losses through floods but has now been made absolutely flood proof.
I refer to these two rivers, the Miami and the Muskingum, because the flood control dams and reservoirs situated on them are comparable with what is needed on the Thames and the Grand rivers in western Ontario. I am glad to know that there is some probability of the Grand river being flood-proofed perhaps in a year's time. That work will give productive employment to many men.
I neglected to say that on the Muskingum river 6,000 men were engaged. On the Tennessee, where I spent some time, I saw
7.000	men at work on one dam. Possibly altogether some 30,000 men were employed flood-proofing the Tennessee, and to-day it is flood-proofed. The total cost will be repaid in a few years by the savings.
To come now to the Grand river, the dams to be erected on that river will, I believe, be situated north of Galt. The watershed of that river north of Galt comprises 1,360 square miles. Any spring, or in summer when there is a heavy rain, a flood might occur. There have occurred on the Grand river floods of such extent that at Galt the flow has been as high as 40,000 cubic feet a second. When such a condition occurs, every industry along the Grand river adjacent to Galt is flooded and men have to be laid off.
Later on if I have time I shall give the cost percentages used in the United States so as to encourage the minister not to be too modest in regard to the amount of money he asks for this work. Unless flood control works are erected on the Grand river there may any year be a flood as great as on the Miami or the Muskingum, where three inches of water fell over the whole watershed in four days. If such a fall occurred in the Grand river basin the flow would not be 40,000 cubic feet a second, it would be 50,000 or 60,000;
50.000	at Galt would be 70,000 at Brantford, and such a flow would wipe the lower end of that city off the map. So I say to the minister: Urge the Ontario government, with which this government offers to cooperate in connection with Grand river works, to speed up the commencement of the Grand river works. One cannot tell what is ahead. A fall of three inches on the Grand River watershed north of Galt would be equivalent to a run-off of about 9,000,000,000 cubic feet of water from that watershed, and when one thinks of that quantity of water flowing down the present course of that river one can picture what would happen to all the works, buildings and so on in the way of a flood like that.

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
Since it has been proposed that the work on the Grand river should be commenced, why not commence work on the Thames as well? Two years ago there was a flood on the Thames river, of which I have pictures in this small treatise, entitled "Water," I have written on the subject of water. These pictures show the railroads tom up, with railroad cars in the bed of the river. I believe that was the flood in which a doctor from Ingersoll, going out on an errand of mercy, was drowned. At that time I believe the flood was about 40,000 cubic feet a second, if there should be a rainfall over the watershed of the Thames anything like the rainfall that caused the Miami disasters of 1913, every city, village und hamlet between the headwaters of the Thames and its outlet into lake St. Clair would suffer vast damage. So any moneys spent in this way return themselves; or in the words used in this house, the cost will be liquidated within a reasonable length of time. I do not look upon money spent on flood control works as a cost to the country at all. because one flood would cost as much as might be spent on works.
In closing I might mention the ratio adopted in the United States, which I obtained after careful consultation with army engineers. I find that on the flood-proofing of the Muskingum river the United States government, through the PWA assistance, which is a plan to take care of unemployment and which works very well, paid 63-23 per cent of the cost, if my figures are correct. The state and certain interested public services such as the railways, telephone and telegraph companies and so on, paid approximately 25-35 per cent, so that the municipalities had to pay only a little over 11 per cent. I imagine that one of the hold-ups to the work being proceeded with on the Grand river is the fact that the municipalities do not want to undertake the payment of 25 per cent of the cost.

speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
I believe the country
would support the minister if he would recommend to the government that they make the burden easier for the municipalities. Let the government of the day assume a larger proportion of the cost. I do not say what the provincial government should do. This is a national problem, too. Let the federal government. rise to the occasion, as the United States government has done, and assume a greater share of the cost, up to at least 60 per rent. Let them say they are ready to do that, and it will be found that the municipalities along the Grand river, the Thames river, the Portneuf river in Quebec and other rivers 
throughout Canada will take advantage of the opportunity. Then, through a long term program of flood prevention, the government could at once give employment to thousands of men. In my judgment that is one sound way of creating employment. If the minister will bring in anything along that line, even if I am the only man in the house to do so I will support him as strongly as I can on such a program. I have made a most exhaustive survey of this whole subject of flood prevention, and I am thoroughly convinced that it is a sound, economic way to provide employment for Canadians, and that in the long run it will not cost the country a dollar. The cost will be repaid as it has been repaid in the Miami valley of Ohio, and as it will be repaid in the Ohio valley by what they save in annual property losses from floods. Fancy, $300,000,000 to be spent along the Ohio; but when they finish flood-proofing the fourteen branches of the Ohio river they will guarantee that never again will there be a flood on that stream. What a blessing that will be to the people living along the shores of that river! Why, Mr. Speaker, if instead of $300,000,000 they paid $2,000,000,000 it still would be cheap, when one figures that one flood alone cost over $800,000,000!
We must realize, as I said earlier, that on account of the cutting down of our forests and the increased rapidity of drainage from the land, the straightening of the rivers and the elimination of refuse at swamp outlets, which in the pioneer days retarded the flow of water into our rivers, this problem has become greater year by year, and with that in mind one can easily grasp what a blessing it will be to the communities along these rivers if we get on with the job in a big way. These are strenuous, grave times, and I believe the minister and the government would have the backing of the people if they would provide employment in this way. I mentioned several other methods but did not discuss them; one cannot cover everything in forty minutes. It would require four hours to deal with all these different subjects. During thp last forty minutes, however, I think I have set out a sound argument for flood-proofing the rivers of Ontario and Quebec, and T do hope the Grand river works will be proceeded with this summer. Then the minister can go on with other rivers in Ontario and Quebec and go right, across the country, thereby placing many thousands of men at. work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) indulged in a marathon; but since he merely marked time or at best ran in circles, I cannot congratulate him upon having won it. There was one fortunate result, however; the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), who followed him, came out of his long sleep, like Rip Van Winkle, and was able to finish the speech which he commenced forty years ago; at least I hope he finished it.
Before sitting down, the hon. member for Greenwood indulged in the usual sneer at the ideas held by those in this corner of the house, without giving any indication of how he proposed to finance the ideas which he presented to the government. I understand the hon. member for Greenwood conducts the largest Bible class in the empire. I would be interested if he could point to one justification in the Bible of lending money at usury, or of charging interest for money. It would seem that teachers and preachers have served their masters better than their Master, because for every critic of sound money there are a tmndred critics of Christianity.
If any hon. members are in doubt as to where money can come from, I would recommend that they sometimes attend the sittings of the committee on banking and commerce. Or is it that they agree with the saying of Professor Soddy. that when the light of scientific truth is directed beyond the affairs of the intellect or even of the soul, to the affairs of the pocket, then the too naked truth is an outrage on all that is fine and respectable.
This debate is on unemployment, and it might be well to make sure just what unemployment is. Would it not be more true to say that it is "unimpayment"? We all know plenty of people who have never done a stroke of work in their lives and never intend to do any. But because they happen to be possessed of money they are classed, not as unemployed, but as highly desirable citizens. The fact is that the crime is not in having no work but in having no money. I remember when I was a young man I was independent, but when I went into a store no
one ever said to me, "Look here, young man, we do not care to take your money; you do not earn it." No, they were glad to get my money, and hoped that I would come in again. Since that time I have done, I believe, a fair share of work, and occasionally I have been in the position of not knowing exactly how I could provide for my family. But nobody ever said to me, "Oh, that is all right, old man. We know you have worked. We will not see you stuck." They did not care twopence whether I worked or not. It is a case of money or starve.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Not always.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Apparently the possession of money confers a divinity upon those who possess it. They are not subject to the laws of ordinary mortals who do not possess it. Unemployment is not a disease; it is a symptom of a disease. Employment is like happiness. Happiness is a result of right living. If you go out to look for happiness you are apt to wake up with a bad taste in your mouth and a sore head. You have had a sort of synthetic happiness. I say that when it is urged that you can create work for the sake of work, and if there is an attempt to carry out that idea, we are going to wake up with a very bad head. To say that you can cure the disease by treating the symptom is the equivalent of sending a case of smallpox to the beauty parlour. The disease is not the symptom.
I have heard hon. members, and especially hon. members opposite, say that the reason for unemployment is the provision of relief. In fact I heard one hon. member put the blame for unemployment on the late leader of the Conservative party, because of his introduction of relief measures. While I was not born in Canada I would say on behalf of Canadians that I have yet to meet a Canadian who was too lazy to work. I have met Canadians who refused to work under degrading conditions, and I thank God for such men, because they are the men who stand between us and slavery.
An attempt has been made by the respective parties to place the blame on each other. It is suggested that were the Conservatives in office they could very soon cure our unemployment problem. I am not a politician, nor am I particularly interested in politics, but I am interested in economics. What are the facts? The facts are that the Liberals held office until 1930, and they did nothing, because they could do nothing to stop the depression which caused the unemployment. Then the Conservatives held office for five years. They did their best. It would be unfair to say that

they lacked ability, because they had the advantage of leadership by one of the ablest and hardest working men in Canada, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. But they could do nothing.
Then, my friends to the immediate right say that they could cure unemployment. Well, we know that on two occasions socialist governments held office in England, but they could do nothing. In fact I think they made rather a worse mess of it than the others had done. Then all three got together to form a national government-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take more than a few minutes, but I wish to- refer to the report of the committee which recommended that this bill be not proceeded with.

The principle of the bill is to trust the people. I think the committee might well have recommended the submission of plebiscites so as to cany out the principle of trusting the people on matters of national policy in domestic affairs. If parliament has this power it should be exercised, not in foreign affairs, but in domestic matters such as constitutional and parliamentary reform. For example, the statute of Westminster should have been submitted to the people. It would have been defeated. Other questions that might well foe submitted would be overgovernment, over-taxation, unemployment insurance. Had this bill been enacted into law and plebiscites on these questions submitted to the people, we should not have the over-government and over-taxation that we have to-day, nor would we have the railway policy and the huge railway deficits that we have to-day. Other questions that might well be submitted to the people by a plebiscite would be senate reform, important treaties, radio broadcasting matters and other domestic questions.
While this bill may not now be enacted into law, I trust that the government will consider enacting legislation that will permit the people to decide by their votes these important domestic questions on the same day as they vote in a general election. Had we had such legislation twenty years ago, we would long ago have had unemployment insurance and a redistribution of the work of parliament between the two houses so that one chamber would not be on vacation half of the session, we would have had senate reform, and long ago we would have had a solution of our wheat and coal problems and a national policy with respect to both these products.
While the report of the committee was not printed, I think it would be in the public interest to have the discussion in the committee printed, and I trust that the committee on printing will consider that suggestion.
There is no machinery at present by which a specific question relating to domestic matters can foe submitted to the people. There is simply a general appeal on opposing policies at the time of a general election, and to submit a specific question on matters such as I have mentioned special legislation and a separate act of parliament are required. Our electoral laws are away behind the times and should be brought up to date. I hope that in the next parliament this question will be raised again. Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, in view of the committee's report that the bill be not proceeded with, I now ask leave to withdraw it.
Bill withdrawn.

maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT
SUPREME COURT ACT
subtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO THE JUDICIAL COMMITTEE OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL

speechtext:
Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Supreme Court Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as there seems to be some misapprehension with regard to the terms of this bill, I wish to state that its terms are different from those of the bill which I introduced last session.
The first section repeals section 54 of the Supreme Court Act, chapter 35 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, and substitutes the following therefor:
54. (1) The supreme court shall have, hold and exercise exclusive ultimate appellate civil and criminal jurisdiction within and for Canada; and the judgment of the court shall, in all cases, be final and conclusive.
(2)	Notwithstanding any royal prerogative or anything contained in any act of the parliament of the United Kingdom or any act of the parliament of Canada or any act of the legislature of any province of Canada or any other statute or law, no appeal shall lie or be brought from any court now or hereafter established within Canada to any court of appeal, tribunal or authority by which, in the United Kingdom, appeals or petitions to his majesty in council may be ordered to be heard.
(3)	The Judicial Committee Act, 1833 chapter forty-one of the statutes of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, 1833, and The Judicial Committee Act, 1844, chapter sixty-nine of the statutes of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, 1844, and all orders, rules or regulations made under the said acts are hereby repealed in so far as the same are part of the law of Canada.
Another section provides:
2.	Nothing in this act shall affect any application for special leave to appeal or any appeal to his majesty in council made or pending at the date of the coming into force of this act.
The third section provides:
3.	This act shall come into force upon a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette.
Mr. Speaker, section 101 of the British North America Act, 1867, enacts that:
101. The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this act, from time to time provide for the constitution, maintenance and organization of a general court of appeal for Canada, and tor the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
Pursuant to the powers thus conferred upon the parliament of Canada to provide for the constitution, maintenance and organization of a general court of appeal for Canada, parliament in 1875, by 38 Victoria, chapter 11, enacted the Supreme Court Act. which now appears as chapter 35 of the Revised Statutes
of Canada, 1927. This statute, in section 35, established the Supreme Court of Canada with "an appellate, civil and criminal jurisdiction throughout the Dominion of Canada."
This bill proposes to extend that section 35 by providing that "the supreme court shall have, hold and exercise exclusive ultimate jurisdiction within and for Canada," and then proceeds to abolish all appeals from any court now or hereafter established in Canada, to any court of appeal, tribunal or authority by which in the United Kingdom, appeals or petitions to his majesty in council may be heard.	.
Prior to 1833 the sovereign, by virtue of his royal prerogative, from time to time, by way of special leave, granted appeals from various courts in the plantations, colonies and other dominions of his majesty abroad, to his majesty in council, or in other words to the government of the United Kingdom.
Such appeals to his majesty in council were first regulated by statute by the Judicial Committee Act, 1833. The Judicial Committee Act, 1844, subsequently enacted that her majesty in council was competent by order to provide for the admission of appeals from "any judgments, sentences, decrees or orders of any court of justice within any British colony or possession abroad".
That act of the parliament of the United Kingdom still applies to the "British colony or possession" now known as the Dominion of Canada, and, under its terms, the government of the United Kingdom, on the advice of its judicial committee, may provide for and grant special leave to appeal to his majesty in council from the judgment of any county court, court of sessions or magistrate's court within Canada.
The Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, which was enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom two years before the enactment of the British North America Act 1867, precluded the parliament of Canada from repealing or amending either of the two judicial committee acts which I have mentioned.
However, sections 2 and 3 of the statute of Westminster (1931) have now removed the fetters which the Colonial Laws Validity Act had previously placed upon the legislative jurisdiction of this and other dominions.
This bill, provided that it is within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament, will vest in his majesty's Supreme Court of Canada, instead of in his majesty's privy council at Westminster, that is, in the government of the United Kingdom, exclusive and ultimate appellate jurisdiction within and for Canada in civil and criminal matters.
Privy Council Appeals

For my own part, I fervently favour that imperial connection which is established by our allegiance to the crown and by Canada's membership, as an autonomous dominion, in the British commonwealth of nations, but nevertheless, I am fully persuaded that the continuance of Canada's amicable relations and good understanding with the government of the United Kingdom will best be promoted by the repeal, so far as applicable to this dominion, of such imperial statutes as, the Judicial Committee Acts, which now confer upon the government of the United Kingdom the political authority and the legal right to intervene, at its discretion, in the administration and enforcement of the laws of Canada. Such intervention the people of an autonomous dominion, in my opinion, should not continue to tolerate.
The more free the people of Canada are from the officious intervention in our domestic affairs by the government of the United Kingdom, the more readily will our people assume and fulfil the duties and responsibilities which are implied in our continued membership in the British commonwealth.
From the communications which I have personally received, I am convinced that public opinion throughout Canada is favourable to this bill. I have, however, received definite notes of warning from those whose legal learning and business experience command respect.
It is suggested that in all prospective constitutional changes it is advisable to proceed slowly and, so far as reasonably possible, to make sure that the reform legislation proposed is within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament.
I have, therefore, provided that this measure, when enacted by parliament, shall come into force only by proclamation of the governor in council; and I trust that the government will, at the earliest convenient date, refer this measure to the supreme court and thence to the judicial committee for an advisory opinion as to its constitutional validity. At such hearings both at Ottawa and at London, the attorneys general of the several provinces will be able to appear and present their views or their objections, if any, to the bill, in its entirety or in part.
Those corresponding with me have expressed a profound regret that the present chief justice of Canada, than whom no Canadian judge ever more fully enjoyed the respect, confidence and esteem of the Canadian people, is about to retire on account of the age limit prescribed by statute.
But since that correspondence was received by me, public apprehension on this account

will be relieved upon the enactment of a bill now before parliament for an extension for three years of the term of office of the present chief justice.
Moreover, there is also a widespread regret that physical frailties preclude two or more other justices from that active and onerous participation in judicial work which their official duties really demand.
There is serious concern in the province of which I am one of the representatives in this house that important issues concerning the interpretation of the civil code of Quebec may be left under present circumstances to the final decision of a quorum of judges, none of whom has been appointed from the bar of that province.
I am persuaded therefore that public opinion will not be billy satisfied until, in due time, the government shall have taken effective measures to change, increase and strengthen the present personnel of the supreme court, so that, when invested with exclusive and ultimate appellate jurisdiction, the members of that court may have and enjoy the full confidence of the Canadian people.
It is therefore important, I think, that this bill should proceed to a stage which will permit the government to refer the question of its validity to the Supreme Court of Canada and thence to the judicial committee of his majesty in council; and, though this is a private member's bill and entitled to no special privileges, I earnestly request the cooperation to that end of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and of all hon. members of this house.
It will otherwise be futile for hon. members to discuss, night after night as opportunity arises, the supreme legal issue, as to whether the bill in its present form is within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament, as only the judicial committee may render a conclusive opinion on that issue.
When this bill has been referred by the government to the Supreme Court of Canada and the final judgment of the judicial committee has been rendered on such reference, then and then only may this parliament deal intelligently with the provisions of this bill; and then effective measures may forthwith be taken to reconstruct the Supreme Court of Canada and readjust its personnel, as public opinion assuredly demands. Thereafter, a bill similar to this or one which conforms to the final judgment of the judicial committee may be enacted at a future session of parliament and brought into force by order in council.

Privy Council Appeals
I therefore move the second reading of the bill in the hope that I may enlist the cooperation of the Minister of Justice who undoubtedly prefers a bill in this form, in securing a reference to the supreme court and to the judicial committee for a final opinion as to whether the bill is within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. P. A. ROBICHAUD (Kent, N.B.):
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT
subtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO THE JUDICIAL COMMITTEE OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yesterday I got the notion, perhaps a foolish one, that I would take part in the discussion of this bill, but only to-day did I make up my mind definitely on the point and I am sorry that I have not set down in writing what I have to say. I trust the house will bear with me in the few disjointed and possibly laboured remarks I shall make.
I am in complete agreement with the principle of the bill, and I think it is unfortunate that such a law could not have been enacted at the time of confederation. The result has been, in my opinion, constitutional malaise and uncertainty in the country. Frankly, as far as I can see, the judicial committee has narrowly interpreted the Canadian constitution in the mistaken belief that by curtailing the powers of the central government to the advantage of the provincial governments it was strengthening, or at any rate preventing the loosening of, the ties that bind this dominion to the mother country. For that reason the judicial committee has given exaggerated powers to the provinces, so much so that the provinces to-day look upon this parliament as simply their creature.
I would direct hon. members to the Ferguson memorandum which was sent to the Right Hon. R. B.-Bennett in 1930, and in which is quoted part of a judgment by Lord Watson in a certain case. I quote:
The object of the act was neither to weld the provinces into one nor to subordinate provincial governments to a central authority, but to create a federal government in which they should all be represented, entrusted with the exclusive administration of affairs in which they had a common interest, each province retaining its independence and autonomy. . . . But, in so far as regards these matters which, by section 92, are specially reserved for provincial legislation, the legislature of each province continues to be free from the control of the dominion and as supreme as it was before the passing of the act.
In the case of Hodge v. the Queen, Sir Barnes Peacock, delivering the opinion of the board, said:
When the British North America Act enacted that there should be a legislature for Ontario, and that its legislative assembly should have
exclusive authority to make laws for the province and for provincial purposes in relation tc the matters enumerated in section 92, it conferred powers not in any sense to be exercised by delegation from or as agents of the imperial parliament, but authority as plenary and as ample within the limits prescribed by section 92, as the imperial parliament in the plenitude of its power possessed and could bestow.
Within the limits of subject and area, the local legislature is supreme and has the same authority as the imperial parliament or the parliament of the dominion.
To my mind it is not so. How can a provincial legislature be said to be supreme, even in its own limited field of legislative powers conferred upon it by section 92, when the dominion governor in council can disallow any of the laws of the provinces, even those that come within the limited scope of provincial legislative jurisdiction? I contend that the provinces cannot be said to be as supreme as the imperial parliament. As I say, the provinces have come to look upon the dominion parliament as their creature and to regard themselves as legally supreme. But let us refer to the British North America Act. How can it be said that the provinces created the dominion parliament, that the dominion parliament is simply their creature, when as a matter of fact, at the time this parliament was created, the provinces were not yet born as legal entities? They existed as territorial entities, but as legal entities they were still unborn, and they were as much created	by	this	act as was	the dominion
parliament. In fact the dominion parliament comes first; it was the first-born, so to speak, and then came the provinces as legal entities.
Let me quote section 3:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice of her majesty's most honourable privy council, to declare by proclamation that, on and	after a	day therein	appointed, notbeing more than six months after the passing of this	act,	the	provinces of	Canada, Nova
Scotia and New Brunswick-
Only three provinces; Quebec did not exist as a province nor did Ontario. How, therefore, could	the	provinces be	said to have
created a legal entity when they themselves did not at that time exist?
-shall form and be one dominion under the name of Canada; and on and after that day those three provinces shall form and be one dominion under the name accordingly.
Listen to section 4:
The subsequent provisions of this act shall . . . commence and have effect on and after the union, that is to say, on and after the day appointed for the union taking effect in the queen's proclamation. . . .
Privy Council Appeals

It will be observed that Canada as a legal entity was first created in section 3, and in section 5 the provinces were likewise created. Section 5 reads:
Canada shall be divided into four provinces, named Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Then section 6 provides:
The parts of the province of Canada (as it exists at the passing of this act) . . . shall be deemed to be severed, and shall form two separate provinces.
That is, the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Then section 7:
The provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall have the same limits as at the passing of this act.
The same territorial limits; but at the same time they were created as legal entities after the creation of this central legal entity. The only way in which they could be said, collectively, to be the father of this parliament is, to use an illustration, in the way a grain of wheat might be said to be the father of the ripened ear. These three provinces were first destroyed as legal entities and recreated; so that, so to speak, of three grains of wheat five blades sprouted from the one root-the dominion parliament and four provinces, one province being split into two.
Another illustration: Suppose Nova Scotia at the time of confederation were represented by the East block, New Brunswick by the Langevin block, Ontario and Quebec-being one province, Canada-by the West block. How did they create this main block out of those three blocks? Did they pick out a stone here and there? No; they demolished those three blocks and out of the heaps of stones that remained they built first this main block, afterward they rebuilt the East block, representing Nova Scotia, on a much smaller scale, and the Langevin block, representing New Brunswick, likewise on a smaller scale, and of the West block they made two blocks, Ontario and Quebec.
After all, to my mind the constitution is not a dead organ; it is a living organism, which grows with the body which it animates, and the only way in which we shall ever grow to be a country is by looking at it in that way.
On the second question, whether we have the legislative power to pass this proposed bill, section 101 no doubt is the section that gives the power if there is any power given. But it might be argued, and I suppose at one time it was argued, that this section does not give the power to create a court of appeal in all respects. It was read by my predecessor; it says:
The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this act, from time to time,

provide for the constitution, maintenance, and organization of a general court of appeal for Canada, and for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
I wonder if those three words "laws of Canada" apply to the first part, the organizing of a court of appeal, as well as to the latter part.
Referring to the Quebec resolution, one provision was this: "The establishment of a general court of appeal for the federated provinces." But the London resolution read differently. It said, "The establishment of a general court of appeal for the confederation." I say that it could have been argued at one time that this general court of appeal wras simply to hear appeals on cases that arose out of dominion laws, not provincial law's. But I think the question has been settled by a case decided by the privy council in 1908, the case of Crown Grain Company v. Day. It was a matter of a lien under a provincial statute; the provincial legislature had attempted to take away the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada; the grain company appealed and were given the right to appeal to the privy council, and the privy council decided that the provincial legislature had not the power to take aw'ay that right of appeal.
Finally the statute of Westminster is the one that really gives us the right and power to pass this bill. The statute of Westminster gives us the power to repeal any act of the United Kingdom applying to the dominion.
Now I am rushing to the end. To come to the third consideration, does this bill go far enough to give the right which it purports to give? With all due deference to the draftsman of this bill, I have my doubts. Subsection 3 of section 1 of new section 54 purports to repeal only the Judicial Committee Act, 1833, the Judicial Committee Act, 1844, and all orders, rules and regulations made under the said acts. But may I remark that the Judicial Committee Act was not the act which created the right of appeal from the dominion to the imperial courts. That act simply regulated the mode of appeal. We should perhaps go behind that act and repeal as well the commissions or letters patent or whatever instrument gave the right in the first place. I think if we repealed only the Judicial Committee Act, which deals only with regulating the mode of appeal we would not be going far enough, because I see that the explanatory note says:
. . . from the decisions of various courts of judicature in the East Indies and in the plantations, colonies and other dominions of his majesty abroad, an appeal lies to his majestr in council.

Privy Council Appeals
Before that, there was the word "whereas"- "whereas an appeal lies." So that the right of appeal must have been created before the date of this act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPREME COURT ACT
subtopic: ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO THE JUDICIAL COMMITTEE OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
similar bill, not exactly as this one, was introduced last year by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan), I gave my views rather extensively at that time, said I was in agreement with the principle of the bill, and even suggested that it should go further than it did and do away with appeals of all judgments from any court in Canada to his majesty in council. But I suggested that this matter should be left for further study and investigation not only by hon. members of this house but by legal associations and bodies in the country. And the matter was left over until this year.
In this bill my hon. friend has incorporated the suggestion I made last year when we discussed the bill he then introduced, and I am free to say that I am personally in entire accord with the substance and the form of my hon.' friend's bill. Personally I have no doubt that this parliament has complete jurisdiction to do away with appeals to any other tribunal than the final court of appeal in Canada, that is the Supreme Court of Canada, because of the residuary powers which this parliament has to legislate on any matters, of peace, order and good government, as well as under section 101 of the British North America Act. As the privy council itself said in the British Coal Corporation case:
. . . such appeals seem to be essentially matters of Canadian concern, and the control and regulation of such appeals thus seem to be a prime element in Canadian sovereignty as appertaining to matters of justice. . . .
There is no doubt that the provinces have no jurisdiction to abolish appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada and still less, or equally, they have no power to do away with appeals to the privy council, because under section 92 of the British North America Act the administration of justice, including procedure, in the province is left to the province; but it is limited to within the province and, as the courts have decided, the provinces have no authority to abolish appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada because it is without the limits of the provinces. If we have in Canada full jurisdiction it is clear, as I have said, that it is the parliament of Canada that has the power to establish a final court of appeal under section 101 of the British North America Act as well as under the residuary powers which this parliament possesses. There is no doubt as to the power to abolish appeals in any matters within the competence of the parliament of Canada; but, as the former leader of the opposition said last year, he had some doubts whether or not we had full power to do away with appeals from provincial courts. This doubt has been expressed also by some.writers; and as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has said, in such an important matter it is essential that there should be no doubt whatever as to the jurisdiction and powers of parliament to deal with the matter.
My hon. friend has suggested that his bill should be given second reading and that it might then be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada and even to the privy council as to the power of this parliament to enact it. I have been told that some members of this house approve the suggestion that the supreme court and the privy council should pass on the jurisdiction of this parliament in the matter but that they would prefer to have this reference made before they are called upon to vote on the principle of the bill. Under section 55 of the Supreme Court Act we may refer the question of the constitutionality of any legislation, whether federal or provincial, to the supreme court. Paragraph (d) of section 55 reads:
. . . the powers of the parliament of Canada, or of the legislatures of the provinces, or of the respective governments thereof, whether or not the particular power in question has been or is proposed to be exercised. . . .
My intention, therefore, is to recommend to the governor in council that this power be used and the bill referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for the purpose of ascertaining the jurisdiction and powers of this parliament to enact the proposed legislation. I
Privy Council Appeals

intend to have this done in the very near future, so that when the matter comes before parliament again there will be no doubt whether or not we have the right to deal with it.' Therefore, having come to this conclusion, I think I should move the adjournment of the debate in order that the bill may remain on the order paper until the end of the session, and as soon as possible the reference will be made. I accept the suggestion of my hon. friend in this amended form. Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Norman McL. Rogers (Minister of Labour) that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress and for such purpose to authorize the execution of undertakings in the general interest of Canada and requisite for the purposes of the act, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, and also to provide financial assistance to the provinces by way of loan, advance or guarantee, out of unappropriated moneys in the -consolidated revenue fund, and for the appointment of necessary officers, clerks and employees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was saying that no democratic government had cured what we call unemployment. I had said that the Conservative government, the socialist government, and the nationalist government made up of Liberals, Conservatives and socialists, had utterly failed to cure unemployment in Great Britain. It will be remembered that in 1930 the May commission was appointed. The policy recommended and adopted by the then government in Great Britain was one of drastic economy, to stay on the gold standard. The result was to bring the country to the verge of revolution and to force it off gold.
If there is any doubt as to the fundamental causes of what we call unemployment-and I am referring not to seasonal unemployment, but to unemployment as we know it to-day- I shall quote a passage by Mr. R. G. Hawtrey. I have quoted it before, but it is worth quoting again. Mr. Hawtrey is secretary of the British treasury and the author of a book entitled The Art of Central Banking. He says this:
The common factor in pre-war, and postwar, experience is the intimate association of the state of trade with the enlargements and compressions of consumers' income and outlay effected by central banks. If this fundamental causal sequence were understood, the public would hardly acquiesce in the central banks proceeding from their position of complacent detachment to generate depressions, unemployment, bankruptcy, budget deficits and defaults, with all the resulting political and social convulsions while government after government is broken because it can neither stem the flood of ruin nor even provide tolerable palliatives to alleviate the consequences.
Surely Mr. R. G. Hawtrey is an authority of whom this house may take notice. Why is it that when we are told by men whose know-

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
ledge is second to none that the fundamental cause of our difficulties is monetary or financial, every group in the house, with the exception of this little group in the corner, refuses to face the facts? Why is it that as soon as we mention money there are would-be funny remarks from all over the house? Last night the hon. member whom I believe to be the official Liberal economist referred to this group as scrip teasers.

Let us consider the condition of Great Britain in 1930. There were millions of unemployed. and most drastic economies to save the country and the nation. Every social service, including old age pensions and the dole, was cut down. All those services were cut to the bone, until the very sailors in the navy mutinied. But when the country was threatened by bombers of the enemy, did they insist upon drastic economies? No. Then it was a case of building up the armaments of the country to meet the common enemy. Did anyone then say, "Where is the money to come from?"

One might have said that
when man took off on his first flight. If someone had not made the first flight we would still be on the ground. We hear a great deal about putting men to work. To my mind, and to those of my colleagues, that smacks of Hitlerism. We do not like the idea of putting men to work. What we say is that we should adapt and alter the existing financial system so that we can provide opportunities whereby people may put themselves to work-and that is a very different matter.
Let me add that any work to which people are put is not likely to result in benefit to those who do the work. I would say that millions of people in the world to-day have been put to work making munitions, but 1 do not think that the most ardent "putter-to-work" will claim that the result of those admirable occupations is likely to end with very much satisfaction to those making the munitions. To some extent it has healed the unemployment problem in Great Britain.
Why is money available to make munitions but not available for purposes of peace? Any bank manager will say that there are no good borrowers, and that there is no use in lending money to industry because industry cannot sell what it produces. In other words the producer cannot recover his costs. But if you can work the people up into a state of mind where they are thoroughly frightened of what the enemy may do to them you can borrow money, and the banks will very kindly create it and lend it to the country, knowing very well that the people will consent to any amount of taxation to secure protection. That was the reason why the city of London imposed the policy of deflation and retrenchment. Poverty did not threaten them. But when the bombs of the enemy threatened the city of London we heard no more about economy.

speechtext:
When we consider that no
government has attempted to cure or even to alleviate in any real sense this problem of unemployment, I find it hard to believe that any member of the house is naive enough to believe that there is any intention of curing it. The financial policy is simply part and parcel of a policy of rationalization. If anyone has any doubts of that may I remind the house
