how the . most exalted person was thrown on the scrap-heap for saying that something should be done for those who were already on the scrap-heap; and such being his fate, what fate can be expected by those who dare to challenge the power of finance to-day? Of course, we in this corner have nothing to lose in position, so all they can do to us is to tiy ridiculing us. But increasing number of people both in Great Britain and in Canada are becoming more and more aware of where the trouble is; unless the world is overwhelmed by some disaster in the meantime, these people are going to see that their ideas are carried out, and here in Canada they are going to see that this parliament shall solve our problems and no longer remain under the command of international financiers as it is to-day.
What is the real trouble with the world to-day? Some say that we need moral rearmament, I say that the trouble with the world to-day is that we are no longer ruled by human beings; we are ruled by institutions, and means have been elevated above the end. A machine or an institution has no soul and no responsibility, and when I say that machinery and plants are scrapped, human beings are scrapped along with them because we are controlled, not by human beings, but by institutions. I should like any hon. member who follows me in this debate or addresses the house between now and the end of the session to explain why it is that in peace-time we must remain under a policy of what is called sound money that results in the conditions we have to-day; yet at the very first threat of war all ideas of sound money are forgotten and the government has to adopt the very method which we in this corner propose. Why is that? It is because in war-time canons of sound finance are silenced by the cannons of the enemy.
The hon. member for Greenwood suggested a dozen or so ideas for the government to adopt. I am not saying that they were not good ideas because any idea that would be helpful is a good one, but nobody outside this corner has any suggestion to offer as to how those ideas are to be financed.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Good for you.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
No one else suggests a method by which those ideas are to be financed.
We are told that there cannot be a shortage of money because production is at the same time consumption, and orthodox economics is, I think, founded on that very idea. I forget the exact words which Mill used-no doubt the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is more

familiar with them than I am-but they were to the effect that, were you to double production you would automatically double consumption. I never learned economics until I was old enough to think for myself. Thank God I was spared that fate; my mind was not warped or twisted by being told a lot of palpable untruths before I had formed the habit of thinking for myself.
We who follow Douglas say that there must be a chronic shortage of purchasing power. Douglas says that the rate of flow of prices must be greater than the rate of flow of purchasing power, and I remember last session seeing nearly the whole cabinet in fits of laughter over that doctrine. Let me put it in this way. Orthodox finance says that that is impossible, that there cannot be any shortage of money because production is consumption. All right, let me give an illustration. Every person who is born must die; therefore deaths must equal births; therefore, by the argument of the orthodox it is impossible for the population to increase. But it does increase. How does it increase? Just as Douglas says it increases, because the rate of flow of births is greater than the rate of flow of deaths. Perhaps some hon. member can detect a flaw in that argument. If he can I shall be interested to hear what it is. Let me repeat it. Everybody who is born must die; therefore deaths must equal births; therefore there cannot be any increase in the population. But we know that the population does increase. How does it do it? Merely because the rate of flow of births is greater than the rate of flow of deaths. So there the A plus B theorem is proved, and if it is true there, it is true in the application which Douglas makes of it. It is a little harder to see, but it is there just the same.
I am not blaming this or any other government. I know that no government and no combination of governments can effect any real cure of our troubles until there is a fundamental change in our financial system. What we must do is so to alter that system that anything physically possible and desirable becomes financially possible. That is so in time of war. We can do as we please then. Nobody ever says that we cannot afford to enlist any more soldiers or that we cannot make any more shells or ammunition because we have no more money. And let it not be thought that war is financed out of taxation. True, taxes rise, but the money is first distributed and then taxed back.
I will make a very simple suggestion which could be acted upon at any time the house cared to do so. Since there are more men than jobs, and since thousands of old people

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
who have earned a bit of leisure are still working, while thousands of young people are wearing out their hearts looking for jobs, why not pension off the older people and make room for the younger ones? What we have to do is not to put people to work but to provide careers for the young people, and if we remove a sufficient number of the older workers we shall make room for younger ones. I shall be asked, how are you going to do it? Well, from my point of view it is quite simple with the set-up we have, with the central bank and the power over that bank which is possessed by this house. All we have to do is to pension off those over sixty. I do not say we should force them to retire, because some men are more valuable at sixty than they are at thirty, but let those who are doing physical work and are under physical handicaps have an opportunity to retire and enjoy a little leisure; reduce the old age pension age to sixty and make the pension worth while, at least thirty dollars a month, and do not pay for it out of taxation; for that does no good; create the money and pay the pensioners with debt-free, state-created money. You will thus achieve a double benefit: you will make room for numbers of young people, and you will reward thousands who have worked a lifetime and have earned some leisure. This could be done through the extra purchasing power so distributed. It would not constitute a debt; that would be useless, because when money is issued as a debt it has to be collected and paid back with interest. I should be interested to hear one of the economists in this house who is outside our group explain just where that interest comes from. It is a question which I have never heard answered. If the people of Canada borrow, let us say, one hundred dollars, they get only one hundred dollars. How then do they pay back one hundred dollars with interest? Where does the interest come from? No man in Canada is allowed to create one cent of money. When I was farming I was told, "Why. that is simple."

speechtext: I will simply conclude what I was saying, and suggest that the government lower the pension age to sixty and try this experiment. We shall be told that this will cause inflation. But can it be worse than what we have now? And, with the few millions which it will cost, is there any possibility of inflation? There is none. Why not try it? Surely we are in a desperate enough condition. Why not try that simple experiment which has already been tried and has worked. It was tried in the island of Guernsey. It worked; there was no inflation. If a little island like Guernsey could stand it, surely a country as big as Canada can stand it. Pension off these old people; give the young ones a chance to find a career for themselves; give them an opportunity to marry and raise children to populate this country. Surely for Canada there is no better stock than that raised by Canadians themselves. Why say that we cannot afford to have families and that in order to populate the country we must go to Europe and bring back people some of whom it takes generations to make into good Canadians? Why not give our young people a chance, and at the same time lower the pension age and pay for the experiment with debt-free, state-created money? Surely conditions warrant that very small experiment. Are the authorities afraid to introduce the principle because when it was found to work on this small scale it would have to be enlarged until all our financing would be done with national, debt-free money? Is there any better solution? The only time the Founder of our religion lost His temper was when He drove the money-changers out of the temple, and His words were, "The love of money is the root of all evil."

speechtext:
There is less unemployment there.
.Mr. BRADETTE: The question before the house to-night is not merely national in its scope, it is universal; it is a question that

will call for all the energy and the attention not only of members of parliament but of every Canadian citizen.
Before I proceed to discuss that question may I pay one more compliment, a greatly deserved one, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). If ever there was a man who was really humanitarian, a man who put his heart, his talents and his whole soul into an effort to try to solve a problem as great as the one that faces the government to-day, that man is the present Minister of Labour. I feel perfectly free to make that statement because I happen to have had some personal contact with the previous Minister of Labour, and I can say that on many occasions he told me how difficult the task was, not to solve the problem, but to tackle it from every angle. I believe the people of Canada fully realize that the present Minister of Labour is doing his utmost to provide a solution for a problem which, as I say, extends beyond the boundaries of the nation and is universal.
We are in a position to-day to study the situation as it affects the world at large and the experiments that have been made in regard to that problem. I am going to discuss for a short time what has been done in the United States. Owing to the fact that there is a democratic government in that country, the United States is a sort of glass hive, and we can see the functioning of the administration there. At the head of that administration is one of the greatest presidents that country has ever had; he is one of the greatest men this world has known; a courageous man, a man with high ideals, and a man who previously had taken an active part in the public life of the American people, having been for many years governor of the state of New York. He was elected by a huge majority and his motto during the election was to fight for the so-called "forgotten man," and to improve his lot. Immediately after his election, not content to be surrounded by those who had been elected to support him, he gathered about him men of great mental calibre, the so-called "brain trust," men of special training in different fields, university professors, men well versed in economics and in all the theories of social government. He had to deal with the wealthiest country in the world and with one of the finest populations, industrious, thrifty and inventive.
I should like the house to study what happened in that country. It is not so easy for us to tell what has been done and what is being done in the totalitarian states, for the very good reason that in those countries the press has been practically suppressed,

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
and their peoples have no right to express their sentiments. No one at the present time knows what is happening in Russia. The same is true of Italy and Germany, although there are fine people in those states. But there has not been either a free press or a free electorate. The people have no right to self-expression, and therefore whatever may have been done with regard to the unemployment situation in that part of the world, we cannot form as clear an idea of the state of affairs there as we can of what has happened in the United States.
It is true the President of the United States was elected in 1933 by a large majority, but he has always "been surrounded by a free press and a free opposition; and when I hear some groups in this house declare that the present capitalist system is one that produces want and misery, I suggest that they have not studied the history of the United States prior to the last depression. Had they done so they would have realized that the leaders of finance and industry in that great republic desired to maintain a policy of plenty. That was their philosophy; they believed that poverty was unavoidable in any part of the civilized world, and they tried to put that conception into practice. Industries throughout the country were working full-time for a number of years, and the people were able to consume more and more of the goods produced. Skilled artists, the best writers and painter^, the best minds in the United States were enlisted in an endeavour to induce the American people to buy more and more of the manufactured goods of the country, thinking the public had unlimited power to consume and they could supply these requirements. Hon. members will recall the statement of Mr. Hoover that the objective should be two radios in every American home and two automobiles in every garage. In short, they believed in the policy of plenty. They not only believed that such a policy could be practised for a certain number of years, but had the idea it could go on indefinitely. Suddenly, however, they discovered that the buying power of the American people had dried up at its source, and that industry could not maintain the pace at which it had been going.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Because to some extent there was over-production, and because also great advances had been made in scientific improvements; technocracy and the displacement of man by machinery were highly accentuated. We should not call the present system the capitalist system; it is a scientific
system. We know what happens after the introduction of any invention. The inventor is outside the realm of politics. Every invention which is thrown into the social order, without previous preparation to take care of its disruptive effects, throws men out of work. We know what happened when steam power came into use, what happened with the advent of electricity and the automotive industry, and the internal combustion engine. In all these instances, added burdens were thrown upon civilization, and the machine, which was supposed to make the lot of the working man easier and to save him from the drudgery of manual labour for ten or fifteen hours a day, adversely affected him. It was supposed to lighten to a large extent the load of the worker, of the drudgery of long hours and arduous physical efforts.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It has done that.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: It has done it to the extent of 10,000,000 unemployed in the United States.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Even those workers who are using machinery are working to-day under conditions of greater drudgery than existed forty or sixty years ago. The machine has turned man into an automaton. He is no longer a craftsman; he has no right to be a craftsman; he is deprived of all initiative because the machine which was supposed to be the servant has become the master. Until every citizen of the world puts his mind to a solution of the unemployment situation, to the new problems that have to be faced from day to day, adaption to this new tyrant, the conditions that exist to-day will become more and more aggravated.
It is all right for some on the other side to murmur when I make that statement. What has machinery done? It has created a great army of unemployed. It certainly has displaced men; but I would be the last man in this house to say that we should stop invention and stop using machinery. But we must insist on finding a ratio, whatever it may be, so that those displaced may be reestablished in some way. Human labour displaced by the machine should be compensated in some way so that the people may be in a position to buy not only tbe necessities of life but all the things created by the inventiveness of the scientist and produced by the machine. It will be a slow process, no matter what form of government we may have, whether communism, fascism, nazism or democracy; it will probably take us a long time to adapt
2822	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
ourselves to the new conditions. Everyone here present, every citizen of this country, everyone throughout the world feels deeply in his heart and mind for the young who are suffering, the old people who are also suffering and for whom a full and fruitful life is almost impossible. Surely the human mind and human inventiveness which were capable of building the great mechanical civilization which we have will not be incapable of solving the problems that these new conditions have created.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Hon. members will
not use their brains.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Well, be patient. Surely you cannot claim a monopoly on that score.
Coming back to the situation in the United States, no one will deny that President Roosevelt was courageous. To work on he had the most advanced industrial country in the world, and industry on its own initiative has shown to everyone that it is possible to give to all not only the necessities of life and to help agricultural production, but also to provide comfort and even luxury for the masses of the people. Working under a democratic system against an alert public opinion and political opposition he tried to put some of his theories into practice. We all remember the National Recovery Act that was put on the statutes of the United States, which required the industrialists and financiers of that country to make certain sacrifices. It was said at that time that industrialists were making too great profits and too large a proportion of those profits was going into replacements and the building of new industries. They were asked to be satisfied with smaller profits, and by that means it was sought to increase the buying power of the people. Appeals were made to the patriotism of the people of the United States. But these theorists, these economists, even these industrialists soon realized that working with the human factor is entirely different from dealing with the mechanical side of industry. They were in the position of a little boy whose rubber ball has been punctured with a pin and the wind has gone out of it; while they were trying to smooth the surface on one side of the ball, the cavity appeared on the other side. Study what they tried to do in the United; States. They used up all the letters of the alphabet over and over again in new bureaux and institutions trying to solve the problem. They formed sixty-five new bureaux, many of which are familiar to us, like the NRA. the CCC, the CWA. the ABC, the XYZ and so on. But, after all that work

and expenditure of energy, has the unemployment situation been overcome in the United States? It has not. To some extent, of course, it has been alleviated-

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They abolished poverty though, to a large extent.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Not any more than in this country, and our standard of living is at least as high as theirs. My hon. friend may be sure of that. With all their courage, energy and expenditure of brain power they arrived at this result, that the national debt has almost doubled since 1&30; in June, 1938, the total was $41,000,000,000 in round figures. Has unemployment entirely disappeared? No, not iby long odds. Yet we must realize and appreciate the courage that the Roosevelt administration has shown. It has been an incentive to other nations, not altogether to copy, but at least to forge forward as far as that big question is concerned. In 1933 there were 14,000,000 unemployed in the United States; in 1937, 8,000,000; in 1938, 11,500,000, and in 1939, 9,000,000. While I am quoting these figures, hon. members must remember that these policies I mentioned a few minutes ago have been put into operation. In 1935 there were 5,700,000 persons working on general work relief schemes; in 1937 the number was 7,650,000, and in January, 1938, 4,500,000 and in October last, 5,500,000. And the public debt which was $155 per capita in 1933 had risen to $305 in 1939.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: What is it in Canada?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Will my friend hold his peace? I do not think I interrupted him when he was speaking at any time during the present session. I visited the United States last year, and it is true that under those schemes the natural resources of the United States have not decreased but have been increased. Nevertheless the fact remains and is glaring for any unbiased person to see that the unemployment situation there is far from being cured. At the present time they have a big armament program on which many thousands are employed; they are putting hundreds of thousands of young men into the. army and the navy, and still unemployment is the great plague in the national life of that nation. Surely if it had been possible to cure unemployment, that nation would have found the cure long ago. It was a cause of great astonishment to the people of the United States to find themselves in that situation, and no one will doubt for a moment that they have been trying earnestly to break those cables that were holding the nation and the individuals in bondage, because if there

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
is any nation that possesses the qualities and the courage that should enable it to solve that problem, it is that nation.
However, in the present evolution of things there are some hopeful features. I mentioned a few minutes ago that at the beginning of the present century it was still the firm belief that poverty was unavoidable. I would be one of the last to believe that we can have plenty for everyone unless we exert ourselves. We hear from time to time in this house of our unlimited natural resources. But there is no such thing as unlimited resources. I have just returned from my own section of the country where lumbering operations have been in progress for the last six months. This work necessitates people trudging through snow five or six feet deep, and no one would tell me that is an easy occupation; that would be an absolute fallacy. This applies to the development. However, I repeat that in this country, as in Great Britain and the United States, we have the finest asset any nation could desire, that is the quality of its population. Our people want to be active and enterprising; the great majority of them are willing and eager to play the game on all occasions and in all circumstances. But this country, like others, has been paralyzed to a large extent by the unemployment which is rampant throughout the world.
Coming down to our national politics, again I do not want to be a partisan; I have spoken on this important question both in opposition and on the government side. If we put all our energies together, we in this house and those in the senate, and find a solution of this problem, there will be enough glory and satisfaction for every hon. member of both houses to share.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Your party is in power, do you know any solution?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
We all have some remedies for that problem, but are they all practical? It means more than being the government in power, my hon. friend. It was beyond the power of the government of the United States, with all the power it has at the present time. It needs more than an autocratic power, an oligarchy, such as they have in Russia at the present time; it needs more than a Hitler in Germany or a Mussolini in Italy to solve the unemployment situation. Even countries blessed with democratic governments and possessing almost unlimited natural resources and territory, such as England and France, experience at the moment the fears that unemployment has created in the hearts of all civilized people.
What I am about to say is not intended in a partisan way. In 1930 the Canadian people, of their own volition, chose a new government. At its head was one of the finest Canadians this country ever produced, a man who had been highly successful in his profession, and in finance, a man who, as far as his own records were concerned, was unequalled in his own section of the country and for that matter, I might say, in the whole of Canada; a man who showed his foresight, vision and ability and whose administrative ability had been felt on boards of directors of several great corporations. He believed in his heart that with these great qualities and the policies of his own party, properly applied, unemployment in this country could be cured. I do not need to remind this house of the statements he made during the campaign of 1930; they still resound in the minds of every Canadian who heard or read them. He thought at the time unemployment was only a passing mood as far as the national life of this country was concerned, and he was really convinced that it would be possible to clear it up in a very short time.
Parliament was called together in the fall of 1930, immediately after the election, and we passed a bill, with the principle of which I did not agree and in which I do not believe any parliamentarian had faith, under which we voted the sum of 820,000,000 to start direct relief so as to relieve or cure unemployment. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker-and I also address these remarks to the Minister of Labour

if it were possible for this parliament to do away with direct relief and substitute fruitful, healthy employment, I believe the people of Canada would be immensely better off. However, it was easier to implant that policy than it is to uproot it. I well remember when it was first applied in my own section of the country, and this refers equally to the rural and urban sections of my constituency. The people thought direct relief was mendicity; they thought they should not take it. They did not want to believe they had reached the point where they had to beg some government official to give them $15 or $20 or $40 a month. However, the idea sank deeper and deeper into the minds of the people, and I believe that to-day some are on relief who only a few years ago never dreamed that they would come to the point of asking for such assistance. It was a palliative; perhaps it- was the only policy the government could establish in the fall of that year.
At the same session-and again I am not being critical in making this statement-the then Prime Minister and his government increased the tariff, with implicit faith that in

2824	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
so doing they would enrich the national life of the country. At the moment I am not discussing whether or not the results were beneficial, but I want to give credit where credit is due. The then Prime Minister worked almost day and night for five successive years. There was not a man in this whole country who worked as earnestly and as hard as he did. However, with all his sincerity of purpose; with all the administrative qualities that he put forward while in power; with all his industry and energy, he was crushed finally by the unemployment situation. With all his ability; with the majority he had in the House of Commons, and with the aid of the policies he implemented to the fullest extent, he was not able to cure unemployment.
That is why I can readily understand the difference between the speeches of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). I must say the hon. member for Greenwood showed wonderful talent in his speech on this subject. I had the pleasure of hearing the first part of that address and carefully read the second part. The hon. member stated that he was not going to go over ancient history, that he was not going to mention anything that occurred from 1930 to 1935. I believe he might derive some benefit from studying the struggle of his own party, when it was in power, to solve the unemployment situation.
The story of unemployment goes back much further than 1930. If we read history as far back as the dawn of civilization in this world we find that even thousands of years ago, under the tribal system, they had to face unemployment. Ever since life appeared on this planet, there has been a keen struggle for life. When one reads ancient history one is astonished, if not ashamed, to realize that unemployment or inactivity has been responsible for at least two-thirds of the wars that have occurred between nations. The present situation is but a repetition of what has occurred many times in the past. A country found its youth unoccupied; the people were able and willing to work but were handicapped by the lack of tools. The only way whereby the power and energy of those people could be used was by throwing them against their neighbours in war. We have that situation again to-day, perhaps intensified more than it ever has been. I do not know whether it was done to appease England or France, but the present leader in Spain, General Franco, made the statement that he had to retain his troops on a war footing; that it was impossible for him immediately to release hundreds of thousands of his young men; that

if he did so, these young men would find themselves suddenly without occupation and might become a cause of disorder. So it does us some good to study this question from all angles and to envisage the future not with absolute pessimism but nevertheless with the complete realization that no one party or no particular section of the people is entirely responsible for the situation in which we find ourselves.
It may be that at times when I was in opposition I sinned by being too much of a partisan, but when we were dealing with the great question of unemployment I always made it a point to praise the government as highly as I could. I praised the then Minister of Labour when he started the back-to-the-land movement, because I believe that if to-morrow we could solve the problems of agriculture we would solve at least fifty per cent of the problem of unemployment in this country. But I warned the government at that time that I thought they were not going far enough in that direction, that the scheme had not been sufficiently studied. I was not surprised, although I was a little astonished, to see that in speaking the other day the hon. member for Greenwood made the statement that the boys left the farms for better days. I do not believe that. That statement might be acceptable in one way, but I maintain that if it were possible to keep fifty per cent of our young people on the land we would solve in large measure the unemployment problem of this country, and in many instances it is still more fruitful for our farmers' sons to stay on the land.
Perhaps I may divulge a family secret. I have a brother who is a good dairy farmer three miles north of the town of Cochrane. He has been there for thirty-two years. He has five healthy, strapping young sons but, Mr. Speaker, I think he will be very lucky indeed if he manages to keep one of them on the farm. He is able to give each boy a good farm, absolutely free of debt, fully equipped with machinery and so on. More than that, I offered one of the eldest boys of that family one of my own farms, 140 acres under cultivation, with a good home, a good barn, a good span of horses and equipment worth at least 83,000; but he said, "No, uncle; I am going to work in the mines." There is something wrong in our present social and educational system when we find that attitude being taken. We must endeavour to maintain the greatest possible percentage of our native rural population on the land; otherwise we shall have a repetition of what happened in old Rome. It will be remembered

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
that practically all the victorious Roman soldiers, who covered almost the whole of the then civilized world, came from farms. Instead of going into productive occupations they remained in Rome, and that was one of the greatest causes of the destruction of the Roman empire.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: They should have stayed on the farm.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
To some extent at least in this country we should maintain our industrialization. But surely it should be possible to some extent also to make it attractive enough for the average young farmer, at least fifty per cent of them, to remain on the farm. I presented a resolution a few years ago asking the government to help them directly on that score. Perhaps we shall have another session before an election, and I may have another opportunity to speak and elaborate my ideas on that problem.
In this house we have other sections of the opposition, but they are not in the same position as the Conservative party has been. They never have had the responsibility of government. And there is nothing that has a more sobering effect on any party than when it happens to be in office for a few years. I highly respect some of the ideology and ideals of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. Personally I am not speaking with any spirit of trying to dictate to them, but I believe they would be fairer to themselves if they called themselves the socialist party. I say that because to the average Canadian the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation does not mean anything, and they are not known under their proper qualification. Here time and again they have mentioned the fact that they are socialists. This afternoon, and I believe with all sincerity, their house leader made a statement respecting the deplorable situation in the country, but I would even go so far as to accuse them of having capitalized on the depression since it started. They have been destructive in their criticism. I still have to find any resolution or any legislation brought in by any party since I have been in the house with which they seemed to be in agreement. Is that a fair way to deal with national problems? Is that the way to help in relieving national suffering and malaise? Certainly it is not.
Generally they build up their philosophy on an individual case. I, too, could do that.
I could tell about the fine type of men we have in this country. During the last provincial election campaign in Ontario we had a (big rally in the rural town of New Liskeard.

I thank hon. members for their courtesy. I shall take only two minutes more. I believe that with all the intelligence we have in this country, with all the energy and all the cooperation of all groups and parties, and if it were possible for us to have a parliamentary committee consisting of the whole house where the people of this country could present their views-and we are getting briefs from them by the dozen week after week-we should be able to solve our unemployment problem at least to a large extent.
Before taking my seat, I just wish to say that I intended no personal reflections in anything I said during this debate, and that if through our concerted efforts we could alleviate to a large extent the present serious unemployment situation, not only would there be enough glory and merit for everyone, but we should also have the satisfaction of having fulfilled a great duty and obligation towards our country and our constituents.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the house that I shall take only a very few minutes. I had not intended to speak at all, but so many things have been said with which I do not agree that probably it is up to me to make a few observations.
I wish to thank the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) for the nice and fair speech that he has just made and for the kind things that he has said about my former leader, the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett. The hon.
member said that in 1930 Mr. Bennett made certain promises which he was not able to carry out. Nobody denies that. But nobody knew in 1930 that we were going to run into five terrible depression years. Mr. Bennett, however, brought the country through the worst five years of depression this country has ever seen; there is no doubt about that. The party opposite took over the government of this country in 1935 when Canada was convalescing, and immediately they got into power they started to tinker and monkey, making treaties with this country and that, so that they have got the country into such a state that it is back practically to where it was in 1930, and we shall 'have to take over the government again and bring the country back on its feet.
I have no particularly bad feelings for anybody on the other side of the house. In fact I rather like most of the faces over there. They seem to be always decent with me, and I speak of them as I find them.
I do not share the views of some hon. members who have told us how to cure unemployment. Some of the suggestions made were radical, while others were fine. It is a difficult thing to bring this country back to normal, I admit, but' I feel that the present government have not done all they could have done. They have been lacking in their duty; I do not think they deserve the approval of the people at another election, and I am satisfied they will not get it. We have given them every opportunity in the last few years to try to cure unemployment, but they have tinkered with tariffs and interfered with business so much that the people of Canada have lost all confidence, and this interference with business and industry has resulted in greater unemployment.
May I say to my hon. friends opposite that there are millions of dollars in this country ready for investment in business and industry if people could only feel that their investment was safe and there would be some stability. But most of the Canadian people have lost confidence and there is a lack of stability everywhere. My opinion is that if this government could restore the confidence of the people, then even at this late hour this would do more to eliminate unemployment than spending millions of dollars on anything they can think of, and the cost would be nothing. Just do the right thing. Get the people behind you. Let them understand that you are going to give them fair treatment and that they have a chance of investing their money with a prospect of getting a fair return. Then you will bring back confidence and improve conditions generally. I have said that
2828	COMMONS
Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
to my own party in the past, and I am of the same opinion still. All that is wrong is that the people have lost confidence-and you cannot get them to invest money when they lack confidence. All they will invest in now is government bonds paying about two per cent interest. Nobody but a coward will do that. No one with any back-bone will put his money in government bonds at two per cent when he should be taking a risk in business and making from five to ten per cent.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext: And employing people.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
And employing people is right. A program of public buildings which some members advocate is not, in my opinion, the proper thing. It is purely a temporary expedient. If you get into a policy of building buildings you will be building buildings where they are not needed. Both parties have done that in the past ever since I have been in this house. So I say that a policy of public buildings is no good. It must be something permanent.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) made some really good suggestions this afternoon. I am familiar with some of the work that he suggested: for example, the building of national highways. I think we all realize that is a good investment. We in Ontario have good national highways, good provincial highways, and good county highways, and we get many tourists and a good deal of their money. Nothing will bring more money into the country than good national highways, and money spent in that way will meet with criticism from nobody.
National airways have also been spoken of. I am not fond of travelling by air, but certainly people are becoming air-minded to-day and I would not object to money being spent to develop air travel, although personally I do not like it. But we must recognize chat the days of the narrow-gauge railways and the old canals with the boats drawn by a horse on the bank, have gone and we can never go back to them, so I suppose we shall all be riding in aeroplanes after a while.
Flood relief has also been suggested by my hon. friend. That is another good way of spending money. A great part of Ontario from London to Paris and around Brantford is flooded every year or two years, hundreds of thousands of dollars of damage being done by the water overflowing the banks, flooding the surrounding country and endangering people's lives. Money could well be spent there. We have also floods between here and Toronto, at Port Hope, for instance, and Peterborough. I remember going down on the train to Toronto from Ottawa on one occasion;
I Mr. Spence.]
when we got within twenty miles of Toronto
a train was standing there which had left that city the night before at eleven o'clock; the bridge behind her had gone and the bridge was down in front of her. We had to stay there for a while, and then we backed up through Lindsay. We could not get into Toronto at all. The Canadian Pacific offered to take us in by bus, but water had flooded the Kingston road four feet deep, and so we could not take the bus. Therefore I think money might well be spent on flood control, and I know many places where one could spend it as I am familiar with highways, particularly in Ontario.
Then there is the conservation of water. That would be another useful project.
But one project which I would particularly draw to the attention of the Minister of Labour is reforestation. In the county of York, where I happen to be on the good roads commission, there is a place called Mount Albert, thirty or forty miles out of Toronto, and there they have been reforesting for the last ten years hundreds of acres of land. It is really not land at all; it is simply blow sand. It is wonderful to what a height these trees have grown in the last ten years. It seems to me that the government should adopt a policy of reforestation on practically all the vacant and waste land in this country, because some kind of tree will grow there. Of course all sorts of trees will not grow on the same land, but the forestry branch can supply a man who will give advice as to what species should be planted in certain kinds of soil. If that were done, I believe in fifty years' time it would pay off the national debt, because trees will grow to a great size in half a century. I planted two maples on my own lot, and after twenty-five years they are a wonderful size. Trees are growing in this blow sand around Mount Albert, on the east side of Toronto, and they are growing rapidly. At one time the blow sand would be piled up on the roadway as high as a big stack of hay, and we had to use scrapers and other machines to clear the road and let people get by. But with reforestation we have grown good trees and have kept the sand from drifting. Some people say that fifty years is a long time to wait. Practically everyone in this house will be gone by that time. But we must look to the future and do something for the people who are coming after us.
As regards the flood conditions mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport, I am familiar with them because I happened to be in the Pittsburgh area in 1887, when one of the worst floods occurred. I went there in 1886, and the next year there was the worst

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
flood I ever saw. The Allegheny, the Monon-gahela and the Ohio meet at a place they call the Point, on the south side of Pittsburgh, and I never saw the like of that flood. The rivers were up to the second storey of some buildings close to the water side. I did at that time what I should not like to do to-day; I helped the engineer and a couple of other fellows build a pontoon bridge on that water, and I assisted in moving people from the second stories of their houses and shifting pianos from the ground floor to the second storey. Certainly floods are disastrous things.
I know all about the Johnstown flood because I happened to be there a few days after it happened. It is the part of the country where I lived first after I came from the old country. I am also familiar with the Miami river of which the hon. member for Davenport spoke. At the present time in the United States they are spending millions of dollars on flood prevention work, and probably in the near future there will be no danger from this source. Not long ago I was down at Cincinnati inspecting a sewage disposal plant. The river had been very low, and the banks were as high as the ceiling of this chamber, but when the flood came it rose to the top of the banks. No one ever saw worse scenes of havoc and ruin; millions of dollars were lost. Those three rivers are just as bad as the Mississippi.
Our duty in this country is to restore business to normalcy and get the people working. I shall be glad to do anything I can in a quiet way. I would suggest that we get together with our feet on the table and eliminate the press and the Hansard reporters. Most hon. members talk to get their names in Hansard. I shall be glad to sit in with the gang and take part in a really confidential talk, where we could consider suggestions which would be of benefit to the country. But people will rise in this house and make long speeches. I am not hinting at anybody, because the hon. member who made the last long speech in this chamber is quite competent to make a speech at any time; it was one of the best speeches that have been made in this house, and I do not think anyone could controvert what he said, because his speech was sincere and honest. However, I do say that there is too much talking by hon. members in order to get their names in Hansard. So far as I am concerned I do not care whether my name or my remarks ever appear in Hansard. I would rather sit with others quietly round a table getting the views of those who are talking common sense in an effort to eliminate the difficulties we are under to-day. That is the way in which our
problems will be solved, not by talking nonsense, playing to the gallery and taking up the time of the house.
There is a little more than a month to go before their majesties arrive, and I hope we shall all pay some attention to business and try to get the work of the house done by that time. Possibly I should not be saying that, because some of my colleagues on this side may not agree with me, but that is my view. At the same time I appeal to the government to use every bit of influence they have in order to find employment for the people who are unfortunately out of work. Many suggestions have been made to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). I hope he will benefit by what he has heard, and no doubt he will, because I am satisfied that he is sympathetic. Although so far he has not done very much, I believe he is willing to try to do something.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF

speechtext: And without shoes to wear.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS- UNDERTAKINGS IN GENERAL INTEREST AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Those are the facts. I am a social crediter so-called. I believe that before this parliament can act democratically-by that I mean that democracy is given an opportunity really to function, by making available to the people the wealth we have-we must have a measure of monetary reform. It is gratifying to me to stand here to-night and



Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
know that the plan which we have put forward in this house in the last three years has never been successfully challenged. We have the goods, we have the consumers, we have the machines to produce more, we have the natural resources and the mental and physical energy of a million people who to-day are unemployed; every ingredient for a happy Canada is there. But when it comes to the question of money that is a subject which is vetoed in this house. Does any lion, member think I believe for one moment that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is not doing his best? I do believe that he is doing his best. But I know that the Minister of Labour, like every other minister, cannot do the things he would like to do, because they are in a monetary strait-jacket. The activities of the various departments are dependent upon the amount of money available through orthodox channels.
This afternoon the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) suggested as a measure to relieve unemployment in this country the building of dams for flood control. I believe those dams should be built; we have the concrete, we have the labour, we have the machinery. But we have not the money. Those who hold the money-bag of the nation control the nation. The people of this nation and of every other nation in the world are going to have to make the choice very shortly whether they will have real democracy, in which people can not only vote but get what they vote for, or chaos. It is one or the other. The monetary system is the keystone; without that keystone the arch of the economic system cannot bear any further weight. All across this country to-day in all sorts of organizations such as service clubs, the question of unemployment is being aired. In many churches across this country unemployment is being discussed. I tried an experiment in the last few days; I asked twelve men, at different times and in various walks of life, hat would you do with regard to unemployment if you were charged with the responsibility of dealing with it?" There was not one but said, "Put them to work." But when I asked them the same question that we asked of the hon. member for Davenport or the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) who spoke yesterday for three and a half hours, and that we ask of the government, "How are you going to finance it?" they are stumped right there.
I know that on every question which comes up in this house this group has a tendency to discuss the question of money. Why should we not? Money is the problem. It is the mechanism that passes goods from the pro-

ducer to the consumer; and if industry is producing more goods with less labour, then there is less wages and therefore less purchasing power, while there are higher costs of production in terms of machinery.
We must make the choice, Mr. Speaker, whether we enter an age in which for the first time in the history of man the people will enjoy the fruits of 2.000 years of science, or whether this industrial machine will destroy us, because of this incomplete and inadequate mechanism of money. This parliament must choose. In 1935 the people of this country had some hope that unemployment would be solved, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) told us he would issue credit in terms of public need. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) told us he would issue 8500.000,000 in new currency. He has sat in his place in this house for the last three years, but not one further word has been said on the subject. I know many Liberals feel as we do in this corner of the house.
If at any time, Mr. Speaker, in speaking in this house I left the impression that I had no respect for parliament I want to correct it. I have; but as one of the youngest members of this house I am determined to make parliament what it should be; to see, so far as I am able, that it turns out the kind of legislation that will bring happiness to my people. Parliament is a useless instrument unless it controls the money-bag of the nation, unless it has the right to issue credit, unless it has the right to control the instrument that makes things go. I have before me a pastoral letter from the archibishop of Toronto, who said that poverty in the midst of Canada's plenty must be attacked. His excellency charged as follows:
The Catholic conscience must arise to attack the problem of the world's distress and its poverty in the midst of plenty.
He goes on to say that unemployment is fertile soil for all the evils and insidious organizations that might destroy a nation. The archbishop further stated:
In conformity with the wishes of our holy rather, the pope, and keeping before us his lcIe soc^ justice and charity for the masses oi the people, with all the authority at my C?mi?an<^ an(^ w*th all the conviction of the shepherd s heart I ask the clergy, religious communities and faithful of all classes in this archdiocese to join in a holy crusade of prayer tor the development of christianism in the social life of all communities.
During the last election campaign the Prime Minister said that in the next parliament the greatest battle ever to be waged in any parliament would be carried on between the people

Unemployment and Agricultural Distress
on. the one hand and finance on the other. It must be tiring to hon. members opposite to listen to us here hammering away on this monetary question, but we will continue to do so; we will continue that fight, because we have the sure conviction that this is where the evil lies.
The direction of the Bank of Canada has not been satisfactory, as far as I can find out. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) persistently tells us that the issuance of more money would mean inflation. The other day he went back to 1935 and said that we are now inflating, that we have a measure of controlled inflation. Why did he not go back to 1929, the year of the high price level in this country? Here we talk of relief for the distressed farmers who are facing an impossible situation. They cannot meet their obligations. According to every present indication the world price of wheat will be lowered, so the income from agriculture will be less, while debts and interest will compound and compound. And year after year those men who are not unemployed, the farmers, have been going behind. People come to me every year when I go home and say, "What would you do with this?" They want to place their case under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, or desire to get some relief through the debt adjustment board. But when I study their individual cases I can see how hopeless it really is. Even if they had crops for the next five years at a guaranteed price of ninety cents a bushel they could not possibly meet their obligations. Some suggest that others should go on the land. Why, to-day people on farms are suffering from malnutrition. They may have the things they can produce on the farms, but they cannot get the other things that are not common to farm production. So the problem of unemployment is identical with the problem of agriculture. There is no solution for it outside monetary reform, the issuance of credit in terms of public need.
Hon. members speak about Alberta breaking its promises; hon. members tell us we made promises that we had no intention of keeping; hon. members say that our record is worse than that of any other province. Let me say this: In terms of health legislation, in terms of debt, in terms of unemployment relief. I think we lead the field of the nine provinces. If this parliament is not prepared to bring about the necessary monetary reform then give that one province an opportunity to do so. We will go ahead and do it. If you do not want to do it. at least give us the opportunity; that is all we ask We are 71492-179J
facing the facts squarely. This year a relief committee operated in Alberta, and the recommendations of that committee were brought into the legislature. Just to show how we are facing these facts I want to quote one passage from a speech made by Doctor Cross, minister of health of Alberta:
As a result of their investigation, they came to this'conclusion: that the only hope for the people on relief as far as the powers of this province go, and under the present economic system, is rehabilitation-rehabilitate them in the industries or on farms; and, in order to do this successfully, the government must be prepared to subsidize them for an indefinite period of time with the hope that they may eventually become partially self-supporting. They suggest that this government go on fighting for monetary reform. It's the only real hope they can see for these people.
This year I was in Nordegg, a town built up on the one industry, the production of coal. There we find men working one day a week, as they have been doing for some years. If they happen to work a full week they do not benefit because the mine operators own the property, and everything the men make beyond the one day a week goes to pay the rent of the houses in which they live. What a hopeless future! What a mad system! And we have been sitting here for three years, or rather for eight years, because I do not differentiate between one party and the other. I am not blaming the parties. What I do want to do is to impress upon the government that when you analyse the problem you find the solution lies in money. That is what we are short of in this country. You can bring about monetary reform without inflation. The Minister of Finance has never yet successfully contradicted that statement.
The other day he spoke about velocity. He said that we do not take that into consideration, and that the danger was that with the velocity speeded up after the issuing of more money we would have chaos, and inferred that if velocity were not speeded up we might have prosperity. I do not know how you speed up the velocity of money. If you can tell me how those thousands of people in Canada who are existing on $6.42 per month can increase their prosperity by increasing the velocity of their money, then you have a convert.
Let me appeal to the government along these lines. Let me say this: We have the desire, as you have, to solve the problems of Canada. So much depends upon it-possibly the whole of civilization. I know how the generation to which I belong feel about it, and I want to give them an opportunity to restore to themselves some vestige of manhood. Once again there must be not only
Privy Council Appeals

the desire to live, but that bubbling health which impels the youth of a nation into a glorious future.
Let us combine our forces in the house. Let us find out if we are right or wrong. We can cut across all party lines, and submerge politics. If we can unite by finding that one common denominator, if we can think in terms of Canada first, then this problem is already solved and happiness is here.
On motion of Mr. Pelletier the debate was adjourned.

subtopic: QUESTION OF REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF BILL NO. 9, APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house adjourns, there is a matter I should like to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister. I notice the Minister of Justice is not in his seat, but an incident occurred this, evening which rather disturbed me. The Minister of Justice announced that Bill No. 9, would be referred to the supreme court. Some of us desired to speak on the bill, but the Minister of Justice having moved the adjournment of the debate, it was impossible for us to express any views thereon. What I suggest to the Prime Minister is that it should not be allowed to go out to the public, at this stage of the disturbed conditions of the world, that Canada was definitely at this time contemplating repudiating or doing away with appeals to the privy council. Some of us hold strong views on the matter, contrary to those contained in the bill. We feel that this is not a time when it should go out to the world that definite steps were being taken. It might appear, in the absence of some protest such as I am making now, or such as we would have made had we had an opportunity to speak, that there was unanimity of opinion in the house that this bill should pass, and that the reference to the supreme court is based upon that assumption.
I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister, if he would give it thought^and I repeat I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not here -that it might be considered over the weekend, and perhaps a statement could be made on Monday. I am making this request on behalf of myself and a number who have spoken to me and who hold similar views.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I cannot speak positively as to what the Minister of Justice has in his mind in the matter, but I would assume it would be that, among other things, [Mr. Poole.)
the reference to the supreme court would be for the purpose of avoiding the very impression my hon. friend has suggested might be created. If that step were not taken the government would wish to have the opinion of the supreme court on the measure, before - the next step would be taken.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT
subtopic: QUESTION OF REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF BILL NO. 9, APPEALS TO PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: The point I am emphasizing is that it should not go out to the world that the house is in any sense unanimous in either the reference to the supreme court or the abandonment of the system of appeals to the privy council. I really feel that it would perhaps be interpreted abroad as an indication of Canada's lukewarmness. I think we would all desire to avoid any such impression-a false one, perhaps; but nevertheless there would be the very great danger that that would be the interpretation placed upon such action.
